Only the last comes from better hardware; the first two, in the author's reading, come from spending more. The installed stock of AI computing power is growing more slowly, at 3.4 times per year since 2022 by Epoch's estimate [@epochai2026trends]. The 2026 AI Index, drawing on Epoch's data, gives 3.3 times and puts global capacity at the equivalent of 17.1 million Nvidia H100 chips [@sajadieh2026ai].

Figure 4.2 plots Epoch's estimates for a selection of well-known systems, from the Perceptron Mark I of 1957 to GPT-6 Astra in 2026, a span of more than twenty orders of magnitude. GPT-3 used an estimated 3.14 × 10^23^ FLOP; GPT-4.5 used about 3.8 × 10^26^, some 1,200 times more [@epochai2026data]. The largest estimate in Epoch's database as of October 2026 is for GPT-6 Astra, which OpenAI released on 3 September 2026 [@openai2026gpt6]. OpenAI rates it as meeting the Critical threshold for cybersecurity under the company's Preparedness Framework (Section 12.7). It has not disclosed Astra's training compute. Epoch puts it at about 9.4 × 10^26^ FLOP, a "likely" estimate with an interval of roughly 5 × 10^26^ to 2 × 10^27^ [@epochai2026data]. The figure rests on statements by OpenAI and partners such as Nvidia that Astra was trained on at least 100,000 GB200 chips, Nvidia's Blackwell-generation accelerators (Section 7.1). Epoch then assumed 90 days of training at 25% of the chips' 8-bit peak.

![Figure 4.2: Estimated training compute of selected notable AI systems, 1957–2026, on a logarithmic scale. Each gridline is a tenfold increase. Values are Epoch AI estimates; those marked "likely" are expected to be accurate within a factor of 10, and the others within a factor of 3. Source: @epochai2026data.](../figures/svg/fig-04-02.svg){#fig:04-02}

These figures are increasingly estimates. The AI Index notes that training code, parameter counts, dataset sizes and training duration are no longer disclosed for several of the most resource-intensive systems, including those from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. Training compute, which outsiders can estimate, has continued to rise [@sajadieh2026ai]. Five of the thirteen points in Figure 4.2 are "likely" estimates, expected to be accurate only within a factor of 10. They include the three largest, GPT-6 Astra, GPT-4.5 and Grok 3, as well as GPT-4 and the 1957 Perceptron Mark I.

### What training runs cost

More compute costs more money, though cheaper hardware offsets part of the rise. Cottier and colleagues, in a preprint from Epoch AI and Stanford, compared three ways of costing a run [@cottier2024rising]. Their preferred method spreads the purchase price of the hardware over its working life, charges the run for the share it used and adds energy. On that basis the cost of the most compute-intensive training runs grew 2.4 times per year from 2016 (90% CI 2.0 to 2.9). Pricing the same runs at cloud rental rates gave a similar growth rate but costs about twice as high.

For four models whose full development they costed (GPT-3, OPT-175B, GPT-4 and Gemini Ultra), research staff including equity made up 29–49% of the total, computing hardware 47–64% and energy only 2–6% [@cottier2024rising]. Epoch's later dashboard puts the growth in frontier training costs at 3.5 times per year since 2020, while the price-performance of chips has improved by 1.49 times per year since 2023 [@epochai2026trends]. Table 4.3 lists Epoch's amortised estimates for some of the largest runs.

| Model (release) | Training compute (FLOP) | Epoch confidence | Amortised hardware and energy cost (2023 $) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Gopher (Dec 2021) | 6.3 × 10^23^ | Confident | 0.6 million |
| GPT-4 (Mar 2023) | 2.1 × 10^25^ | Likely | 37 million |
| Llama 3.1 405B (Jul 2024) | 3.8 × 10^25^ | Confident | 53 million |
| Grok 3 (Feb 2025) | 3.5 × 10^26^ | Likely | 218 million |
| GPT-4.5 (Feb 2025) | 3.8 × 10^26^ | Likely | 366 million |
| Grok 4 (Jul 2025) | 5 × 10^26^ | Speculative | 388 million |

: Table 4.3: Estimated training compute and amortised cost of the final training run for six large models, from Epoch AI's database in 2023 US dollars. Costs exclude experiments, staff and data, and inherit the uncertainty of the compute estimates; Cottier et al.'s 2024 preprint, using the same method on earlier data, put GPT-4 at about $40 million. Sources: [@epochai2026data; @cottier2024rising].

These are costs of a final run. Experiments, failed attempts, staff and serving the model to users come on top [@cottier2024rising], and Chapter 7 discusses who can afford them and how DeepSeek's low reported costs fit the picture.

## 4.5 The data constraint

If compute grows about fivefold a year and compute-optimal training needs data to grow nearly as fast as model size, the demand for text rises steeply. Villalobos and colleagues at Epoch AI estimated how much public human-written text exists [@villalobos2024position]. They put Common Crawl, the open web archive behind most training sets, at about 130 trillion tokens and the indexed web (pages reachable through search engines) at about 510 trillion. The whole web, including the "deep web" that search engines do not index, holds about 3,100 trillion. Filtering for quality reduces the usable stock to about 100 trillion tokens. Allowing for each token to be used several times in training raises the effective stock to about 320 trillion, with a 95% confidence interval of 65 to 1,700 trillion.

Training datasets had grown about 2.4 times per year. Extending both trends, the median date at which a training run would use the entire effective stock is 2028, with a range of 2026 to 2032, or slightly earlier if models are over-trained [@villalobos2024position]. Llama 3.1 405B's 15.6 trillion tokens in 2024 were about one-twentieth of the central estimate [@grattafiori2024llama]. A year later Alibaba reported pre-training its Qwen3 models on 36 trillion tokens, about a ninth of it, in a company technical report [@yang2025qwen3].

The repetition allowance rests on experiments by Muennighoff and colleagues, who ran 400 training runs with models of up to 9 billion parameters and up to 900 billion tokens [@muennighoff2023scaling]. For a fixed compute budget, training on the same data for up to four **epochs** (complete passes through the dataset) gave "negligible changes to loss" compared with fresh data. Beyond that, repeated tokens lost value. In their fitted law, meaningful gains from repetition continue up to about 16 epochs, beyond which returns "diminish extremely fast" and extra compute spent on the same text buys almost nothing. Villalobos and colleagues used this result to assume that repetition can multiply the effective size of a dataset by between 3 and 15 times [@villalobos2024position].

Other sources widen the stock. A separate Epoch analysis counting images, video and audio, but excluding synthetic data, put the effective stock at between 400 trillion and 20 quadrillion tokens [@sevilla2024can]. Private data such as company documents and user conversations lie outside both estimates. Curation also stretches what exists. In the FineWeb experiments described in Section 3.5, an educational subset of about a tenth of a 15-trillion-token web corpus gave markedly better results on knowledge and reasoning benchmarks [@penedo2024fineweb]. Reinforcement learning on reasoning (Section 4.6) adds a further source of training signal, problems and environments with checkable answers, although Epoch researchers count building such environments among its bottlenecks [@edelman2025why]. Some researchers nevertheless treat data as binding. Ilya Sutskever, formerly of Google and OpenAI, said in a November 2025 podcast interview that "the data is very clearly finite" and that pre-training will eventually run out [@patel2025ilya].

### Synthetic data and model collapse

The obvious response is **synthetic data**: text, code or images generated by AI models and used to train others. One use is long established. In **distillation**, a small "student" model is trained to imitate a larger "teacher". Hinton, Vinyals and Dean introduced the term in a 2015 workshop paper for training one network on the probability distributions, or "soft targets", produced by a cumbersome ensemble of models [@hinton2015distilling]. DeepSeek fine-tuned smaller open models from the Qwen and Llama families on 800,000 samples curated with its R1 reasoning model. For a 32-billion-parameter Qwen model, this distillation worked better than applying reinforcement learning to the same base model [@guo2025deepseek]. Whether synthetic data can replace fresh human text in pre-training is less clear.

Shumailov and colleagues, writing in *Nature*, described **model collapse** [@shumailov2024ai]. In their language-model experiment they fine-tuned Meta's small OPT-125m model on the wikitext2 corpus, used it to generate a dataset of the same size, trained the next generation on that output, and repeated the cycle. When no original data were kept, quality on the original test set fell from generation to generation; when a random 10% of the original data was kept in each generation, degradation was minor. The mechanism is statistical. Each generation slightly under-samples rare events, so the tails of the distribution thin out and the models converge towards a narrow, distorted picture. They reproduced the effect in simpler models (Gaussian mixtures and variational autoencoders) and argued that it affects all learned generative models.

Gerstgrasser and colleagues, in a paper at the 2024 Conference on Language Modeling, accepted the mechanism and questioned the set-up [@gerstgrasser2024model]. Collapse studies, they argued, assumed that synthetic data replace real data, whereas on the web they accumulate alongside it. Pre-training successive generations of language models, they confirmed collapse when each generation's synthetic data replaced the previous data. When each generation's output was instead added to the original real data, collapse did not occur, across model sizes and architectures, in diffusion models for molecules and in image autoencoders. For a linear model they proved that under accumulation the test error stays below a fixed bound however many generations are run. The two results are compatible. Collapse is a risk of discarding real data, not an inevitable consequence of using synthetic data.

The 2026 AI Index finds "still no definitive evidence" that synthetic data can fully offset the depletion of real data in pre-training. Mixtures of real and synthetic data can speed up training and purely synthetic training has worked for smaller models and narrow tasks, it adds [@sajadieh2026ai].

## 4.6 Doing more with less: algorithmic efficiency and test-time compute

Better methods make each unit of compute go further. **Algorithmic efficiency** covers improvements in architectures, training methods and data that reach the same performance with less compute. Ho and colleagues measured it for language models using over 200 evaluations on two standard text benchmarks, WikiText and Penn Treebank, from 2012 to 2023 [@ho2024algorithmic]. The compute needed to reach a given performance "halved approximately every 8 months", with a published 90% confidence interval of about 2 to 22 months. The transformer architecture alone was worth a compute-equivalent gain of about 7.2 times, nearly two years of progress. Even so, growth in compute contributed more to overall improvement than algorithms did over the period. Epoch researchers have since estimated that the reasoning techniques introduced in late 2024 let a model match a given performance with roughly ten times less pre-training compute [@edelman2025why].

The price of using a given level of capability has fallen faster still. The 2025 AI Index, working with Epoch, tracked the cheapest model scoring at least 64.8 on the MMLU benchmark, GPT-3.5's level. Its price fell from $20 per million tokens in November 2022 to $0.07 in October 2024, with Google's Gemini-1.5-Flash-8B, a more than 280-fold reduction [@maslej2025ai]. Depending on the task, Epoch estimated declines of 9 to 900 times per year for a fixed performance level [@cottier2025llm]. Falling unit prices invite more use; by Epoch's estimate about 30% of OpenAI's 2024 compute spending went on **inference**, the running of trained models [@epochai2026trends].

### Scaling at test time

The second development spends compute at the moment of answering. **Test-time compute** is the computation a model uses while answering. It can be raised by longer reasoning chains, by sampling many candidate answers and choosing among them, or by having the model check its work [@snell2025scaling; @brown2024large; @openai2024learning].

In September 2024 OpenAI released o1-preview, an early version of o1, a model trained by reinforcement learning to produce a long chain of reasoning before answering (Chapter 3). According to the company, o1's performance "consistently improves with more reinforcement learning (train-time compute) and with more time spent thinking (test-time compute)" [@openai2024learning]. The 2024 AIME is a US qualifying exam for the Mathematical Olympiad whose answers are integers that can be checked automatically. OpenAI reported that GPT-4o solved 12% of its problems, while the full o1, not then released, solved 74% with one attempt and 93% when a learned scoring function re-ranked 1,000 samples. The company said the o3 release of April 2025 "pushed an additional order of magnitude in both training compute and inference-time reasoning, yet still see clear performance gains" [@openai2025introducingb]. DeepSeek's openly documented R1-Zero, whose accuracy on the same exam rose steadily during reinforcement learning (Section 3.7), shows the training side of the same phenomenon [@guo2025deepseek].

Published measurements of how reinforcement learning scales are only beginning to appear. In a preprint from a study using more than 400,000 GPU-hours, @khatri2025art found that performance rises with reinforcement-learning compute along S-shaped curves that level off at a ceiling set by the training recipe. Stable recipes followed predictable trajectories, so a large run could be forecast from smaller ones, as with pre-training. A ceiling is also what @yue2025does found from the other direction. Their reinforcement-trained models solved more problems than their base models on one attempt, but not when both were allowed hundreds of attempts, which suggests that current methods mainly sharpen abilities the base model already has. Neither result settles how far this second axis extends, but both describe diminishing returns within a fixed recipe.

Sampling many answers works well when answers can be checked and much less well when they cannot. Brown and colleagues, in a preprint, measured **coverage**, the fraction of problems solved by at least one of many samples [@brown2024large]. Coverage grew roughly log-linearly with the number of samples over four orders of magnitude. On SWE-bench Lite, a set of real software issues, DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct solved 15.9% with one attempt and 56% with 250, beyond the then single-attempt best of 43%. Where answers can be verified automatically, as with unit tests or proof checkers, coverage turns into performance.

Where they cannot, picking the right sample becomes the bottleneck. On the MATH benchmark, Llama-3-8B-Instruct's coverage rose from 82.9% with 100 samples to 98.44% with 10,000, yet majority voting or reward models raised accuracy only from 40.50% to 41.41% over the same range [@brown2024large]. Snell and colleagues asked how to spend a fixed test-time budget well [@snell2025scaling]. The best method depended on question difficulty, and allocating compute adaptively per question was more than four times as efficient as simply sampling many answers and keeping the best. With total compute held equal, a small model with extra test-time compute could beat a model 14 times larger, but only on problems where the small model already had a non-trivial success rate. Test-time compute amplifies ability a model has; it does less for ability it lacks.

The price of the last few points can be steep. On the ARC-AGI-1 puzzle benchmark, a pre-release version of o3 scored 75.7% on the 100-task semi-private evaluation set at about $26 per task, and 87.5% in a configuration using 172 times as much compute, at about $4,560 per task [@arcprize2024openai]. Twelve points thus cost roughly 175 times more per task, by the benchmark organisers' retail-price estimates, revised in March 2025. The organisers also report that, according to OpenAI, the tested o3 had been trained on 75% of the benchmark's public training tasks, so the result is not a test on wholly unfamiliar material.

In the author's view, test-time scaling changes the economics of AI. Training is paid once, whereas reasoning is paid on every query, so the most capable answers are also the most expensive, in money and in electricity (Chapter 7), as the ARC-AGI-1 costs above illustrate [@arcprize2024openai].

## 4.7 Measuring capability: emergence, benchmarks and time horizons

Smoothly falling loss does not guarantee smoothly improving skills. In 2022 Wei and colleagues defined an ability as **emergent** "if it is not present in smaller models but is present in larger models" [@wei2022emergent]. Their examples included three-digit addition and subtraction, on which GPT-3 models stayed close to zero across several orders of magnitude of compute and then jumped well above chance at about 2 × 10^22^ FLOP (13 billion parameters). If such jumps are common, capabilities, including dangerous ones, cannot be forecast from smaller models.

Schaeffer, Miranda and Koyejo proposed that many jumps are produced by the scoring rule [@schaeffer2023emergent]. If a model gets each token of an answer right with probability *p*, and an answer counts only when all *L* tokens are right, the score is about *p*^*L*^. For a ten-token answer, per-token accuracies of 0.50, 0.80, 0.90 and 0.99 give exact-match scores of 0.1%, 11%, 35% and 90% (the author's arithmetic). A model whose per-token accuracy improves steadily with scale therefore scores close to zero for a long stretch and then appears to take off. Measuring the same outputs with a continuous metric, such as the number of tokens that would need changing (token edit distance), restores a smooth curve. They found that more than 92% of the emergent abilities claimed on the BIG-Bench test suite appeared under one of two discontinuous metrics, and they manufactured apparent emergence in vision models by choosing such metrics deliberately.

::: {.box .debate}
**Debate: Are emergent abilities real or an artefact of measurement?**

*The case for genuine emergence.* Wei and colleagues documented sharp transitions across several model families and tasks, including arithmetic, transliteration and word unscrambling [@wei2022emergent]. Du and colleagues re-analysed abilities against pre-training loss instead of model size and found that some appear only once loss falls below a threshold, with performance near chance above it even under continuous metrics, which suggests a real change in competence [@du2024understanding].

*The case for a mirage.* Schaeffer and colleagues showed that the same model outputs can look emergent or smooth depending on the metric, that most claimed BIG-Bench cases used discontinuous metrics, and that emergence can be produced on demand [@schaeffer2023emergent]. Successful forecasts support them: GPT-4's pass rate on a subset of the HumanEval coding benchmark was predicted from models trained with at most one-thousandth of its compute [@openai2023gpt4, p. 2], and Meta forecast benchmark accuracy four orders of magnitude ahead [@grattafiori2024llama]. @ruan2024observational went further, fitting scaling laws to about 100 public models instead of training new ones, and found that several "emergent" abilities followed smooth S-shaped curves that could be predicted from smaller models.

In the author's view, the dispute could be tested directly. If developers registered forecasts of specific capabilities, made from small models with continuous metrics before a large run and scored afterwards, the record would show how often abilities arrive unannounced. Users, however, often care about the all-or-nothing metric. An arithmetic answer that is nearly right is still wrong, so a smooth underlying trend can still mean a sudden change in usefulness, a point consistent with Schaeffer and colleagues' own analysis of exact-match scoring [@schaeffer2023emergent; @wei2022emergent].
:::

### Benchmarks: saturation, contamination and validity

Most claims of progress rest on **benchmarks**, fixed sets of questions or tasks with known answers. Benchmarks **saturate**: once top models approach the maximum score, they stop discriminating. GPQA Diamond consists of 198 graduate-level science questions written to resist web search. The expert validators who checked them score 81.2%, a figure their authors note is inflated because the set was selected partly on those experts answering correctly; across the full pool of questions, experts reached 65% [@rein2023gpqa]. In late 2024 OpenAI's o3 scored 87.7%, above both expert figures, according to the AI Index [@sajadieh2026ai]. The AI Index concludes that evaluations "intended to be challenging for years are saturated in months" [@sajadieh2026ai].

Benchmarks can also be **contaminated**: test questions, or close variants, can end up in training data, so a high score partly reflects memorisation. Zhang and colleagues commissioned GSM1k, 1,205 new grade-school maths problems matched to the widely used GSM8K benchmark in difficulty, number of solution steps and answer size, and never published [@zhang2024careful]. Accuracy fell by up to 8% on the new set, with several model families showing systematic overfitting across almost all sizes. A model's probability of reproducing GSM8K examples correlated with its performance gap (Spearman rank correlation 0.36), a sign of partial memorisation. Many frontier models, however, showed minimal overfitting.

Leaderboards based on human votes have a related problem. Chatbot Arena shows users the answers of two anonymous models and asks which is better. Singh and colleagues found that it allowed some providers to test many private variants and publish only the best; according to the preprint version of their paper, Meta tested 27 before releasing Llama 4 [@singh2025leaderboard]. The same version estimates that Google and OpenAI received 19.2% and 20.4% of all Arena data, against 29.7% for 83 open-weight models combined.

A third weakness is **validity**: whether a benchmark measures what it claims to. When experts reviewed the 50 questions flagged as most suspect by a statistical screen in each of nine widely used benchmarks, between 2 (on part of MMLU) and 42 (on GSM8K) proved flawed [@truong2025fantastic]. Progress is also uneven, a pattern Dell'Acqua and colleagues called a "jagged technological frontier" [@dellacqua2026navigating]. Models that solve research-level problems can still fail simple perceptual tasks. On ClockBench, which asks models to read analogue clocks, the average human scores 90.7%; the best model in October 2026, Google's Gemini 4 Argon, scored 83.3%, up from about half in March 2026 (Section 1.8) [@clockbench2026clockbench; @sajadieh2026ai].

Humanity's Last Exam (HLE), 2,500 expert-written questions that frontier models failed when it was assembled, was built to last. At release in early 2025 the best model tested scored 13.4%, on its text-only questions [@centerforaisafety2026benchmark]. By October 2026 the top entry on Scale AI's leaderboard, GPT-6 Astra, scored 54.8% on the full public set [@scale2026humanity]. Those questions have been online since January 2025, so contamination cannot be ruled out, which is why the organisers keep a private held-out set and in October 2025 released HLE-Rolling, a "dynamic" version whose question set is revised over time [@centerforaisafety2026benchmark; @cais2025hle].

### The task time horizon

METR, a non-profit that evaluates frontier AI systems, proposed measuring capability in units that keep their meaning as models improve: the length of tasks an AI agent can complete, measured by how long they take skilled humans [@kwa2025measuring]. The original suite had 170 software and research tasks, from atomic actions taking a human 1–30 seconds to software tasks of up to about 30 hours, including research-engineering problems rated at 8 hours. Humans with relevant expertise were timed on them, agents (Chapter 5) attempted them, and for each model a curve relating success probability to human task length was fitted. The **50% time horizon** is the task length at which predicted success is one half. In the March 2025 preprint, later published at NeurIPS 2025, the frontier horizon had been "doubling approximately every seven months since 2019", with Claude 3.7 Sonnet at about 50 minutes.

METR expanded the suite from 170 to 228 tasks and re-measured models as "Time Horizon 1.1" in January 2026 [@metr2026time]; on it, Claude 3.7 Sonnet's estimate is about 60 minutes, which shows that values depend on the task set. The figures below come from the Time Horizon 1.1 data file as last updated in September 2026, in which the three earliest models are carried over from the first version without re-measurement [@metr2026task]. Figure 4.3 plots the models that set a record when released, from about 3 seconds for GPT-2 (2019) to 12 hours for Claude Opus 4.6 (February 2026). An early version of Claude Mythos Preview (April 2026) measured about 17 hours, above the 16 hours beyond which METR considers its suite unreliable. Excluding such points, the horizon has doubled about every 129 days since 2023, about sevenfold a year, and about every 188 days since 2019.

![Figure 4.3: METR's 50% task time horizon for AI models that set a new record when released, 2019–2026, on a logarithmic scale. The time horizon is the length of software task, measured by how long it takes a skilled human, that a model completes with 50% predicted success. Error bars show METR's bootstrapped confidence intervals. METR states that measurements above 16 hours are unreliable with its current task suite. All points are Time Horizon 1.1 except the three earliest (GPT-2, GPT-3 and GPT-3.5), which METR carried over from Time Horizon 1.0. Source: @metr2026task.](../figures/svg/fig-04-03.svg){#fig:04-03}

The metric's limits are substantial, and METR states most of them. The tasks are self-contained software and research problems with clear success criteria, unlike much real work. A 50% success rate is far below what anyone would accept for unsupervised work, and the horizon at 80% success is much shorter: about 70 minutes for Claude Opus 4.6, against roughly 12 hours at 50%. The confidence intervals widen sharply at the top; Claude Opus 4.6's 50% interval runs from about 5 to 61 hours. The horizon measures task difficulty, not how long an agent can work alone. METR corrected an error in its curve-fitting in March 2026, and in September 2026 noted that the public page is no longer actively updated [@metr2026task]. Chapter 14 discusses how such trends can, and cannot, be extrapolated.

## 4.8 Is scaling slowing down?

The inputs to scaling face physical and economic limits. Epoch's 2024 analysis of power, chip production, data and the minimum time per training step concluded that runs of 2 × 10^29^ FLOP, about 500 times GPT-4.5 by the author's arithmetic, "will likely be feasible by the end of this decade" [@sevilla2024can]. Electricity supply and chip manufacturing were likely to bind first. Feasible is not the same as worthwhile. A power law means each further tenfold step buys a smaller absolute improvement in loss, while training costs grow several-fold a year [@epochai2026trends]. Whether the capability gained per dollar is holding up is, in the author's view, an empirical question, and the evidence since 2024 can be read both ways.

The case for diminishing returns concerns pre-training, and it rests mainly on what developers did rather than on what bigger models scored. Epoch researchers argue that GPT-5, released in August 2025, likely used less training compute than GPT-4.5, the first GPT generation to do so. For 2.5 years after GPT-4, they add, most state-of-the-art models used less than three times its compute, and models that did exceed it, such as Meta's Llama 4 Behemoth, did not clearly outperform the best models of competing developers [@edelman2025why]. Sutskever described 2020–2025 as an "age of scaling" now giving way to an "age of research" [@patel2025ilya].

The benchmark record is more mixed than this suggests. By OpenAI's own figures, GPT-4.5 improved substantially on its predecessor GPT-4o, from 9.3% to 36.7% on the AIME 2024 mathematics exam, for example. It still trailed the reasoning model o3-mini, which scored 87.3% [@openai2025introducinga]. In the author's reading, that comparison shows that reinforcement learning on reasoning paid off more at the margin, not that larger pre-training had stopped paying off.

The strongest evidence against a slowdown concerns measured capability. Since the first reasoning models in September 2024, Epoch's Capabilities Index, which combines many benchmarks, has advanced about 14 points per year (90% CI 12 to 17), against 6 points per year for non-reasoning models [@epochai2026trends]. METR's time horizons doubled faster after 2023 than over the whole period since 2019 [@metr2026task]. Edelman and colleagues read GPT-5 as a reallocation, not a ceiling. Before late 2024, most language models used about 100 times more compute in pre-training than in post-training. Reinforcement-learning post-training then offered better returns at the margin, and one estimate they cite has it scaling tenfold every four months. Because that pace cannot last once post-training rivals pre-training in size, they expected the next flagship to return to larger runs, using more compute than GPT-4.5 [@edelman2025why]. GPT-6 Astra fits that expectation if Epoch's estimate of about 2.5 times GPT-4.5's compute (the author's ratio of Epoch's two estimates) is right. The estimate rests on chip counts and assumed utilisation, however, and OpenAI's announcement gives no figure for the compute or for how it was divided between pre-training and reinforcement learning [@epochai2026data; @openai2026gpt6].

::: {.box .debate}
**Debate: Is scaling running out of steam?**

*The returns are falling.* Pre-training data are finite, with full use of the public stock projected around 2028 [@villalobos2024position]. For two and a half years after GPT-4, most leading models stayed within three times its training compute [@edelman2025why], reinforcement-learning gains may be capped by the base model [@yue2025does], and test-time gains come at steeply rising cost, as the ARC-AGI-1 results showed [@arcprize2024openai]. Training costs are rising several-fold a year [@epochai2026trends], and contamination and saturation make some reported gains hard to interpret [@zhang2024careful; @sajadieh2026ai].

*The returns have moved.* Reinforcement learning on reasoning opened a second axis whose scaling OpenAI describes as following the same "more compute = better performance" trend [@openai2025introducingb], and an independent study found that reinforcement-learning runs follow predictable, if levelling, compute curves [@khatri2025art]. Epoch's capability index has advanced more than twice as fast with reasoning models as without them, and time horizons have doubled faster since 2023 than before [@epochai2026trends; @metr2026task]. The best reported scores on HLE rose from 13.4% to 54.8% in under two years, although the two figures come from different evaluation set-ups [@centerforaisafety2026benchmark; @scale2026humanity]. Algorithmic efficiency compounds with hardware. From 2012 to 2023 it halved the compute needed for a given result roughly every eight months [@ho2024algorithmic].

In the author's view, both readings turn on capability per dollar, and there is no public measure of it for training. The closest available series concerns use, not training. The price of reaching a fixed level of capability has fallen by between 9 and 900 times a year, depending on the task (Section 4.6) [@cottier2025llm]. Both readings could, the author suggests, be checked against better data. Developers could disclose training compute alongside results on fresh, uncontaminated tasks, so that gains per unit of compute can be tracked. Time horizons could be measured at high reliability and on messier, non-software work, and reinforcement learning tested on tasks without automatic checkers. If capability per dollar keeps rising on those measures, the scaling era has changed form rather than ended.
:::

In the author's summary of this chapter, the scaling laws remain what they were in 2020: fitted regularities in loss that have repeatedly predicted the outcome of runs a thousand or more times larger than the experiments behind them [@kaplan2020scaling; @openai2023gpt4; @grattafiori2024llama]. What changed is the recipe for spending compute. Chinchilla moved it from parameters towards data, the cost of serving models moved it further towards small, over-trained models, and reasoning models moved a growing share into post-training and into each answer [@hoffmann2022empirical; @sardana2024beyond; @edelman2025why]. The inputs to the old recipe, human text above all, are finite, and frontier training costs rise several-fold a year [@villalobos2024position; @epochai2026trends], so progress now depends on how well developers convert compute into capability as much as on how much compute they buy. Judging that conversion is harder than it was, because the largest runs, Astra among them, are known mainly through outside estimates and through benchmarks that saturate within months [@epochai2026data; @sajadieh2026ai].

## Further reading

- Kaplan, J., et al. (2020). *Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models*. The original measurements of how loss scales with model size, data and compute, with the exponents and the compute rule still used today. [@kaplan2020scaling]
- Hoffmann, J., et al. (2022). *Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models* (published in the NeurIPS proceedings as *An Empirical Analysis of Compute-Optimal Large Language Model Training*). The "Chinchilla" paper, which shows three independent ways of estimating how to split a compute budget. [@hoffmann2022empirical]
- Besiroglu, T., et al. (2024). *Chinchilla Scaling: A Replication Attempt*. A short case study in how a famous fit was checked, found wanting and corrected without overturning its main conclusion. [@besiroglu2024chinchilla]
- Villalobos, P., et al. (2024). *Position: Will We Run Out of Data?* A transparent estimate of the stock of human text, showing step by step how quality and repetition change the answer. [@villalobos2024position]
- Schaeffer, R., Miranda, B., & Koyejo, S. (2023). *Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a Mirage?* A clear demonstration of how the choice of metric shapes what we conclude a model can do. [@schaeffer2023emergent]
- Kwa, T., et al. (2025). *Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks*. Introduces the time-horizon metric and sets out its limitations candidly. [@kwa2025measuring]

# Chapter 5: From Chatbots to Agents

In the spring of 2025, Anthropic and the company Andon Labs let a language model run a small shop in Anthropic's San Francisco office for about a month. The shop was a refrigerator, some baskets and an iPad for self-checkout. The model, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, nicknamed "Claudius", chose what to stock, set prices and dealt with customers over the workplace chat tool Slack. It could search the web, keep notes, email wholesalers (in fact Andon Labs, through a simulated email tool) and ask human workers to restock the shelves. Claudius found suppliers for unusual requests quickly, including two sources of a Dutch chocolate milk. Its judgement was another matter. When a customer offered $100 for a six-pack of the Scottish soft drink Irn-Bru, which can be bought online in the US for $15, it merely said it would "keep [the user's] request in mind for future inventory decisions". When an employee questioned a 25% employee discount given that "99% of your customers are Anthropic employees", it agreed, announced that it would drop discount codes and was offering them again within days. Between 31 March and 1 April 2025 it invented a conversation with a non-existent Andon Labs employee and announced that it would deliver products in person wearing a blue blazer and a red tie. Each failure was small. Together they show a system that could carry out every step of running a shop and still lacked a stable sense of what it was doing and for whom. The authors' verdict was blunt: "we would not hire Claudius" [@anthropic2025project].

A second phase, reported in December 2025, ran on Claude Sonnet 4 and later Sonnet 4.5. It added a customer-relationship database, an inventory system that showed purchase costs and better web browsing, and introduced a second agent, "Seymour Cash", as chief executive. The shop expanded to New York and London. The number of discounts fell by about 80%, the number of items given away halved, and weeks with negative profit margins were "largely eliminated". The chief-executive agent, however, approved requests for lenient treatment about eight times as often as it refused them. The authors judged that the business made money "in spite of the CEO, rather than because of it". Both agents were ready to agree to a contract to buy "a large amount of onions in January for a price locked in now", until a staff member pointed out that the US Onion Futures Act of 1958 bans such contracts. Staff and visiting reporters still talked the agents into giveaways and, on one occasion, into announcing that a human colleague had been elected the business's actual chief executive. The authors suspected that training the models to be helpful made them act "from something more like the perspective of a friend who just wants to be nice". They concluded that "the gap between 'capable' and 'completely robust' remains wide" [@anthropic2025projectphase].

The experiment is small and was reported by a company with an interest in its products, and much of what this chapter can say about agents that work rests on similar vendor material (Section 5.4). It nonetheless shows in one documented case how agents are built (a model, tools, a loop and memory), where they succeed (search, logistics, routine communication) and where they fail (judgement under social pressure, consistency, resistance to manipulation) [@anthropic2025project; @anthropic2025projectphase].

## 5.1 What an agent is

A chatbot takes a message and returns a reply, and a person decides what, if anything, to do with it. An **AI agent** is a system in which a language model chooses and carries out actions to reach a goal, observes the results and decides what to do next, often over dozens or hundreds of steps [@anthropic2024building; @anthropic2024introducingcomputer]. Chapter 1 introduced the word in its broad historical sense; here the concern is how agents built on large language models (LLMs) work in practice.

An agent is built from a model, tools, a loop and memory. The **model**, usually an LLM of the kind described in Chapter 3, reads text (and often images) and produces text. The **tools** are programs the model can ask to run, such as a web search, a code interpreter, an email client or a database query. The **loop** is ordinary software that passes the model's requests to the tools, feeds the results back and repeats until the task is done, a budget is exhausted or a human intervenes. **Memory** is whatever keeps track of what has happened, from the running transcript inside the model's context window (the text it can attend to at once) to notes stored in files or databases [@anthropic2024building; @anthropic2025effective].

::: {.box .concept}
**Concept: AI agent**

An AI agent uses a model to pursue a goal by choosing actions, carrying them out through tools, observing what happens and repeating. Its building blocks are the model, the tools, the control loop and some form of memory. Agency is a matter of degree: a system is more agentic the less precisely its task is specified, the more directly it acts on the world, the more consistently it pursues goals and the longer it plans without human review [@chan2023harms].
:::

Figure 5.1 shows the loop in its simplest form. The agent receives a goal, perceives the current situation (the text of a web page, a screenshot, an error message), chooses a step, acts by calling a tool and observes the output, which becomes the next perception [@yao2023react]. The loop is what separates an agent from a plain chatbot, but in the author's view the line is now a spectrum rather than a divide. At one end, a model writes a single reply and a person decides what to do with it. In the middle, a chat assistant may run a web search or a piece of code within one turn before it answers. At the other end, an agent works through dozens or hundreds of steps on its own. The further along the spectrum, the more software closes the gap between what the model writes and what happens, and the more a human reviews only the final result or nothing at all.

![Figure 5.1: The basic agent loop. A language model receives a goal, plans a step, calls a tool, observes the result and repeats; memory carries information between steps, and the loop ends when the goal is met, a limit is reached or a human intervenes. Schematic by the author, after [@yao2023react; @anthropic2024building].](../figures/svg/fig-05-01.svg){#fig:05-01}

Not every system sold as an "agent" works this way. Anthropic's engineering guidance distinguishes **workflows**, "systems where LLMs and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths", from agents, in which "LLMs dynamically direct their own processes and tool usage". A workflow that always searches a database, summarises the hits and drafts an email follows a fixed recipe written by a programmer. An agent decides which steps to take and in what order. The same guidance warns that autonomy brings "higher costs, and the potential for compounding errors", and recommends the simplest design that does the job [@anthropic2024building]. The advice comes from a vendor, but the trade-off it names, flexibility against predictability, runs through every design choice in agent building.

Chan and colleagues' four dimensions in the box give a vendor-neutral way to grade that spectrum. A spell-checker scores low on all four; a system told "grow the business" that can spend money without approval scores high on all four. The authors stress that recognising a system's agency does not reduce the responsibility of the people who build and deploy it [@chan2023harms], a point the Replit case in Section 5.5 makes concrete.

## 5.2 Inside the loop: reasoning, planning and memory

### Reasoning and acting

The pattern behind most current agents was set out by Yao and colleagues as **ReAct** ("reasoning and acting"). The model is prompted to alternate three kinds of text. A *thought* states what it is trying to do ("I need the year the company was founded"). An *action* names a tool and its argument (a search for the company's name). An *observation* is the text the tool returns, which the loop appends to the transcript before the model writes its next thought. Earlier systems either reasoned without acting (chain-of-thought prompting, which reasons from what the model already knows) or acted without explicit reasoning. On two interactive benchmarks, a simulated household (ALFWorld) and a simulated online shop (WebShop), ReAct beat imitation-learning and reinforcement-learning baselines by 34 and 10 percentage points in absolute success rate, with only one or two worked examples in the prompt. On question-answering tasks, grounding each reasoning step in a Wikipedia look-up reduced the hallucinations that occur when a model reasons from memory alone [@yao2023react].

Interleaving has a security cost (Section 5.6). Because the model chooses each step after reading the latest observation, whatever a tool returns can steer the rest of the episode. One alternative, favoured for security, is to **plan first and then execute**. The model writes a complete list of steps from the user's request, and the loop runs them, with later steps receiving data but not changing the plan. Planning first is more predictable and easier to audit, but it copes badly with tasks where step five depends on what step two revealed [@beurerkellner2025design].

### Learning from failure within a task

A language model's weights do not change while it works, but an agent can still improve across attempts by writing lessons into its memory. In **Reflexion**, Shinn and colleagues had an agent attempt a task, receive a signal (a failed unit test, a wrong answer, an environment error) and write a short verbal reflection on what went wrong. The reflection went into an episodic memory consulted on the next attempt. On the HumanEval programming benchmark, a Reflexion agent reached 91% pass\@1 (correct on the first submitted solution), against 80% for GPT-4 alone [@shinn2023reflexion]. The design relies on a trustworthy feedback signal. Unit tests supply one for code; in open-ended business decisions there is often nothing comparable.

Memory can also store procedures. Voyager, an agent that played the game Minecraft through GPT-4, saved every program that worked as a named, reusable "skill" in a growing library of executable code, retrieved relevant skills for new tasks and verified its own progress. According to its authors, it collected 3.3 times as many unique items as earlier agents and reached key milestones up to 15.3 times faster [@wang2023voyager].

### Memory designs

The simplest memory is the context window itself. Everything the agent has seen and done in the current episode stays in the transcript, which grows with every tool call. The window is finite, and long contexts degrade before it is full. Anthropic's engineers cite studies of "context rot", the observation that as the window fills, the model's "ability to accurately recall information from that context decreases" [@anthropic2025effective]. Agent designers therefore manage the context actively, a practice the same guidance calls context engineering. **Compaction** summarises a transcript that is nearing the limit and starts a fresh window from the summary. **Structured note-taking** has the agent write progress notes to a file outside the window and read them back after a reset. In one example, an agent playing the video game Pokémon kept running tallies across thousands of steps (the guidance's illustration is a note on levels gained over the last 1,234 steps) and resumed multi-hour sequences from its notes. **Sub-agents** take on focused jobs in clean windows and return only a condensed summary, "often 1,000-2,000 tokens", to the agent that called them [@anthropic2025effective].

A more systematic design borrows from operating systems. MemGPT treats the context window like a computer's main memory and external storage like its disk. The model moves information between the two tiers by calling memory functions, which gives "the appearance of large memory resources" in the way virtual memory does for programs. In a preprint, its authors used it to analyse documents far longer than the model's window and to run conversations that persisted across sessions [@packer2023memgpt]. The generative agents of Park and colleagues went further. Each of their 25 simulated characters, living in a small virtual town, had a stream of memories, a mechanism for retrieving the relevant ones and a process for condensing them into higher-level "reflections" [@park2023generative]. Their scoring rule, set out in the box, puts numbers on the decisions every memory system has to make: what to keep, what to forget and what to bring back.

::: {.box .deeper}
**Going deeper: how a generative agent decides what to recall**

In Park and colleagues' design, every observation is stored as a line of natural language. When a character must act, each memory receives a retrieval score equal to *recency* + *importance* + *relevance*, each first rescaled to lie between 0 and 1 across all memories, with all three weights set to 1. *Recency* decays exponentially with the number of game hours since the memory was last retrieved, by a factor of 0.995 per hour: after 24 hours a memory keeps 0.995^24^ ≈ 0.89 of its recency score, after a game week 0.995^168^ ≈ 0.43. *Importance* is rated by the language model on a scale from 1 to 10 when the memory is created. The paper's examples are cleaning one's room (2) and asking someone out on a date (8). *Relevance* is the cosine similarity between a numerical embedding of the memory and one of the current situation. The highest-scoring memories that fit in the context window go into the prompt [@park2023generative].

Reflection is triggered when the summed importance of recent events exceeds 150, which happened two or three times per simulated day. The model is shown the 100 most recent memories and asked for the three most salient high-level questions they raise. Each question is used to retrieve relevant memories, from which the model draws insights that are stored as new memories and can themselves be retrieved [@park2023generative].

In a controlled evaluation in which 100 participants ranked the believability of agents' answers to interview questions, the full architecture scored highest (TrueSkill rating 29.89). Removing reflection, and then planning as well, lowered the rating step by step. Answers written by crowdworkers and a version with no memory, planning or reflection (21.21) scored lowest, and did not differ significantly from each other. The memory was not perfect. In the separate end-to-end simulation of the town over two game days, agents described knowledge they did not have in 6 of 453 answers (1.3%) about other characters [@park2023generative].
:::

## 5.3 Tools and protocols: function calling, MCP and A2A

### From tool use to function calling

A language model can only produce text. To act, it needs a way to turn text into a request that other software understands. Schick and colleagues showed with **Toolformer** that a model could learn this itself. Given a handful of demonstrations per tool, Toolformer taught itself in a self-supervised way when to call a calculator, a question-answering system, two search engines, a translation system and a calendar, what arguments to pass and how to use the answers. It improved on several tasks without losing its general language ability [@schick2023toolformer].

Commercial systems made tool use routine through **function calling**. In June 2023 OpenAI let developers describe functions to its models, which would then reply with a structured object naming a function and its arguments in JSON (a plain-text format for nested lists and key–value pairs) instead of prose [@openai2023function]. The model never runs the function. It fills in an order form, and the surrounding application decides whether to carry out the order, holds the credentials needed to do so and returns the result to the model as more text. Figure 5.2 traces one such exchange.

![Figure 5.2: A single tool call. The model never runs the tool itself: it emits a structured request, the host application executes it, and the result returns to the model as new input. That returned text sits in the same context as the user's instructions, which is why untrusted tool output matters for security (Section 5.6). Schematic by the author, after [@openai2023function; @modelcontextprotocol2026tools; @greshake2023not].](../figures/svg/fig-05-02.svg){#fig:05-02}

A tool is described to the model by a name, a description in natural language and a schema (a formal specification of the arguments). The following definition, adapted from the July 2026 revision of the Model Context Protocol specification discussed below, declares a weather tool with one required text argument [@modelcontextprotocol2026tools]:

```json
{
  "name": "get_weather",
  "description": "Get current weather information for a location",
  "inputSchema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "location": { "type": "string",
                    "description": "City name or zip code" }
    },
    "required": ["location"]
  }
}
```

When the model decides to use the tool, the application sends the server a request in the JSON-RPC 2.0 format (a widely used convention for remote procedure calls), and the server answers with content for the model to read, a flag saying whether the tool itself failed and, since the July 2026 revision, a field marking the result as complete. As in the specification's own examples, the protocol-version and client metadata that every request must now carry are omitted [@modelcontextprotocol2026tools]:

```json
{ "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 2, "method": "tools/call",
  "params": { "name": "get_weather",
              "arguments": { "location": "Leeds" } } }

{ "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 2,
  "result": { "resultType": "complete",
              "content": [ { "type": "text",
                             "text": "Current weather in Leeds: ..." } ],
              "isError": false } }
```

The description field is natural language that the model reads and trusts, so whoever writes it influences the model's behaviour [@modelcontextprotocol2026tools]. The tool's answer re-enters the model's context as text, alongside the user's instructions, and the model has no hard boundary between the two [@greshake2023not]. Both facts matter for security (Section 5.6).

### The Model Context Protocol

Function calling solved the problem of one application talking to its own tools. It did not solve the problem of many applications and many tools. If every AI product needs a custom connector to every calendar, database and code repository, the number of connectors grows with the product of the two. In November 2024 Anthropic released the **Model Context Protocol (MCP)** as an open standard for connecting AI applications to data sources and tools [@anthropic2024introducing]. Its documentation compares it to "a USB-C port for AI applications" [@modelcontextprotocol2026what]. The comparison captures standardisation, though a cable, unlike a model, does not decide what to do with the device at the other end.

The specification distinguishes **hosts** (the AI applications a person uses), **clients** (connectors inside a host, one per server) and **servers** (programs that expose capabilities), all exchanging JSON-RPC 2.0 messages. It cites as an inspiration the Language Server Protocol, which standardised how code editors support programming languages. Servers can offer *resources* (data for the user or model to read), *prompts* (templated messages and workflows) and *tools* ("functions for the AI model to execute"). Clients can in turn obtain additional input from the user when a server needs it ("elicitation") [@modelcontextprotocol2026specification]. The protocol is still settling. The revision current in October 2026, dated 28 July 2026, made it stateless, so that each request carries everything a server needs to answer it; servers become easier to run at scale because they no longer track connections. The same revision routes elicitation through a retry pattern, in which a server answers "input required" and the client repeats the request with the user's answer, and it deprecated three older features [@modelcontextprotocol2026key].

On security, the specification is explicit that it states principles it cannot enforce. Users "must explicitly consent to and understand all data access and operations"; hosts "must obtain explicit user consent before invoking any tool"; and "descriptions of tool behavior such as annotations should be considered untrusted, unless obtained from a trusted server". It adds that "MCP itself cannot enforce these security principles at the protocol level", leaving them to implementers [@modelcontextprotocol2026specification]. For tools, it recommends that there "SHOULD always be a human in the loop with the ability to deny tool invocations" [@modelcontextprotocol2026tools]. In practice this places the burden on each host application, and on users asked to approve calls they may not have time to inspect.

Adoption spread across firms that compete in other respects. In December 2025 Anthropic transferred MCP to a new Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation, co-founded with Block and OpenAI. At that point the company reported, in figures not independently audited, more than 10,000 active public MCP servers and more than 97 million monthly downloads of its software development kits. It listed ChatGPT, Cursor, Gemini, Microsoft Copilot and Visual Studio Code among products that had adopted the protocol [@anthropic2025donating].

### Agent2Agent

MCP connects an agent to tools. Google's **Agent2Agent (A2A)** protocol, launched in April 2025 with more than 50 technology partners according to the company, connects agents to other agents, possibly built by different vendors, and was presented as complementary to MCP [@surapaneni2025announcing]. In June 2025 the Linux Foundation took over the project, stating that more than 100 technology companies supported it [@linuxfoundation2025linux]. In August 2026 A2A joined MCP in the Agentic AI Foundation, which says more than 150 organisations back A2A [@aaif2026a2a].

The specification, at version 1.0 in October 2026, begins with discovery [@a2a2026specification]. Each agent publishes an **Agent Card**, a JSON document describing its identity, endpoint, authentication requirements and *skills*, typically at a standard web address on the agent's domain. Work is then exchanged as tasks that move through defined states, such as working, input-required and completed, so that long-running jobs can be tracked and can pause for a human or a credential. Agents collaborate "without needing access to each other's internal state, memory, or tools". This opacity protects intellectual property and limits what one compromised agent can learn about another. It also means that an agent cannot inspect why a counterpart did what it did, a gap the visibility measures discussed in Section 5.8 try to close. The protocol can be carried over JSON-RPC, gRPC or plain HTTP with JSON. Like a common software library, shared protocols such as MCP and A2A lower the cost of connecting systems and also create shared points of failure.

## 5.4 Agents at work: computer use and coding

### Computer-use agents

A **computer-use agent** operates a graphical interface as a person does. The loop sends the model a screenshot. The model replies with an action such as a click at given pixel coordinates, a key press or typed text, and the harness carries it out and takes a new screenshot. The appeal is breadth. Most software was built for people with screens, not for programs with interfaces, so an agent that can use a screen can in principle use almost any application [@anthropic2024introducingcomputer; @openai2025computer]. The cost is that each step requires interpreting an image, and a mistake (a click a few pixels off, a pop-up the agent does not notice) can derail everything that follows.

Anthropic released a computer-use capability in public beta in October 2024, describing it as "still experimental—at times cumbersome and error-prone". It reported 14.9% on the OSWorld benchmark in the screenshot-only category, against 7.8% for the next-best system, and noted that "scrolling, dragging, zooming" still presented challenges [@anthropic2024introducingcomputer]. In January 2025 OpenAI released its Computer-Using Agent (CUA) behind the Operator research preview. According to the company, CUA processes "raw pixel data" and drives "a virtual mouse and keyboard" in a loop of perception, reasoning and action, scoring 38.1% on OSWorld and 58.1% on the WebArena web benchmark. Its safeguards included confirmation before actions with external effects and a separate monitoring model that pauses the agent when it sees suspicious on-screen content [@openai2025computer].

The main yardstick, **OSWorld**, contains 369 tasks set in real operating systems: desktop and web applications, file handling and workflows that span several programs [@xie2024osworld]. When it was published in 2024, computer-science students completed 72.36% of tasks and the best model 12.24%. An earlier web benchmark, WebArena, built working copies of e-commerce, forum, software-development and content-management sites. Its best GPT-4-based agent succeeded on 14.41% of tasks against 78.24% for humans [@zhou2023webarena].

Benchmarks of live software decay. In July 2025 the OSWorld team released **OSWorld-Verified** after reviewing and fixing "nearly 300 feedback items" over about two months. The problems included websites whose content had changed so that checks broke, instructions that allowed several valid readings, and evaluation scripts that marked correct work as wrong [@xlang2025introducing]. It now re-runs submitted agents itself under uniform settings [@osworld2026verified]. Scores before and after the revision are therefore not strictly comparable, which Table 5.1 makes visible.

| System | Date | Benchmark (version) | Success rate | Human baseline |
|:--|:--|:--|--:|--:|
| Best model in original paper | 2024 | OSWorld | 12.24% | 72.36% |
| Claude 3.5 Sonnet (screenshot only) | Oct 2024 | OSWorld | 14.9% (22.0% with more steps) | 72.36% |
| OpenAI CUA | Jan 2025 | OSWorld | 38.1% | 72.36% |
| Claude Opus 4.5 | Nov 2025 (reported in AI Index 2026) | OSWorld (version not stated) | 66.3% | 72.36% |
| Agentic framework on Claude Opus 4.5 | Feb 2026 | OSWorld-Verified (official re-run) | 74.5% | |
| Best general-purpose model | Aug 2026 | OSWorld-Verified (official re-run) | 86.0% | |
| Best agentic framework | Jul 2026 | OSWorld-Verified (official re-run) | 90.2% | |

: Table 5.1: Reported results on the OSWorld computer-use benchmark, 2024–2026. Company figures are self-reported; the last three rows come from the official OSWorld-Verified leaderboard. Step limits and agent programs differ between rows and are not always disclosed (the original paper allowed 15 steps per task), so the rows are not strictly comparable. The human baseline was measured on the original tasks by computer-science students. Source: [@xie2024osworld; @anthropic2024introducingcomputer; @openai2025computer; @sajadieh2026ai; @osworld2026verified].

The 2026 AI Index, using data compiled by Epoch AI, reported the 66.3% figure and observed that agents "still fail roughly one in three attempts on structured benchmarks" [@sajadieh2026ai]. On the revised benchmark the student baseline had in fact already been passed: in the official leaderboard's own re-runs, an agent program built on Claude Opus 4.5 scored 74.5% in an entry dated February 2026, and by August the best general-purpose model reached 86.0% [@osworld2026verified]. That baseline, however, was measured once, on the original tasks, by students rather than experienced office workers, and says nothing about work that has not been packaged as a test. Its successor, OSWorld 2.0, described in a June 2026 preprint, consists of 108 long workflows that take people a median of about 1.6 hours each. The best agent tested completed about 21% of them, and earned 54.8% of the available credit when partly finished work was scored [@yuan2026osworld]. OpenAI reported 72.6% for GPT-6 Astra on an offline subset of OSWorld 2.0 scored with partial credit [@openai2026gpt6]; the comparable figure for the paper's best agent is that 54.8%, on the full task set.

### Coding agents

Software engineering has the most developed agent benchmarks, partly because a project's own tests can check an answer. **SWE-bench**, published by Jimenez and colleagues, collects 2,294 real problems from the issue trackers of 12 popular Python projects on GitHub. An agent receives the code and the text of the issue and must produce a change (a "patch") that makes hidden tests pass. When the benchmark appeared in 2023, the best model, Claude 2, resolved 1.96% [@jimenez2024swebench].

Some problems turned out to be unfair, because the description was too vague or the tests rejected valid solutions. In August 2024 OpenAI and the benchmark's authors released **SWE-bench Verified**, 500 problems selected after professional developers had screened 1,699 candidates, and reported that GPT-4o resolved 33.2% of them [@openai2024introducing]. By February 2026, with every model run inside the same minimal agent program, the leading models clustered in the low-to-mid 70s and the top score was about 76.8% [@sajadieh2026ai].

In February 2026 OpenAI announced that it would stop reporting SWE-bench Verified results. According to the company, an audit of 138 problems that its o3 model had not solved consistently across 64 runs found that 59.4% had material flaws in their tests or descriptions. Newer models from three developers (GPT-5.2, Claude Opus 4.5 and Gemini 3 Flash) could also reproduce some of the original human fixes or problem details from memory, a sign that the public solutions had entered training data [@openai2026why]. The sample was chosen because it was hard, so 59.4% does not describe the benchmark as a whole. The episode illustrates two problems that Chapter 4 discusses in general, saturation and contamination.

A successor illustrates how much the number depends on the test. **SWE-bench Pro**, described in a 2025 preprint, contains 1,865 problems from 41 actively maintained repositories, split into a public set, a held-out set and a commercial set drawn from 18 private codebases of start-ups. Its tasks may take a professional engineer hours to days. The paper's main results use one agent program (SWE-Agent), at most 50 turns, and problem statements supplemented with written requirements and interface details. In that setting the best model, Claude Sonnet 4.5, resolved 43.6% of the public problems. On the commercial set, reported in a separate table, the best score was 17.8% (Claude Opus 4.1). In an earlier run capped at $2 per task, GPT-5 at its high reasoning setting resolved 25.9% of the public set [@deng2025swebench]. On Scale AI's public leaderboard, mostly run in a minimal agent program, the top entry in October 2026 resolved 61.5% [@scale2026swebench]. Table 5.2 summarises the three versions.

| Benchmark | Released | Tasks | Source of tasks | Result reported |
|:--|:--|--:|:--|:--|
| SWE-bench | 2023 | 2,294 | 12 public Python projects | best model 1.96% at release |
| SWE-bench Verified | Aug 2024 | 500 | human-screened subset | GPT-4o 33.2% (2024); top ≈76.8% (Feb 2026) |
| SWE-bench Pro | Sept 2025 | 1,865 | 41 repositories, incl. 18 private | best 43.6% on public set (50 turns, no cost cap reported); best 17.8% on commercial set; leaderboard top 61.5% (Oct 2026) |

: Table 5.2: Three generations of the SWE-bench coding benchmark. Scores depend on the agent program, turn limits and cost caps used, and are not comparable across rows. Source: [@jimenez2024swebench; @openai2024introducing; @sajadieh2026ai; @deng2025swebench; @scale2026swebench].

A different yardstick asks how long a task an agent can finish. The non-profit METR's "50% time horizon" is the length of software task, timed on skilled humans, that an agent completes half the time [@kwa2025measuring]. On METR's data it doubled roughly every four months from 2023 to early 2026 (129 days, with a 95% confidence interval of 104 to 158). Claude Opus 4.6 (February 2026) measured about 12 hours, with an interval of roughly 5 to 61 hours. The last model METR measured before it stopped updating the series in September 2026, an early version of Claude Mythos Preview (April 2026), reached about 17 hours, with an interval of roughly 8 to 55 hours [@metr2026task]. A 12-hour task is of the order of a skilled engineer's day and a half of work on a self-contained software problem with a clear test of success. Chapter 4 (Section 4.7) explains the method and its caveats, among them that "time horizon is not the length of time AIs can work independently" [@kwa2026clarifying]; a 50% success rate is also far from the reliability most employers expect.

### Agents in use

Evidence on how agents were actually used in 2025–26 is thinner than the benchmark record, and most of it comes from the companies that sell them. Coding was the clearest case. Anthropic's own usage report of September 2025 found that "77% of API transcripts show automation patterns", meaning that businesses calling its models through software mostly delegated whole tasks rather than working through them in conversation, and that a little under half of that traffic concerned computing and mathematical tasks [@anthropic2025economic]. Independent data come from public code repositories. A dataset compiled by academic researchers and described in a 2025 preprint holds more than 456,000 pull requests (proposed code changes) opened by five coding agents, among them OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot and Claude Code, across 61,000 repositories by mid-2025 [@li2025rise]. Using it, another preprint, from 2026, compared projects before and after they adopted an agent with matched projects that did not. Output rose sharply at first, but mainly in projects that had not already used AI coding assistants, while static-analysis warnings and code complexity rose by about 18% and 39% and stayed higher [@agarwal2026ai]. Beyond coding, the positive evidence for agents at work is mostly vendor-reported, from case studies and usage figures that outsiders cannot audit; the critical evidence in this chapter, by contrast, is mostly academic.

Laboratory benchmarks and workplace outcomes can diverge. In a randomised trial run by METR in early 2025 and reported as a preprint, 16 experienced open-source developers completed 246 real tasks in their own projects. When allowed to use AI tools they took 19% longer, although they had expected to be about 24% faster [@becker2025measuring]. One small study of early-2025 tools is not decisive, and Chapter 8 places it among the wider evidence on productivity.

Kapoor and colleagues argue that the field's evaluation habits overstate progress [@kapoor2025ai]. Many leaderboards rank agents by accuracy alone, so complex and expensive agents top tables that much cheaper designs nearly match. The SWE-bench Pro results show how much a score depends on turn limits, cost caps and the agent program. Many benchmarks have weak or missing hold-out sets (tasks kept secret from developers), which lets agents overfit, and inconsistent evaluation practices make results hard to reproduce. Benchmarks also tend to use cooperative or simulated users. In Project Vend, the failures that mattered most came from real people who asked for discounts, invented stories or claimed that a leadership election had taken place [@anthropic2025projectphase].

## 5.5 Reliability: the mathematics of many steps and many tries

### Compounding error

A chatbot that is right 95% of the time is useful, because a person reads each answer. An agent that must take 20 steps in a row, each 95% reliable, is a different matter. If every step must succeed and steps fail independently, the probability that the whole task succeeds is the product of the step probabilities [@goodfellow2016deep], *p*^*n*^ (the per-step success rate *p* multiplied by itself once for each of the *n* steps), here 0.95^20^ ≈ 0.36. This is **compounding error**, plotted in Figure 5.3. In the author's calculation, over 50 steps, a per-step rate of 99% still leaves about a 60% chance of finishing, while 95% leaves about 8%. At 90% per step the chance falls below 1%.

![Figure 5.3: How per-step reliability compounds over a multi-step task. Each curve shows the probability that every step succeeds, for per-step success rates of 99, 95 and 90%, assuming steps fail independently and every step must succeed. Simple arithmetic, not measured data; real agents can recover from some errors, and their errors are rarely independent. Computed and drawn by the author using the product rule for independent events [@goodfellow2016deep].](../figures/svg/fig-05-03.svg){#fig:05-03}

Real agents depart from this model in both directions. They can notice an error and try again, which is why the observe step of the ReAct loop helps [@yao2023react]. A calculation by the author shows that the effect of recovery is large. If every failed step is detected and retried once, with an independent second chance, a step's success rate rises from 0.95 to 1 − 0.05^2^ = 0.9975. Twenty such steps then succeed 0.9975^20^ ≈ 95% of the time instead of 36%. The calculation assumes that failures are detected, which is exactly what is hard when there is no test to run. Errors can also be correlated, as when an agent misreads a whole class of web page the same way. An early wrong step can also send all later steps in the wrong direction. The curve is best read as an argument for short tasks, checkpoints that can detect failure, and measuring end-to-end success directly.

### pass\@*k* and pass^*k*^

**pass\@*k*** and **pass^*k*^** have similar names and answer opposite questions. **pass\@*k*** asks whether *at least one* of *k* attempts succeeds. Chen and colleagues at OpenAI, in a 2021 preprint, introduced it for code generation, where a test suite can pick out the working attempt. Their Codex model solved 28.8% of the HumanEval problems with a single sample, but 70.2% when 100 samples per problem were drawn and any working one counted [@chen2021evaluating]. **pass^*k*^** ("pass hat *k*"), introduced by Yao and colleagues for τ-bench, asks whether *all k* attempts succeed, which is the relevant question for an agent that will handle the same kind of request unsupervised every day [@yao2025taubench].

If an agent solves a given task with probability *p* and its attempts are independent, pass\@*k* = 1 − (1 − *p*)^*k*^ and pass^*k*^ = *p*^*k*^. The same *p* gives very different pictures. For *p* = 0.7 and *k* = 8, pass\@8 ≈ 0.99993 while pass^8^ ≈ 0.06. In practice *p* is unknown and is estimated from *n* trials of which *c* succeed. Both papers use estimators that avoid the bias of simply inserting *c*/*n* for *p*. They are written with binomial coefficients C(*a*, *b*), the number of ways of choosing *b* items from *a*:

pass\@*k* = 1 − C(*n* − *c*, *k*) / C(*n*, *k*) and pass^*k*^ = C(*c*, *k*) / C(*n*, *k*),

each averaged over the benchmark's tasks [@chen2021evaluating; @yao2025taubench]. A worked case: an agent attempts a task *n* = 8 times and succeeds *c* = 6 times. Its pass\@4 is 1 − C(2, 4)/C(8, 4) = 1, because any four attempts must include a success. Its pass^4^ is C(6, 4)/C(8, 4) = 15/70 ≈ 0.21: of the 70 possible sets of four attempts, only 15 consist entirely of successes. The naive calculation (6/8)^4^ ≈ 0.32 overstates it.

A benchmark's pass^*k*^ is an average over tasks, and tasks differ: some are easy for a given agent (*p* close to 1) and others hard (*p* close to 0). Because easy tasks keep contributing however large *k* becomes, the observed pass^*k*^ is never lower than the average single-attempt rate raised to the power *k* (a mathematical consequence of averaging, apart from sampling noise), and with mixed difficulty it is usually much higher. On τ²-bench's retail tasks, Claude Opus 4.5's pass^1^ of 0.80 would predict a pass^4^ of about 0.40 if every task were equally hard; the observed value is 0.52 [@sierra2026taubench]. The simple formula still makes the essential point. An agent that looks good on one try can look much worse when it must be right every time.

### Customer-service agents under test

τ-bench (tau-bench) simulates customer service. A language model plays a customer following instructions the agent cannot see. The agent must converse, call the company's tools (looking up orders, changing bookings) and follow a written policy. Success is judged by comparing the database at the end with the correct final state. The original 2024 benchmark had 115 retail and 50 airline tasks. GPT-4o, the strongest function-calling model tested, had a single-attempt success rate (pass^1^) of 61.2% on retail and 35.2% on airline tasks. In retail its pass^8^ was below 25% [@yao2025taubench].

Its 2025 successor, **τ²-bench**, published at ICML in 2026, added a telecoms domain with "dual control": the simulated customer must also take actions on their own device, as in technical support. The authors report "significant performance drops" when agents must guide a user instead of acting alone [@barres2025tau2]. In 2026 its maintainers at the company Sierra released a further extension, τ³-bench, which fixed more than 50 flawed retail and airline tasks and added a banking domain in which the agent must search a knowledge base of about 700 documents [@sierra2026taubench]. Averaged over the four domains, the leading models' first-attempt scores in early 2026 ranged from about 63 to 70%, according to the AI Index [@sajadieh2026ai]. Table 5.3 shows how much that average hides.

| Domain | What the agent must do | Claude Opus 4.5, pass^1^ |
|:--|:--|--:|
| Airline | Book, change and cancel flights under airline policy | 84.0% |
| Retail | Returns, exchanges and order changes | 79.6% |
| Telecom | Troubleshoot while the customer acts on their device | 92.3% |
| Banking | Answer and act using ~700 policy documents | 24.7% |
| Four-domain mean | | 70.2% |

: Table 5.3: One model's first-attempt success on the three τ²-bench domains and the τ³-bench banking domain. The figures come from Sierra's own run in 2026, a company-run evaluation of a model from another developer. By August 2026 the best banking score on the leaderboard was about 55%. Source: [@sierra2026taubench].

### A documented failure

Benchmarks measure success rates; deployments reveal what a failure costs. Project Vend's shopkeeper showed the cheap end of the range, selling metal cubes for less than it had paid and, for a time, directing customers to a payment account that did not exist [@anthropic2025project]. The case below shows a more expensive one.

::: {.box .case}
**Case study: A coding agent and a production database (2025)**

In July 2025 Jason Lemkin, founder of the software community SaaStr, documented a multi-day experiment building an application with the AI coding service Replit. According to his public posts, reported by *The Register*, the service's agent deleted a live production database even though he had instructed it not to change any code without his permission. It then told him that the data could not be restored, which turned out to be untrue. Screenshots he shared appear to show the agent calling its own action "a catastrophic error of judgement" [@sharwood2025vibe]. The OECD's AI Incidents Monitor recorded the event as an AI incident causing economic and reputational harm [@oecd2025replit]. Replit's chief executive called the incident "unacceptable", offered a refund and announced changes, including automatic separation of development and production databases [@sharwood2025replit].

The case rests largely on one user's account, so details should be treated with care. In the author's view its structure is nonetheless typical. An instruction written in plain language was one more input that the model could outweigh, while the agent held a real permission to delete data.
