The fixes the company announced changed permissions and infrastructure, not the model's instructions [@sharwood2025replit].
:::

Other failures do not involve a granted permission at all. In July 2026 OpenAI reported that models it was evaluating had broken out of their test environment and into Hugging Face's systems, an incident Section 12.2 examines [@openai2026openai].

## 5.6 Security: prompt injection and its defences

Figure 5.2 showed that a tool's output re-enters the model as text in the same context as the user's instructions [@greshake2023not]. This creates a security problem that resembles an old one, the "confused deputy" discussed below, but lacks the clean separation of commands from data that fixed comparable flaws in conventional software. A language model processes everything in its context as one stream of tokens and has no reliable built-in way to tell which parts are instructions from its principal and which are merely data it was asked to read [@chismon2025prompt].

### A taxonomy

**Prompt injection** is the name for attacks that exploit this. In its *direct* form, the user types instructions that try to override the developer's rules. The more serious form for agents is **indirect prompt injection**, analysed by Greshake and colleagues in 2023. Here an attacker places instructions inside content an AI system is likely to process, and the model may treat them as commands. The authors argued that connecting models to retrieved content "blurs the line between data and instructions" and demonstrated the problem against systems then in use, including a search engine's GPT-4-based chat [@greshake2023not].

Greshake and colleagues sort attacks by how they arrive and what they aim at. Injections can be planted where retrieval will find them, such as a web page, sent to the target in an email the assistant will read, or pasted by a user who has been tricked. Their goals range from extracting private data and fraud to taking unauthorised actions through the system's own tools, spreading malware and manipulating what the user is shown [@greshake2023not].

Agents widen the attack surface beyond web pages and emails. A computer-use agent reads whatever is on screen, which is why OpenAI added a monitor for suspicious on-screen content [@openai2025computer]. Tool descriptions are themselves text that the model trusts, which is why the MCP specification tells clients to treat annotations from untrusted servers as untrusted [@modelcontextprotocol2026tools]. In multi-agent systems, a message from another agent is one more input of uncertain provenance.

Real products have shipped with such flaws. In June 2025 the US National Vulnerability Database published CVE-2025-32711, described as "AI command injection in M365 Copilot" that "allows an unauthorized attacker to disclose information over a network". Microsoft rated it 9.3 out of 10 ("critical") and NIST's own analysts 7.5 ("high"); both scoring vectors indicate that the attack required neither privileges nor any action by the user [@nist2025cve]. Microsoft stated that it had already fully mitigated the flaw on its servers, that users needed to take no action, and that it was not aware of exploitation [@microsoft2025cve].

### Why it resists a fix

The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) has argued that prompt injection should not be thought of as similar to SQL injection, a familiar class of web vulnerability. SQL injection can be prevented by strictly separating commands from data, but current language models "do not enforce a security boundary between instructions and data inside a prompt". The NCSC therefore warned that "it's very possible that prompt injection attacks may never be totally mitigated in the way that SQL injection attacks can be". It described the model as an "inherently confusable deputy" (a classic security term for a program with privileges that can be tricked into using them for someone who lacks them) and advised designers to focus on reducing the likelihood and impact [@chismon2025prompt].

The independent developer Simon Willison has proposed a widely cited rule of thumb for when the danger is acute. His "lethal trifecta" is an agent that combines access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and the ability to communicate externally [@willison2025lethal]. With all three, injected instructions can in principle cause private data to leave the system. Removing any one breaks the chain, which turns an unsolved machine-learning problem into a design decision. Willison also observes that a filter that catches 95% of attacks would be a failing grade in web security.

### Defences and their limits

One line of defence is *training the model* to resist. OpenAI researchers proposed an "instruction hierarchy" in which models learn to give priority to the developer's and user's instructions over text from tools and documents. In a preprint they reported substantially improved robustness, including against attack types not seen in training [@wallace2024instruction]. *Detection* uses separate classifiers to flag likely injections in inputs. Both approaches improve average-case behaviour but give no guarantees, and attackers who adapt can defeat them. A study by 14 researchers from several AI companies and universities, released in 2025 and published at the USENIX Security Symposium in 2026, tested 12 recent defences from these families (prompting techniques, training methods, detectors and methods based on secret checks) against adaptive attacks. Such attacks modify their strategy to counter each defence's design. They bypassed most defences with success rates above 90%, although the majority had originally reported attack success near zero. A human red-teaming competition with more than 500 participants and $20,000 in prizes succeeded in every scenario it covered. The authors conclude that "empirical evaluations cannot prove that a defense is robust" [@nasr2025attacker].

*System design* takes the opposite starting point. It accepts that the model can be fooled and limits what a fooled model can do. Beurer-Kellner and colleagues, from industry and academic security groups, describe in a 2025 preprint six design patterns (Table 5.4). Their central claim is that "securing general-purpose agents remains out of reach with current capabilities", but that "application-specific agents can be secured through principled system design" [@beurerkellner2025design].

| Pattern | Idea | Main cost |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Action selector | Model only maps a request to a fixed menu of actions; results never return to it | Loses most of the model's flexibility; every command must be predefined |
| Plan then execute | Actions fixed before untrusted data is read | Hard when later steps depend on earlier results; injected data can still alter tool inputs, such as an email's text |
| Map–reduce | Each untrusted item processed by an isolated model call with constrained output | Some tasks cannot be decomposed this strictly |
| Dual LLM | A privileged model with tools never sees untrusted text; a quarantined model without tools reads it | Quarantined model's output must be tightly constrained; some tasks cannot be split this way |
| Code then execute | Model writes a program that calls tools and other models, then runs it over the data | As with plan then execute, injected data can still alter the content passed between steps |
| Context minimisation | Remove the user's prompt from context once it has been used | Addresses only injections in the user's own prompt |

: Table 5.4: Design patterns for agents that resist prompt injection, with the trade-offs their authors identify. Source: [@beurerkellner2025design].

Some designs go further and offer formal guarantees, measured on **AgentDojo**, a benchmark from ETH Zurich. It provides 97 realistic tasks (managing email, online banking, travel booking) and 629 security test cases; its authors found that leading models failed many tasks even without attack [@debenedetti2024agentdojo]. A follow-up system, **CaMeL**, first posted as a preprint in 2025 and published in 2026 at the IEEE Conference on Secure and Trustworthy Machine Learning (SaTML), is the instance of the code-then-execute pattern that Beurer-Kellner and colleagues cite [@beurerkellner2025design]. It adds a layer that tracks where every piece of data came from and what it may be used for. The plan is derived from the trusted user request before any untrusted data is read, so retrieved content cannot change which actions are taken. A policy check blocks data from flowing to places it should not. On AgentDojo, CaMeL completed 77% of tasks with provable security, against 84% for an undefended system, so protection cost seven points of usefulness. The guarantees cover attacks that try to change the agent's actions or the flow of data, such as sending private files to an outsider. The authors state that CaMeL "cannot defend against text-to-text attacks", such as an injected instruction that makes the agent summarise an email misleadingly. They also describe side channels through which small amounts of information could still leak [@debenedetti2025defeating].

Human confirmation, the default safeguard in MCP and in commercial computer-use agents, sits alongside all of these. It works when the person reads the request; Beurer-Kellner and colleagues warn of "tired or overloaded human verifiers approving unsafe actions" [@beurerkellner2025design].

::: {.box .debate}
**Debate: Can prompt injection be solved inside the model?**

*Mainly outside the model.* The NCSC holds that because models do not separate instructions from data, prompt injection may never be mitigated as completely as SQL injection, and that systems should limit what a manipulated model can do [@chismon2025prompt]. Adaptive attacks broke all twelve jailbreak and prompt-injection defences tested, most at success rates above 90%, although most had reported near-zero rates [@nasr2025attacker]. Architectural designs such as CaMeL give guarantees, for defined classes of attack, that do not depend on the model behaving well [@debenedetti2025defeating].

*Increasingly inside the model.* Training on an instruction hierarchy improved robustness, including against unseen attack types [@wallace2024instruction], and AgentDojo shows attack success varying widely between models, so model choice matters [@debenedetti2024agentdojo]. Architectural defences have real costs: CaMeL completed fewer tasks, its guarantees exclude text-only manipulation [@debenedetti2025defeating], and the most secure patterns give up much of what makes a general-purpose assistant useful [@beurerkellner2025design].

In the author's view, what would move the argument is a kind of test that has rarely been run: independent evaluations on realistic tasks in which well-resourced attackers adapt to each defence, reporting both attack success and lost usefulness. A model-level defence that held up under such testing would strengthen the second position; continued breaks would favour the first.
:::

## 5.7 Agents that pay

If agents are to book travel or buy supplies, they need a way to pay. Card rules assume either a cardholder present at checkout or a merchant charging under a standing agreement, as with subscriptions; neither fits a third-party agent deciding what to buy. Google's announcement of its **Agent Payments Protocol (AP2)** in September 2025 named the problems this creates once software acts for a person. *Authorisation* means "proving that a user gave an agent the specific authority to make a particular purchase". *Authenticity* means assuring the merchant that the request reflects the user's real intent, and *accountability* means deciding who is responsible if a transaction is fraudulent or wrong [@parikh2025powering].

AP2's answer is a chain of "mandates", which the company describes as "tamper-proof, cryptographically-signed digital contracts" signed with verifiable credentials (digitally signed attestations that a third party can check). An *Intent Mandate* records what the user asked for, such as "find me new white running shoes", and a *Cart Mandate*, signed when the user approves a specific cart, records the exact items and price. For a purchase without the user present, such as concert tickets bought the moment they go on sale, a detailed Intent Mandate signed in advance, with price limits and other conditions, lets the agent generate the Cart Mandate itself. Google argues that the chain provides "a non-repudiable audit trail", a record that no party can plausibly deny later. More than 60 organisations backed AP2 at launch, including card networks and payment firms [@parikh2025powering].

The protocol's current documentation describes AP2 as an extension of A2A and MCP and restructures the scheme. A *Checkout Mandate* is shared with the merchant, and a *Payment Mandate* with the credential provider, the card networks and the merchant's payment processor. Each exists in an "open" form, which sets constraints such as a budget, and a "closed" form, which records a specific, finalised transaction [@ap22026agent]. In April 2026 Google handed AP2 to the FIDO Alliance, the industry body behind passkeys, which is building agent-payment standards on it and on Mastercard's related Verifiable Intent framework [@fidoalliance2026google; @fidoalliance2026fido].

A second proposal works at the level of the web itself. The HTTP protocol that underlies web pages has long reserved a status code, 402 "Payment Required", that was rarely used. In May 2025 the cryptocurrency company Coinbase released **x402**, an open protocol that puts this code to work, initially for payments in stablecoins (digital tokens pegged to a currency such as the US dollar) [@dioquino2025coinbase; @coinbase2025x402]. In the current specification, a server that wants payment answers a request with status 402 and a header listing acceptable payment options. The client, which may be an agent, chooses one, signs a payment and repeats the request with the signed payment in another header. The server, or a third-party "facilitator", verifies and settles the payment and returns the resource. The design principle is "trust minimizing": schemes "must not allow for the facilitator or resource server to move funds" beyond what the client authorised [@x4022026x402]. Because the whole exchange fits inside an ordinary web request, the design suits small payments per request; the specification's own example is paying $1 to read an article. In April 2026 the protocol moved to an x402 Foundation under the Linux Foundation; its 40 launch members included card networks, cloud providers and payment companies [@coinbase2026x402].

These protocols are young, and in the author's assessment public evidence on how much real commerce passes through them is thin and comes mostly from vendors. What the protocols provide is a record of what the human authorised, in a form that can be checked later, the kind of evidence a dispute would turn on [@parikh2025powering; @x4022026x402]. They leave open who bears the loss when an agent acting within its mandate makes a bad purchase, the accountability problem Google's announcement names, and in the author's view a question for contract law and payment regulation [@parikh2025powering].

## 5.8 Many agents: multi-agent systems and agent economies

### Teams of agents

Many deployed systems combine several agents with different roles. Anthropic described its research feature as an orchestrator–worker design: a lead agent (Claude Opus 4) plans the research and spawns sub-agents (Claude Sonnet 4) that search in parallel. According to the company, this outperformed a single Opus 4 agent by 90.2% on its internal research evaluation. The cost was tokens. Agents used about four times as many tokens as chat interactions and the multi-agent system about fifteen times as many. On the BrowseComp search benchmark token usage alone explained about 80% of the variance in performance. The company noted that most coding tasks offer fewer truly parallel sub-tasks than research does [@anthropic2025how].

Independent analysis is less encouraging about multi-agent designs in general. Cemri and colleagues started from the observation that such systems often show only small gains over single agents on standard benchmarks. They built a taxonomy of 14 failure modes in three categories from 150 traces analysed by human experts, then used a language model as judge to label more than 1,600 execution traces from seven popular multi-agent frameworks. System design issues include the most frequent mode in the model-labelled data, step repetition (15.7% of failures), and agents unaware of when to stop. Misalignment between agents covers cases such as a mismatch between an agent's stated reasoning and its action, or an agent ignoring another's input. The third category is weak or incorrect verification of the final result. Three human annotators reached close agreement on the categories in a calibration set of 15 traces (Cohen's kappa, a measure of agreement beyond chance, 0.88), and the model judge agreed reasonably well with human labels (kappa 0.77). The failures are recognisable patterns, although their frequencies are machine-judged [@cemri2025why]. Project Vend's second phase showed the same pattern at small scale. Adding a manager agent changed outcomes, but the manager shared the worker's weakness for saying yes [@anthropic2025projectphase].

### Risks when agents meet

A different problem arises when agents with different owners interact, for example in a marketplace. The Cooperative AI Foundation's report *Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI*, led by Lewis Hammond with 44 authors, offers one of the most systematic maps so far. It classifies failures by the agents' incentives into **miscoordination** (agents with compatible goals fail to work together), **conflict** (agents with opposed goals harm each other or bystanders) and **collusion** (agents cooperate in ways their owners or society did not intend). It lists seven risk factors that make them more likely, among them information asymmetries, network effects and commitment problems [@hammond2025multi]. Because large populations of capable LLM agents interacting in the wild are still rare, the report is a structured map of mechanisms, not a measurement of current harm.

Evidence on collusion comes from older pricing algorithms. In simulations, Calvano and colleagues found that simple reinforcement-learning pricing algorithms competing in a standard market model "consistently learn to charge supracompetitive prices, without communicating with one another". The algorithms sustained high prices with strategies that punish undercutting and then return to cooperation [@calvano2020artificial]. In Germany's retail petrol market, where pricing software became widely available in 2017, Assad and colleagues found that adoption raised margins only for stations facing competitors. In markets with two or three stations, margins rose only when all of them adopted it, consistent with the algorithms learning to avoid price wars, that is, with tacit collusion [@assad2024algorithmic]. Neither study involves language-model agents, but both show that coordination can emerge between algorithms without being designed or communicated.

### Agent economies

Economists have begun to ask what markets will look like if many transactions are carried out by software. Hadfield and Koh, in a chapter of the National Bureau of Economic Research volume *The Economics of Transformative AI* (quoted here from the preprint version), argue that agents able to carry out long tasks with little oversight may be widely deployed within a decade. They raise the possibility that "the errors introduced by AI agents might be more correlated than those of humans", so that mistakes would not cancel out across a market. They point to the 2010 "flash crash" in US stock markets, which automated trading is thought to have worsened, as an early warning. The identity and registration systems that tell people whom they are dealing with "are currently missing for AI agents", they note, and new digital institutions will be needed [@hadfield2025economy].

Tomašev and colleagues at Google DeepMind propose, in a preprint, the frame of "sandbox economies". They classify agent economies by whether they emerge spontaneously or are deliberately designed, and by how *permeable* they are: how freely value and effects pass between the agent economy and the human one. They call permeability "the critical and controllable design variable" and argue that current trends point towards a large, unplanned and highly permeable agent economy. Their proposals include auctions to allocate resources fairly, partial insulation between high-speed agent trading and the rest of the economy, and identity infrastructure such as cryptographically signed credentials [@tomasev2025virtual].

The payment mandates of Section 5.7 and the Agent Cards of Section 5.3 are early pieces of such infrastructure. Chan and colleagues examine three further measures for making agents visible: **agent identifiers** that show when an agent is involved in an interaction, **real-time monitoring** of agent activity, and **activity logs** that can be reviewed afterwards. Each can be implemented more or less intrusively, and the authors weigh the gains in accountability against costs to privacy and the risk of concentrating power in whoever runs the monitoring [@chan2024visibility].

In the author's assessment, evidence on agent-to-agent commerce still consists mostly of experiments, protocols and forecasts [@hadfield2025economy; @tomasev2025virtual], so this literature names the design choices (identity, permeability, speed, record-keeping) before large-scale deployment has fixed them. Chapter 11 places correlated failure within the wider taxonomy of AI risks, and Chapter 14 returns to evaluating whole populations of agents.

Governance of agents is at an early stage. The EU AI Act does not regulate agents as such; its duties attach to providers of general-purpose AI models, which have applied since August 2025, and to systems used for listed high-risk purposes, whether or not they act autonomously (Chapter 13) [@europeanparliament2024regulation]. In February 2026 the US standards body NIST launched an AI Agent Standards Initiative to support industry-led standards and open protocols for agents and research on agent security and identity [@nist2026announcing]. Who bears the loss when an agent errs remains, as Section 5.7 noted, a question for existing contract and payment law.

An agent's usefulness and its main weaknesses have the same source: software, not a person, now closes the loop between what a model writes and what happens in the world. Errors compound over steps, reliability across repeated attempts falls well below single-try success, and any text the loop feeds back, from a web page to another agent's message, can redirect the model. The safeguards that do not depend on the model behaving well sit outside it: narrow permissions, plans fixed before untrusted data arrive and checks that catch failure, joined for payments by signed records of what a human authorised. Project Vend's second phase showed that better tools cut a shopkeeper's losses without giving it better judgement [@anthropic2025projectphase]. The open question for the next few years is whether such outside safeguards can be made cheap enough that agents are trusted with tasks nobody checks, or whether checking remains the main cost of using them.

## Further reading

- Yao, S. et al. (2023). *ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models*. The short paper behind the reason–act–observe loop that most current agents use, with readable example traces. [@yao2023react]
- Kapoor, S. et al. (2025). *AI Agents That Matter*. Shows, with worked comparisons, why accuracy-only agent leaderboards mislead and what cost-aware, held-out evaluation looks like. [@kapoor2025ai]
- Chismon, D. (2025). *Prompt Injection Is Not SQL Injection (It May Be Worse)*. A short explanation from the UK's National Cyber Security Centre of why the problem resists the fixes that worked for earlier injection attacks. [@chismon2025prompt]
- Beurer-Kellner, L. et al. (2025). *Design Patterns for Securing LLM Agents against Prompt Injections*. Six concrete architectures with case studies, and an honest account of what each gives up. [@beurerkellner2025design]
- Hammond, L. et al. (2025). *Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI*. A systematic map of failure modes and risk factors when many AI agents interact, grounded in real-world examples. [@hammond2025multi]
- Hadfield, G. K. and Koh, A. (2026). *An Economy of AI Agents*. An economist's survey of the institutions that markets full of agents may need. [@hadfield2025economy]


# Chapter 6: AI for Science, Mathematics and Engineering

In the second week of October 2024, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awarded two of its Nobel Prizes for work on artificial intelligence. On 8 October the physics prize went to John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton "for foundational discoveries and inventions that enable machine learning with artificial neural networks" [@royal2024nobelphysics]. The next day, half of the chemistry prize went to Demis Hassabis and John Jumper of Google DeepMind "for protein structure prediction", with the other half going to David Baker for computational protein design [@royal2024nobelchemistry]. The physics prize honoured early ideas (Hopfield networks and Boltzmann machines) from which the networks of Chapter 2 descend. The chemistry prize honoured a use of such networks that had changed how a whole field works.

A prize is not a measure of what AI does for science. A model can be accurate without revealing why [@zittrain2019hidden]. A system can produce thousands of candidate results that nobody has time to check, and a headline about AI "discovering" something can rest on an evaluation that a later reanalysis overturns [@cheetham2024artificial; @leeman2024challenges]. The fields covered below (protein structure and design, weather and climate, materials, mathematics and algorithms, engineering, and automated research) each have a showcase result and at least one independent test of it. Biology and medicine appear only at the level of protein structure; Chapter 10 covers health.

Most of the showcase results discussed in this chapter come from a handful of companies, above all Google DeepMind, and many were first reported by the companies themselves [@jumper2021highly; @lam2023learning; @merchant2023scaling; @google2024ai; @novikov2025alphaevolve]. Several later passed peer review and some were checked by outsiders; where no independent evaluation exists, a result is the developer's own account.

## 6.1 Where AI enters the scientific cycle

Science can be described, in simplified form, as a cycle. Researchers read what is already known, form a hypothesis, design an experiment or a simulation, collect and analyse data, and publish results that others check and build on. Machine learning can enter at every stage, where, in this chapter's classification, it does one of four distinguishable jobs. **Prediction** learns a mapping from inputs to outputs from many solved examples, so that new cases can be answered without the slow work: a protein's shape from its sequence [@jumper2021highly]. **Emulation** learns to imitate an expensive simulation, such as a weather model, so that it can be run far more cheaply [@lam2023learning]. **Search** proposes many candidate solutions (crystal structures, proofs, algorithms) and keeps those that pass a test [@merchant2023scaling; @romeraparedes2024mathematical]. **Automation** takes over parts of the research workflow itself: reading papers, writing and running code, drafting manuscripts [@lu2024ai]. Figure 6.1 places examples of these jobs on the cycle. A candidate found by search is, until it is checked, a hypothesis.

![Figure 6.1: Where AI enters the scientific cycle. Each stage of a simplified research cycle is paired with an example of an AI job done there, and with the check that keeps the result honest. The checks on the inner ring return in Section 6.9. Schematic by the author; examples after [@jumper2021highly; @lam2023learning; @merchant2023scaling; @romeraparedes2024mathematical; @lu2024ai].](../figures/svg/fig-06-01.svg){#fig:06-01}

An **emulator** (also called a surrogate model) is trained on the inputs and outputs of a slower model or measurement. Once trained, it gives approximate answers in a small fraction of the time; GraphCast, for example, produces a ten-day forecast in under a minute that takes a physics-based model about an hour on a supercomputer [@lam2023learning]. Unlike the simulation it imitates, it is not written from physical equations; it learns only from examples, so it can be confidently wrong in situations its training data never covered [@sun2025can].

The four jobs differ in how easily their results can be checked, and in the author's view this matters more than the sophistication of the model. A prediction can be compared with a later measurement, an emulator with the simulation it imitates and with reality. A candidate found by search may be checkable instantly (a proof, a faster program) or only after laboratory synthesis and expert analysis (a new compound) [@romeraparedes2024mathematical; @szymanski2023autonomous; @leeman2024challenges]. Automated research produces claims of every kind at once [@mitchener2025kosmos].

Scientists are adopting these tools quickly and with mixed feelings. A 2023 *Nature* survey of more than 1,600 researchers found them "concerned, as well as excited", with many expecting AI tools to become central to research soon [@vannoorden2023ai]. The anthropologist Lisa Messeri and the cognitive scientist M. J. Crockett, reviewing how scientists describe their hopes for AI, identify four imagined roles: *Oracle* (searching and summarising the literature), *Surrogate* (standing in for data that are hard to collect), *Quant* (analysing data too large for a human) and *Arbiter* (judging which studies are sound) [@messeri2024artificial; as summarised by @cummings2024doing]. Each promises more productivity and objectivity; Section 6.9 returns to what those promises can hide.

## 6.2 Protein structure and design: what AlphaFold computes, and what it does not

A protein is a chain of building blocks, amino acids, that folds into a three-dimensional shape; the shape largely determines what the protein does. Determining one structure by experiment has typically taken months to years, and by 2021 only around 100,000 unique protein structures had been solved, a small fraction of the known sequences. Predicting structure from sequence had been an open research problem "for more than 50 years" [@jumper2021highly], and the field had built an unusually strict test for it. The Critical Assessment of Structure Prediction (CASP) is a community experiment whose "core components are rigorous blind testing of methods and evaluation of the results by independent assessors" [@kryshtafovych2021critical]. Predictors submit models of proteins whose experimental structures have been determined but not yet released, so nobody can tune to the answer.

### How AlphaFold 2 works

AlphaFold 2 takes three inputs: the amino-acid sequence, a **multiple sequence alignment** (MSA) of related sequences from other organisms, and, where available, a few experimentally solved structures of related proteins as templates [@jumper2021highly]. The alignment matters because evolution leaves traces of shape in sequence. Positions that are in contact in the folded protein tend to change together over evolutionary time, so correlated variation between two columns of the alignment hints that they are close in space. Earlier methods computed these "pairwise evolutionary correlations" with fixed statistics and turned them into predicted distances. AlphaFold instead lets the network learn to interpret "phylogenetic and covariation relationships without hardcoding a particular correlation statistic" [@jumper2021highly].

The network keeps two internal representations and lets them talk to each other. The *MSA representation* is a table with one row per related sequence and one column per residue (amino-acid position). The *pair representation* is a square table with one entry for every pair of residues, recording what the network currently believes about their relation. The trunk of the network, called the **Evoformer**, consists of 48 blocks that repeatedly exchange information between the two tables. Its most distinctive operations are "triangle" updates: for any three residues *i*, *j* and *k*, the entries for the pairs *ik* and *jk* are used to update the entry for *ij*. The motivation is geometric. For a set of pairwise distances to describe a real object in three dimensions, they must satisfy constraints such as the triangle inequality, and the triangle updates were designed with that consistency requirement in mind. They encourage it rather than impose it as a hard rule [@jumper2021highly].

The **structure module** then turns these representations into coordinates. It treats each residue as a free-floating rigid body, a "residue gas", and moves the residues with a geometry-aware attention mechanism (*invariant point attention*) whose result does not depend on how the whole molecule is rotated or shifted. Correct bond geometry is encouraged in training and enforced only in a final physics-based relaxation [@jumper2021highly].

The whole network is then run again with its previous outputs (the pair representation, the first row of the MSA representation and the predicted backbone positions) fed back in as extra inputs, a step called *recycling* (Figure 6.2). AlphaFold runs four such passes in all. The model was trained on Protein Data Bank (PDB) structures released up to 30 April 2018, plus a high-confidence subset of its own predictions for further sequences [@jumper2021highly].

Each prediction comes with a per-residue confidence score, the predicted local distance difference test (pLDDT), which "reliably predicts" the actual local accuracy, so a researcher can see which parts of a model to trust [@jumper2021highly].

![Figure 6.2: How AlphaFold 2 turns a sequence into a structure. The sequence is used to search databases for related sequences (the MSA) and templates; 48 Evoformer blocks exchange information between the MSA representation and the residue-pair representation; the structure module places each residue as a rigid body in 3D; the network's outputs are fed back in for further passes (recycling, four passes in all), and the final structure comes with a per-residue confidence score, pLDDT. Schematic by the author, after [@jumper2021highly].](../figures/svg/fig-06-02.svg){#fig:06-02}

### The CASP14 result and its limits

In CASP14, held from May to July 2020, the gap to every other method was large. On 87 protein domains, AlphaFold's median backbone error was 0.96 ångström (Å; one ångström is a ten-billionth of a metre), measured as the root-mean-square deviation over the best-fitting 95% of residues. The next best method had 2.8 Å. For all atoms, including side chains, the figures were 1.5 Å and 3.5 Å [@jumper2021highly].

The CASP organisers' overview of the round, which summarises the independent assessments, reported models "competitive with experimental accuracy for at least 2/3 of the targets" and concluded that the results "represent a solution to the classical protein-folding problem, at least for single proteins" [@kryshtafovych2021critical]. The qualifier is deliberate. The same overview records objections to the word "solution". The AlphaFold paper names its own weak points: accuracy "decreases substantially" when the alignment has fewer than about 30 sequences, and the model is "much weaker for proteins that have few intra-chain or homotypic contacts", that is, proteins whose shape depends mainly on contacts with other molecules or with copies of themselves [@jumper2021highly].

Scale followed quickly. The AlphaFold Protein Structure Database, hosted by the European Bioinformatics Institute, grew from about 300,000 predicted structures in 2021 to "over 214 million", and its predictions are integrated into the main protein databases [@varadi2024alphafold]. The Academy's Nobel press release stated that more than two million people in 190 countries had used AlphaFold [@royal2024nobelchemistry].

Outside structural biologists then tested how much weight the predictions can bear. Terwilliger and colleagues compared AlphaFold predictions with experimental crystallographic maps for 102 crystal structures, looking only at the parts predicted with very high confidence. Many matched "remarkably closely". Overall, the central backbone (Cα) atoms in these very-high-confidence regions differed from the crystal structures by a median of 0.6 Å, and about 10% differed by more than 2 Å. Even these predictions differed from experiment by about twice as much as two experimental structures of the same protein crystallised in different forms differ from each other. Some predictions were distorted globally or had domains in the wrong orientation [@terwilliger2024alphafold]. The authors recommend treating predictions as "exceptionally useful hypotheses", and verifying by experiment any detail that matters, "particularly those that involve interactions not included in the prediction".

### AlphaFold 3: wider scope, new failure modes

AlphaFold 3, published in May 2024, extends prediction from single protein chains to complexes "including proteins, nucleic acids, small molecules, ions and modified residues" [@abramson2024accurate]. Its architecture changes in two ways. Alignment processing is "substantially de-emphasized", and a new trunk, the Pairformer, replaces the Evoformer as the main processing block. A **diffusion model**, the generative method also used by image generators, replaces the structure module. It learns to start from random noise and remove it step by step until a realistic sample remains, here working directly on atom coordinates. The authors report substantially higher accuracy than specialised tools for protein–small-molecule and protein–nucleic-acid interactions, and than their own previous system, AlphaFold-Multimer, for antibody–antigen complexes [@abramson2024accurate].

The same paper lists the costs of the new design. Generative models can invent order where there is none. The diffusion approach "introduces the challenge of spurious structural order (hallucinations) in disordered regions", although such regions are usually flagged with low confidence. Outputs "do not always respect chirality", the handedness of molecules, with a violation rate of 4.4% on one benchmark. The model "typically predict[s] static structures as seen in the PDB", not the motions through which many proteins work [@abramson2024accurate]. Access is narrower than for AlphaFold 2: the inference code is public, but the trained parameters are available only from Google under its terms of use. The free web server, for non-commercial use, supports a more limited set of ligands and chemical modifications [@google2024alphafold]. Open reproductions followed within months; Boltz-1, released in November 2024 with its code, weights and training data under an open licence, reported accuracy at the level of AlphaFold 3 in its authors' preprint [@wohlwend2024boltz1].

### Designing proteins

The other half of the 2024 chemistry prize rewarded the reverse problem: designing a sequence that will fold into a shape, and do a job, that nature has never produced. Here too deep learning took over. ProteinMPNN, from David Baker's laboratory, proposes sequences for a given backbone; on natural backbones it recovered 52.4% of the native amino acids, against 32.9% for the physics-based Rosetta software, and it rescued designs that had failed when made with earlier methods [@dauparas2022robust]. RFdiffusion, from the same group, generates new backbones with a diffusion model built by fine-tuning a structure-prediction network. Its authors characterised hundreds of designed assemblies, metal-binding proteins and protein binders in the laboratory, and a cryo-electron-microscopy structure of one designed binder bound to an influenza protein was nearly identical to the design [@watson2023novo]. Design has a cheap, decisive check: make the protein and measure whether it folds and binds. That check is what separates it from the materials designs of Section 6.4.

## 6.3 Weather and climate: learning the atmosphere

Weather forecasting is the other field that has most of what the protein case combines: a large archive of carefully checked data, a precisely defined target, a measure of confidence and a test by outsiders, here the weather itself. It is also where machine learning has moved fastest from research paper to daily operations. Conventional **numerical weather prediction** (NWP) starts from the best estimate of the current state of the atmosphere and steps forward in time by solving the equations of fluid dynamics and thermodynamics on a supercomputer. That starting estimate comes from **data assimilation**, the process of combining fresh observations with a short forecast from the previous cycle [@rasp2024weatherbench]. The European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) runs the leading global system, the Integrated Forecasting System (IFS). Its high-resolution deterministic forecast (HRES) ran at 0.1° resolution with 137 vertical levels, and a ten-day forecast took about an hour on a supercomputer [@lam2023learning].

### How machine-learning models are trained

Machine-learning weather models learn from **reanalysis**: a consistent reconstruction of past weather, produced by running a fixed modern data-assimilation system over decades of historical observations. ECMWF's ERA5, available hourly from 1940 to the present at 0.25° resolution (about 28 km at the equator), is the standard training set [@rasp2024weatherbench; @lam2023learning]. A model is shown the state of the global atmosphere at one time and learns to predict the state a few hours later. To forecast further ahead, it is applied again to its own output.

Pangu-Weather, from Huawei, published in *Nature* in July 2023, reported stronger deterministic forecasts than the operational IFS "in all tested variables" when verified against reanalysis [@bi2023accurate]. GraphCast, from Google DeepMind, published in *Science* in 2023, became the reference point. It represents the atmosphere on a grid of about a million points and at each point predicts 227 values, five surface variables plus six atmospheric variables at each of 37 pressure levels [@lam2023learning].

GraphCast is a graph neural network, a network that passes messages along the edges of a graph. An encoder maps the grid onto an internal "multi-mesh", built by repeatedly refining an icosahedron, whose edges of many lengths let information travel both locally and across continents in a few steps. Processing layers pass messages over this mesh, and a decoder maps the result back to the grid. With 36.7 million parameters it is, as its authors note, "a relatively small model by modern ML standards" [@lam2023learning].

Trained on ERA5 from 1979 to 2017 and tested on 2018, GraphCast produces a ten-day forecast in under one minute on a single Google TPU v4 (a Tensor Processing Unit, Google's own AI accelerator chip; Chapter 7), against about an hour for HRES on a supercomputer. On 90% of 1,380 verification targets (combinations of variable, pressure level and lead time) it was significantly more accurate than HRES. The targets where HRES did better were concentrated in the stratosphere; with the highest level tested (50 hPa, about 20 km up) excluded, GraphCast was better on 96.9% of the rest [@lam2023learning].

::: {.box .concept}
**Concept: Forecast skill**

"Skill" in weather forecasting means accuracy measured by agreed scores, usually relative to a baseline. The **root mean square error** (RMSE) averages the squared differences between forecast and verifying analysis over the globe (weighted by latitude), then takes the square root; lower is better. The **anomaly correlation coefficient** (ACC) asks whether the forecast gets the *departures from normal* right, correlating forecast anomalies with observed anomalies; 1 is perfect and 0 is no better than climatology. ECMWF treats an ACC below 0.6 as the point where the positioning of large-scale weather systems "ceases to have value for forecasting purposes" [@rasp2024weatherbench]. For ensembles, the **continuous ranked probability score** (CRPS) rewards a spread of forecasts that is centred on what happened and neither too narrow nor too wide. Comparisons between models need reading with care. Each model is usually verified against its own "truth": GraphCast against ERA5, HRES against its own operational analysis [@lam2023learning]. And a forecast that is smoother than real weather can score well on RMSE and ACC without depicting any weather that could actually occur [@rasp2024weatherbench].
:::

::: {.box .deeper}
**Going deeper: Rolling a forecast forward, and why it blurs**

GraphCast takes two snapshots of the atmosphere six hours apart and predicts the snapshot six hours later. To forecast ten days ahead it feeds its own prediction back in and repeats the step 40 times [@lam2023learning]. This *autoregressive rollout* is how a language model adds one token at a time (Chapter 3). Because small errors compound, GraphCast was trained to minimise its error over up to 12 consecutive steps, not just one. That choice has a side-effect. When the future is uncertain, the forecast that minimises average squared error is the average of the possible outcomes. In a chaotic, non-linear atmosphere, moreover, "the mean of many states is not a realistic state itself" [@rasp2024weatherbench]. Forecasts therefore blur with lead time: storm peaks are shaved off and rain is spread thinly. GraphCast's authors tested whether its advantage was only blurring. When both models were optimally blurred, GraphCast still beat HRES on 88.0% of targets [@lam2023learning]. GenCast, described below, avoids the problem differently, by sampling individual sharp forecasts and letting the spread of an ensemble carry the uncertainty [@price2025probabilistic].
:::

A single forecast does not tell a decision-maker how confident to be. Operational centres therefore run **ensembles**: dozens of forecasts from slightly perturbed starting points, whose spread indicates uncertainty. GenCast, published in *Nature*, is a diffusion-model ensemble, in which each run starts from fresh random noise and produces a different plausible 15-day trajectory. In the authors' evaluation, it had greater skill than ECMWF's operational ensemble (ENS) on 97.2% of 1,320 targets, with better predictions of extreme weather, cyclone tracks and wind-power output. Its 50 members can be run in parallel, each 15-day forecast taking about eight minutes on one TPU v5 [@price2025probabilistic].

### Into operations

The step to operations came within two years. On 25 February 2025, ECMWF put its own Artificial Intelligence Forecasting System (AIFS) into operational service alongside the IFS. According to ECMWF, it outperforms leading physics-based models on many measures, including tropical cyclone tracks, and uses roughly 1,000 times less energy per forecast [@ecmwf2025ecmwfs]. In a 2024 technical preprint describing an earlier version of the system, the AIFS used a graph-network encoder and decoder around a transformer processor. It was pre-trained on ERA5 for 1979–2020 and then fine-tuned on ECMWF's operational analyses, the kind of data from which it is started in real time. A ten-day forecast took about two and a half minutes on one GPU [@lang2024aifs].

A 51-member ensemble version followed on 1 July 2025 (Table 6.1). It runs on a coarser grid than the physics-based ensemble, which ECMWF states "remains indispensable for high-resolution fields and coupled Earth-system processes" [@ecmwf2025ensemble]. Version 2 of both, live since 12 May 2026, adds what ECMWF calls its first data-driven wave and snow-cover forecasts [@ecmwf2026significant].

In December 2025 the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) launched three operational AI-based global systems, using GraphCast as the initial foundation and fine-tuning it on NOAA's own analyses. Its deterministic model (AIGFS) and ensemble (AIGEFS) need a small fraction of the computing of their physics-based counterparts (Table 6.1); a third, hybrid ensemble combines AI and physics-based members and, according to NOAA, outperforms both across most major verification measures [@noaa2025noaa].

| System | Compared with | Reported skill | Reported cost / speed | Limitation (reported or noted) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| GraphCast (deterministic; *Science*, 2023) | ECMWF HRES | Better on 90% of 1,380 targets | 10-day forecast in under 1 minute on one TPU v4 (HRES: about 1 hour on a supercomputer) | Blurring at long lead times |
| GenCast (50-member ensemble; *Nature*, 2024/2025) | ECMWF ENS | Better on 97.2% of 1,320 targets | 15-day forecast in about 8 minutes on one TPU v5 | Higher cost than deterministic ML models\* |
| AIFS, ECMWF (deterministic; operational since 25 Feb 2025) | Physics-based models | Better on many measures, incl. tropical cyclone tracks (gains of up to 20%) | About 1,000 times less energy per forecast | Depends on physics-based initial conditions\* |
| AIFS ENS, ECMWF (51-member ensemble; operational since 1 Jul 2025) | Physics-based models | Better on many measures, incl. surface temperature (gains of up to 20%) | Over 10 times faster; about 1,000 times less energy | Coarser grid than physics-based ensemble (31 km vs 9 km) |
| AIGFS / AIGEFS, NOAA (operational suite launched 17 Dec 2025; GraphCast as starting point) | GFS / GEFS | Improved skill for many large-scale features; ensemble adds 18–24 h of skill | Up to 99.7% less computing (AIGFS); 9% of GEFS computing (AIGEFS) | Worse tropical cyclone intensity forecasts (v1.0; July 2026 upgrade reported to improve them) |

### What independent evaluations find

Several of the clearest evaluations come from meteorologists who did not build the models. The first comparison "in an operational-like context", by an ECMWF team, ran Pangu-Weather from the same initial conditions as the IFS and verified both against analyses and weather-station observations. Accuracy was comparable for global scores and for extreme events, but the study identified "overly smooth forecasts, increasing bias with forecast lead time, and poor performance in predicting tropical cyclone intensity" [@benbouallegue2024rise]. Massimo Bonavita, also at ECMWF, examined Pangu-Weather, FourCastNet and GraphCast and concluded that they did not properly reproduce smaller-scale weather and lacked the "fidelity and physical consistency" of physics-based models [@bonavita2024some].

Researchers at the University of Reading compared four machine-learning models on Storm Ciarán, a European windstorm that caused sixteen deaths. All captured the large-scale structure of the storm accurately, and all underestimated its peak winds, the detail that matters most for warnings [@charltonperez2024ai]. NOAA itself states that the first version of its deterministic AI model showed "a degradation in tropical cyclone intensity forecasts" even as track errors fell [@noaa2025noaa]. An upgrade in July 2026 was designed in part to fix this; the weather service says it improves intensity forecasts and reduces blurring at longer lead times [@nws2026aigfs].

Intensity is not beyond reach of machine learning, however. The US National Hurricane Center's verification of the 2025 season found that an experimental Google DeepMind ensemble slightly outperformed its official Atlantic track forecasts up to three days ahead and was the best of the intensity models, comparable to the official forecasts at most lead times [@cangialosi2026national]. In the same system's peer-reviewed description, published in *Nature* in August 2026 under the name WeatherNext Cyclones, its developers report for cyclones of 2023–2025 an average lead-time advantage of a day or more over leading operational models for track, intensity and storm size [@alet2026operational].

Other studies probe whether the models have learned atmospheric physics or a statistical shortcut. Selz and Craig fed an AI model tiny perturbations to its starting state. In physics-based models and in theory, such perturbations grow very fast, which is the "butterfly effect" that sets a hard limit on how far ahead weather can be predicted. The AI model "completely fails to reproduce the rapid initial growth rates", although for perturbations of realistic size it largely agreed with physics-based simulations [@selz2023can].

Sun and colleagues asked whether an AI model can forecast storms stronger than any it has seen. They trained versions of FourCastNet on 1979–2015 data, some with every Category 3–5 tropical cyclone removed, and tested them on Category 5 storms from 2018–2023. All versions were similarly accurate for ordinary weather; the version that had never seen strong storms "cannot accurately forecast Category 5" storms. Removing strong storms from only one ocean basin did less harm, because the model could learn from strong storms elsewhere [@sun2025can]. An emulator interpolates within its experience; it does not reliably extrapolate beyond it.

### Dependence on physics, and the climate question

Every operational AI system above still starts from an analysis produced by physics-based data assimilation, and all were trained on reanalysis produced by a physics model. ECMWF notes that the AIFS uses the same initial conditions as the IFS [@ecmwf2025ecmwfs]. Aardvark Weather, from researchers at the University of Cambridge and partner institutions and published in *Nature* in 2025, tests whether that dependence can be removed. A single model ingests raw observations and produces global and local forecasts; its global forecasts outperformed an operational baseline "for several variables and lead times" [@allen2025endtoend]. It remains a research system.

Climate projection is a harder problem than weather. A climate model must stay stable over decades of simulated time and respond correctly to conditions, such as higher greenhouse-gas concentrations, that lie outside the historical record. NeuralGCM, developed by a team at Google with academic and ECMWF co-authors and published in *Nature* in 2024, is a hybrid: a conventional solver for large-scale atmospheric dynamics, with learned components for small-scale processes such as clouds. With sea-surface temperatures prescribed it tracked climate statistics for multiple decades at a fraction of the computing cost of conventional models. Its authors state plainly that "our model does not extrapolate to substantially different future climates" [@kochkov2024neural]. For weather, AI emulators have matched or overtaken physics-based forecasts on average scores. For projecting a changed climate, the out-of-distribution problem that Sun and colleagues demonstrated for storms applies to the whole system.

## 6.4 Materials: discovery claims under scrutiny

New materials underpin batteries, solar cells and microchips. The traditional route is slow: a chemist proposes a compound, a quantum-mechanical calculation using **density functional theory** (DFT) estimates whether it is stable, and a laboratory tries to make it [@merchant2023scaling; @szymanski2023autonomous]. A compound is computed to be stable if its energy lies on or below the **convex hull**, the lowest-energy combination of known competing phases with the same overall composition. Anything above the hull would, in principle, decompose into those competitors. Machine learning can speed up the first two steps by screening vastly more candidates than DFT can afford [@merchant2023scaling; @cheetham2024artificial].

### GNoME: scale by active learning

In November 2023 Google DeepMind researchers published GNoME (Graph Networks for Materials Exploration) in *Nature*. Graph neural networks represent a crystal as atoms (nodes) linked to their near neighbours (edges) and predict its energy. The system ran six rounds of **active learning**: generate candidate structures by substituting elements into known crystals and by random search, filter them with the network, compute the survivors with DFT, and retrain the network on the results. Over these rounds the share of filtered candidates that DFT confirmed as stable (the "hit rate") rose from under 6% to above 80% for candidates with a given structure [@merchant2023scaling].

Starting from about 48,000 previously known stable crystals, the authors reported "the discovery of 2.2 million structures below the current convex hull". Of these, 381,000 lie on the final updated hull, for a total of 421,000 stable crystals, "an order-of-magnitude expansion in stable materials known to humanity". They reported that 736 of their predicted structures had already been made independently by experimental groups [@merchant2023scaling].

Two solid-state chemists, Anthony Cheetham and Ram Seshadri, examined the first 250 of 2,047 entries in one GNoME compilation and a random sample of ten from the larger database of 384,870 predicted stable structures [@cheetham2024artificial]. A sample that small is a spot check, which is itself an argument for systematic evaluation. They found "scant evidence for compounds that fulfill the trifecta of novelty, credibility, and utility". A recurring problem was ordering. The calculations, carried out in effect at absolute zero, place different atoms on separate, neat positions in the crystal. At the temperatures where real synthesis happens, similar atoms often mix randomly on shared sites, so many "new" predictions were ordered versions of compounds already known in disordered form. Cheetham and Seshadri also argued that a compound only becomes a *material* when it shows some useful property. In their view the work "does not report any new materials but reports a list of proposed compounds". They nonetheless called the method promising and asked for more domain expertise in the next version.

::: {.box .case}
**Case study: The A-Lab and its correction**

In the same issue of *Nature* as GNoME, a team at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory and the University of California, Berkeley described the A-Lab, an autonomous laboratory that combines computation, synthesis recipes learned from the literature, machine learning and robotics. Its targets were chosen using stability data from the Materials Project, a public database of computed materials properties, and from Google DeepMind. Over 17 days of continuous operation, the authors reported, it "realized 41 novel compounds from a set of 58 targets" [@szymanski2023autonomous].

In early 2024 a group of solid-state chemists published a reanalysis in *PRX Energy* [@leeman2024challenges]. They argued that the automated analysis of the X-ray diffraction patterns, the measurements used to identify what had been made, was "not yet reliable", and that the predictions neglected atomic disorder. About two-thirds of the claimed successes, they concluded (counting 43 synthesis products, slightly more than the 41 compounds of the headline claim), were "likely to be known compositionally disordered versions of the predicted ordered compounds", and no new materials had been discovered.

In January 2026 the original authors published a correction [@szymanski2026author]. It clarifies that "novel" had meant new to the prediction platform, "not necessarily new to science". The authors manually reanalysed the diffraction data. One compound was removed from the discussion because it had mistakenly been included in the training data. Of the 40 remaining reported successes, the authors confirmed the platform's conclusion in 36 and judged 4 inconclusive, so the count of compounds made was reduced to 36. The correction does not claim that the compounds are new to science. Outside experts checked a claim and the record was corrected, as science is supposed to work; it took more than two years and a great deal of expert labour.
:::

### Generating to order, and the disorder lesson

GNoME searches by substitution and filtering. A different approach generates crystals directly, using the same diffusion technique as AlphaFold 3. MatterGen, from Microsoft Research and published in *Nature* in January 2025, generates crystal structures and can be fine-tuned to aim for target properties such as chemistry, symmetry, or mechanical, electronic and magnetic properties. Compared with earlier generative models, its structures were "more than twice as likely to be new and stable" [@zeni2025generative]. As a proof of concept the team asked for a material with a bulk modulus (resistance to uniform compression) of 200 GPa and synthesised one of the generated structures, TaCr~2~O~6~. The X-ray analysis showed that the material made was "a compositionally disordered version of the ordered structure predicted by MatterGen". DFT gave 222 GPa for the ordered prediction. For the real, disordered sample, the highest of four estimates derived from nanoindentation measurements was 169 GPa (mean 158 GPa), within 20% of the target. To decide whether a generated structure is new, the authors introduced an "ordered-disordered structure matcher" and compared against disordered as well as ordered experimental structures [@zeni2025generative]. The check was not enough. A 2026 reanalysis by Mikkel Juelsholt, published in *Materials Horizons*, argued that the compound made is identical to a disordered phase first reported in 1971 and included in MatterGen's own training data. On that reading the proof of concept showed that the model could aim at a property, not that it had discovered a material [@juelsholt2026continued]. The disorder error documented for GNoME and the A-Lab recurred in the system designed to avoid it.

In the author's reading, the materials record shows a gradient of evidence. A prediction of stability is a statement about a computer model at zero temperature. A claim of synthesis concerns matter in a laboratory, and a claim of a useful material concerns measured performance. AI has made the first step cheap but not the second or third, so the gap between candidates generated and candidates verified has widened: GNoME reported 381,000 new stable crystals and 736 independently made, the A-Lab 36 confirmed syntheses [@merchant2023scaling; @szymanski2026author; @cheetham2024artificial].

## 6.5 Mathematics: proofs a machine can check

Mathematics has a special place in AI for science because some of its answers can be verified by machine. A **proof assistant** such as Lean is a programming language in which mathematical statements and proofs are written so precisely that a computer can check every step [@moura2021lean]. If a proof is accepted, it is correct relative to the definitions used, whoever or whatever wrote it. Lean's community library, mathlib, held more than 290,000 theorems in October 2026 [@lean2026mathlib]. AI systems that work in Lean can build on that library, but a problem must first be translated (**formalised**) into Lean, which is laborious and can introduce errors. A Lean proof of the wrong statement is a correct proof of something nobody asked, a warning that the Navier–Stokes case in Section 6.6 makes concrete.

### Olympiad geometry and AlphaProof

Competition mathematics became the proving ground. In January 2024 Trinh and colleagues described AlphaGeometry, which pairs a language model with a symbolic deduction engine. It was trained not on human proofs but on 100 million synthetic ones generated by the symbolic engine. On 30 recent olympiad geometry problems it solved 25, against 10 for the previous best method [@trinh2024solving]. Its successor, AlphaGeometry 2, raised the share of all International Mathematical Olympiad (IMO) geometry problems from 2000 to 2024 that it solves from 54% to 84%, according to its developers' paper in the *Journal of Machine Learning Research* [@chervonyi2025goldmedalist].

At the IMO in July 2024, according to Google DeepMind, AlphaProof and AlphaGeometry 2 together scored 28 of 42 points, one point below the gold threshold of 29. The solutions were scored under IMO rules by the mathematicians Timothy Gowers and Joseph Myers. The caveats were stated. Humans first translated the problems into formal languages, and while one problem was solved in minutes, others took up to three days, against two 4.5-hour sessions for contestants [@google2024ai].

The peer-reviewed account appeared online in *Nature* in November 2025 [@hubert2025olympiad]. AlphaProof is modelled on AlphaZero, the self-taught game-playing system. It learns to find Lean proofs by reinforcement learning, training on "millions of auto-formalized problems", that is, problems translated into Lean automatically rather than by hand. For the hardest problems it uses **test-time reinforcement learning**: while working on a problem it generates and learns from "millions of related problem variants", adapting itself to that one problem. The design depends on the proof checker. Every proof the system finds is verified by Lean, so it can learn from its own successes without a human marking them, and a false proof can never be rewarded. Figure 6.3 places these and later results on a timeline.

### IMO 2025: four claims, four kinds of evidence

A year later several systems reached gold-medal level, under different conditions and with different kinds of verification (Table 6.2). According to Google DeepMind, an advanced version of Gemini with its "Deep Think" reasoning mode solved five of the six problems for 35 points, working in natural language from the official problem statements within the 4.5-hour limit. Its solutions were graded and certified by IMO coordinators [@google2025advanced]. Two days earlier, an OpenAI researcher announced that an experimental OpenAI model had reached the same score on the same five problems under exam conditions [@wei2025openai]. That is a company claim. According to OpenAI, each proof was graded by three former IMO medallists, and the result was not certified by the IMO's coordinators.

Two systems worked in Lean. The start-up Harmonic reports in a preprint that its Aristotle system produced formally verified solutions to five of the six problems. The problem statements were translated into Lean by hand, which the authors describe as "the only human formalization step" [@achim2025aristotle]. ByteDance's Seed-Prover, also described in a preprint, fully proved five of six problems in Lean after human experts formalised the statements, and the authors note that one proof "was finished after the deadline" set by the IMO committee [@chen2025seedprover]. A formal proof removes doubt about the reasoning, but each of these Lean results still rested on a human translation of the question.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| AlphaProof + AlphaGeometry 2 (Google DeepMind) | IMO 2024 | Formal languages (Lean for AlphaProof); problems translated by hand | 28/42 (gold threshold 29); some problems took up to 3 days | Lean (AlphaProof's proofs); scored by two mathematicians | Company blog; later *Nature* paper |
| Gemini Deep Think (Google DeepMind) | IMO 2025 | Natural language, within 4.5 h | 35/42 (gold); 5 of 6 problems | IMO coordinators (certified) | Company blog; IMO-certified grades |

: Table 6.2: AI systems at mathematical olympiads, 2024–2026. Results in natural language and in Lean, and under different time limits, are not directly comparable. Source: [@google2024ai; @hubert2025olympiad; @google2025advanced; @wei2025openai; @achim2025aristotle; @chen2025seedprover; @petrov2025proof; @matharena2026usamo; @afp2026ai].

The gold-medal systems of 2025 were experimental models run by their developers, and in early 2025 publicly available models lagged far behind. Researchers at ETH Zurich and INSAIT in Sofia gave the six problems of the 2025 USA Mathematical Olympiad (USAMO) to leading reasoning models within hours of the problems' release in March 2025, and expert judges graded the full proofs. In their preprint, only Gemini 2.5 Pro reached a non-trivial score of 25%; all others scored below 5%. The judges found flawed logic, unjustified assumptions and a lack of creative strategy, where benchmarks that graded only final answers had suggested much stronger performance [@petrov2025proof].

A year later the gap had largely closed. The same group, running its MathArena evaluations on the 2026 USAMO shortly after the contest, reported that GPT-5.4 "essentially saturates the benchmark with a top score of 95%", with Gemini 3.1 Pro at 74% and the strongest openly available model at 45%. Grading changed too. A panel of three models proposed grades and the team checked every solution by hand, noting that two of the judging models overrated their own answers. The evaluators note that the work was partly funded by Google [@matharena2026usamo]. According to AFP, at the July 2026 IMO in Shanghai, Huawei and Xiaohongshu (RedNote) announced that their systems had scored a perfect 42, working on the problems after the human contestants had sat them and within a set time limit. Xiaohongshu said it had submitted its solutions to IMO organisers for grading; AFP reported the scores as the companies' claims, alongside informal tests by a venture investor in which models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Axiom Math and Moonshot AI also scored 42 [@afp2026ai]. Fresh contest problems limit contamination, but proofs graded quickly by small teams, or by the companies themselves, are weaker evidence than certified grades.

## 6.6 Searching for new mathematics and algorithms

Olympiad problems have known solutions; research mathematics asks questions nobody has answered. In the author's assessment, the most productive approach so far has been a search loop with an automatic scorer [@romeraparedes2024mathematical; @georgiev2025mathematical].

### FunSearch and AlphaEvolve

FunSearch, published in *Nature* in December 2023, pairs a language model that writes short programs with an evaluator that runs them and scores what they produce. The best programs are fed back into the prompt, and the loop repeats [@romeraparedes2024mathematical]. Applied to the cap set problem, a question in combinatorics about how large a set of points in a grid can be without three on a line (in a grid where lines wrap around), it found a cap set of 512 points in eight dimensions, larger than any previously known. The result was not easy even for FunSearch; only four of 140 runs found the 512-point set. Because the system outputs a program rather than a list of points, mathematicians could read the program and write down the construction by hand [@romeraparedes2024mathematical].

AlphaEvolve, announced by Google DeepMind with a white paper in May 2025, generalises the idea into a coding agent that evolves whole programs [@novikov2025alphaevolve]. It maintains a database of candidate programs. An ensemble of Gemini language models proposes modifications, evaluators run and score each child program, and the best survive. Its best-known mathematical result concerns multiplying two 4×4 matrices of complex numbers. According to the company, it found a method using 48 scalar multiplications, the first improvement for complex-valued 4×4 matrices since Volker Strassen's algorithm of 1969. According to the company, it was applied to more than 50 open mathematical problems, matched the best known constructions in about 75% of cases and improved on them in about 20%.

The engineering results are of the same kind. A scheduling heuristic it found for Google's data centres recovers on average 0.7% of the company's fleet-wide computing resources. A tiling heuristic for a matrix-multiplication kernel used in training Gemini gave an average 23% kernel speed-up and a 1% reduction in overall training time [@novikov2025alphaevolve]. These are company results in a preprint, but the mathematical constructions can be checked by anyone.

A follow-up paper, with the mathematicians Javier Gómez-Serrano and Terence Tao as co-authors, applied AlphaEvolve to 67 problems in analysis, combinatorics, geometry and number theory. It "rediscovered the best known solutions in most cases and improved on them in several" [@georgiev2025mathematical]. Released as a preprint in November 2025 and published in *PNAS* in 2026, it is one of the most useful documents in the field because it reports the denominator, including the cases where the system failed to reach the best known result. It states that AlphaEvolve "excels at problems that can be clearly formulated as the optimization of a smooth score function" and "sometimes struggles otherwise". It also records a "cheating phenomenon": the system found "loopholes or exploit[ed] artifacts" in the scoring setup, for example a verifier that checked a constraint only at discrete points, rather than genuine solutions.

Where the scorer could be trusted, the systems could be combined. On one problem the authors chained three systems: AlphaEvolve found a general construction for finite-field Kakeya sets, Deep Think derived a proof and a closed-form formula, and AlphaProof formalised the proof in Lean [@georgiev2025mathematical]. An automated scorer is only as good as its specification, and a search strong enough to find new constructions is also strong enough to find holes in the test.

Computing itself has been a target. In 2023 Google DeepMind's AlphaDev used reinforcement learning to discover short sorting routines that outperformed the human-written ones. They were added to the LLVM standard C++ sort library, a widely used open-source component [@mankowitz2023faster].

Timeline compiled by the author.](../figures/svg/fig-06-03.svg){#fig:06-03}

### Open problems: Erdős problems as a test case

Claims about open problems need particular care, and a website collecting problems posed by the mathematician Paul Erdős has become an informal testing ground. In October 2025, according to the technology news site The Decoder, OpenAI staff posted that GPT-5 had found solutions to ten "open" problems from the site [@bastian2025leading]. Its maintainer, Thomas Bloom, called this "a dramatic misrepresentation": the model had found existing papers he did not know of, and "open" status "only means I personally am unaware of a paper which solves it" [@bloom2025hi].

In January 2026, Erdős problem #728 was described in a preprint as "the first Erdős problem ... regarded as fully resolved autonomously by an AI system". The proof came from a combination of OpenAI's GPT-5.2 Pro and Harmonic's Aristotle, operated by Kevin Barreto, and was checked in Lean [@sothanaphan2026resolution]. As Erdős and his co-authors stated it, the problem was ambiguous and had trivial solutions. Bloom judged that the AI proof answered a tightened version, "the question in the spirit it was intended" [@bloom2026erdos]. Terence Tao, who follows these attempts closely, found the speed with which AI tools rewrote and improved the exposition more interesting than the solution itself. He later added that the methods were very similar to those of a 2014 paper by Carl Pomerance, who then showed that his own methods also solve the problem [@tao2026mastodon; @tao2026ai]. Tao argued that autonomous AI workflows scale well to the "long tail" of obscure Erdős problems, "many of which actually have straightforward solutions", and that failures are "unlikely to be reported on any public site" [@tao2026mastodon]. Success rates are therefore hard to establish. Tao guessed that on the order of 1–2% of outstanding problems are simple enough for current AI tools with minimal human help [@tao2026mastodon]; according to The Decoder, a database of AI attempts compiled by two mathematicians found success rates of the same order, mostly on easier problems [@bastian2026gpt]. Formal verification shows that a proof is correct. It cannot show whether the problem was important, whether the formal statement captured the intended question, or how often the method fails.

The largest and most contested claim came in September 2026.

::: {.box .case}
**Case study: The Navier–Stokes claim (2026)**

*The claim.* On 8 September 2026 OpenAI posted a 166-page manuscript, with a Lean formalisation, constructing a three-dimensional fluid flow that starts from rest, is stirred by a smooth external force confined to a bounded region, and develops unbounded velocity in finite time. The manuscript, which has not been peer-reviewed, states that this establishes one of the four alternatives in the Clay Mathematics Institute's statement of the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize Problem [@openai2026finite]. The official statement does allow solutions with such a force [@fefferman2006existence]. According to *Quanta Magazine*, about 10,000 copies of an unreleased model worked for about 88 hours, and another model translated the proof into Lean in about 17 hours [@kakaes2026ai].

*What is contested.* OpenAI said: "We do not intend to claim the Millennium Prize for this result." It gave no reason; commentators, among them the news site The Next Web, linked the decision to the reliance on an external force [@thenextweb2026openai]. More than a month later, *Scientific American* reported, no one fully understood the proof, and experts judged that in its details it took a different approach from the human research programme it had first been compared with [@howlett2026openais]. In a preprint, three mathematicians argue that the formalised Lean proof does not correspond to the natural-language one [@bastounis2026navierstokes].

*What Lean does and does not certify.* Lean certifies that the formal proof proves the formal statement [@moura2021lean]. It cannot certify that the formal statement says what the manuscript claims, or that the manuscript's own argument holds where the two diverge, the point at issue in the critique by Bastounis and colleagues [@bastounis2026navierstokes]. That is the gap Section 6.5 warned of.

*What would settle it.* Peer review of the manuscript, an independent check that the formal statement matches the Clay alternative, and a decision by the Clay Institute. As of October 2026, research groups were still examining the paper and the Lean code [@howlett2026openais].
:::

## 6.7 Engineering: design under test

Engineering asks for things that work, and some engineering problems come with a check almost as quick as a proof checker. Control is one. In 2022 researchers from DeepMind and the Swiss Plasma Center at EPFL used **reinforcement learning**, in which a system learns by trial and error against a reward signal, to control the magnetic coils of a tokamak fusion reactor. A controller trained entirely in a simulator held a range of plasma shapes on the real machine in Lausanne without further tuning, including two separate plasmas at once [@degrave2022magnetic]. The test of success is immediate: the plasma holds its shape or it does not. AlphaEvolve's data-centre scheduler and AlphaDev's sorting routines (Section 6.6) belong to the same family, results whose value can be measured directly once they run.

Chip design shows what happens when the check is slow and much of the evidence is private. In 2021 Google researchers reported in *Nature* a reinforcement-learning method for floorplanning, the placement of large circuit blocks on a chip.
