The problem is not unique to open weights. @qi2023finetuning removed the safety behaviour of OpenAI's GPT-3.5 Turbo through the company's own fine-tuning service, using only 10 examples at a cost of less than $0.20. The difference is that a provider can monitor its service and roll out fixes, whereas a downloaded model is beyond reach.

Kapoor and colleagues argue that the key question is **marginal risk**: how much an open model adds to what a malicious actor could already do with search engines, existing tools or closed models. Their worked examples point in both directions. For automated searches for software vulnerabilities, they judged the marginal risk of open models to be low at present, partly because defenders can use the same tools. For digitally altered intimate images made without consent, they concluded that open image models "pose considerable marginal risk at present", because such models need few resources, can be fine-tuned on pictures of specific people and are hard to police once released. They also cite a 2023 study finding that most computer-generated child sexual abuse material had been made with the openly available Stable Diffusion family of image models [@kapoor2024position].

Technical defences are an open research problem. Tamirisa and colleagues, in a paper at ICLR 2025, presented a training method, TAR, designed so that safeguards survive "hundreds of steps of fine-tuning" by an attacker [@tamirisa2024tamper]. The International AI Safety Report notes that filtering harmful material out of training data can resist adversarial fine-tuning about ten times more effectively than defences added after training, and that such techniques are now used in some releases. It also notes that other research has disabled such safeguards, and that their robustness against real attacks remains hard to evaluate [@bengio2026international].

::: {.box .debate}
**Debate: Should the weights of the most capable models be released openly?**

*For openness by default.* @kapoor2024position argue that open models spread power beyond a few companies, enable independent safety research and support competition, and that most claimed misuse risks have not been shown to exceed those of existing technologies. In July 2024 the US National Telecommunications and Information Administration concluded that "current evidence is not sufficient to definitively determine" that restrictions on open-weight models were warranted, and recommended that government "actively monitor" risks instead [@ntia2024dual]. Before releasing gpt-oss, OpenAI fine-tuned it to be as capable as possible in biology and cybersecurity. According to a paper by the company's researchers, presented at ICLR 2026, even this version performed below OpenAI's closed o3 model, which it had judged to be under its own "High" risk threshold [@wallace2025estimating]. That is a developer's evaluation of its own product, without independent replication.

*For caution at the frontier.* In a preprint, @seger2023opensourcing accept that open-sourcing has historically brought large net benefits. They argue, however, that for some highly capable future models the risks may be extreme enough that such models "should not be open-sourced, at least not initially". Cheap removal of safeguards [@lermen2023lora] makes release decisions irreversible, and documented harms from open image models show that marginal risk is not only hypothetical [@kapoor2024position].

In the author's assessment, both sides accept that the answer turns on marginal risk at particular capability levels [@kapoor2024position; @seger2023opensourcing], which makes it an empirical question. Independent evaluations of what open models add to specific harms, repeated as each generation improves, would narrow the disagreement, as would evidence on whether tamper-resistant training survives determined attackers; Chapter 12 discusses such dangerous-capability evaluations.
:::

Open weights lower the cost of entry for firms and countries that cannot afford frontier training, partly offsetting concentration. They also complicate export controls. The January 2025 diffusion rule controlled the weights of certain advanced closed-weight models but left the weights of open-weight models outside its scope, on the ground that the most advanced of them were less powerful than the leading closed models [@bis2025framework]. A model trained on restricted chips can be downloaded anywhere the day it is published.

## 7.7 Compute governance and sovereign AI

Data and algorithms are hard to observe and easy to copy, so some researchers argue that hardware is an especially practical lever for governing AI. In a preprint, @sastry2024computing, a group of 19 authors including Yoshua Bengio, argue that AI-relevant compute is "detectable, excludable, and quantifiable" and is produced through "an extremely concentrated supply chain". **Compute governance** uses these properties to give public authorities visibility into AI development, allocate resources and enforce rules. Sastry and colleagues also warn of risks to privacy, economic harms and centralisation of power, and propose guardrails such as collecting only the minimum information needed.

Proposals range from paperwork to hardware. Heim and colleagues argue in a preprint that cloud providers could act as record keepers and verifiers. In their view, information the providers already hold, without seeing customers' data, can reveal whether a workload is large-scale training and how much compute it used [@heim2024governing]. In another preprint, Shavit proposed a more ambitious scheme in which chip firmware would occasionally save snapshots of the weights being trained, so that inspectors could later verify what a training run did. Monitoring of the chip supply chain would ensure that no actor could amass untracked chips [@shavit2023what].

Training compute is already used as a regulatory threshold. The EU AI Act presumes that a general-purpose AI model has "high impact capabilities", and is subject to additional obligations, when the computation used for its training exceeds 10^25^ floating-point operations [@europeanparliament2024regulation, Art. 51(2)]. DeepSeek-V3's pre-training used about 3.3 × 10^24^ operations (Section 4.1), a third of the threshold, yet its developers report that it performed comparably to leading closed models of its time [@deepseekai2024deepseekv3]. Efficiency gains of this kind are one reason fixed compute thresholds are contested; Chapter 13 discusses thresholds and their limits.

The same logic of control over compute underlies **sovereign AI**, the effort by governments to secure national access to AI infrastructure and models rather than depending entirely on foreign providers. The 2026 AI Index notes that "AI sovereignty emerged as a central organizing principle" in national policies during 2025 [@sajadieh2026ai, Introduction]. Strategies differ in scale and emphasis:

- **European Union.** In February 2025 the European Commission launched InvestAI, aiming to mobilise €200 billion for AI investment, including a €20 billion fund for four "AI gigafactories", each with around 100,000 of the latest AI chips [@ec2025eu]. Consortia were to be selected in early 2027 [@eurohpc2026eurohpc].
- **India.** In March 2024 the Indian cabinet approved over Rs 10,300 crore over five years for the IndiaAI Mission, including a plan for public–private compute capacity of more than 10,000 GPUs [@pib2024cabinet]. By February 2026 more than 38,000 GPUs had been made available through the mission [@pib2026democratising].
- **United Kingdom.** The AI Opportunities Action Plan of January 2025 recommended expanding the country's public AI Research Resource "by at least 20x by 2030" and creating "AI Growth Zones" to speed up data-centre construction [@dsit2025ai].
- **United States.** The July 2025 AI Action Plan called for exporting the "full AI technology stack" (hardware, models, software, applications and standards) to allied countries, so that they would not become dependent on rivals' technology [@whitehouse2025winning].

US private AI investment reached $285.9 billion in 2025, against $12.4 billion in China, although the AI Index cautions that the Chinese figure omits much state funding [@sajadieh2026ai, Report highlights]. Even India's 38,000 GPUs are small next to the 17.1 million H100-equivalents of global capacity, and Microsoft alone spent $115.9 billion on equipment in its 2026 fiscal year (Table 7.4). For most countries "sovereignty" therefore means reliable access, local data centres or open-weight models adapted to national languages, not training frontier models from scratch.

Sovereign strategies also run into the chokepoints of Section 7.2. A country can build data centres on its own soil and still depend on Nvidia's designs, TSMC's fabs, Korean and American memory and ASML's machines, dependencies shaped by US export policy, as the UAE arrangement of 2026 illustrates [@bis2026enhanced]. Open-weight models offer a partial route to independence at the model layer, which is one reason governments as different as the United States and China have encouraged them [@whitehouse2025winning; @iea2026key, Box 10.1]. For most countries, then, sovereignty over models is within reach, while sovereignty over the hardware that runs them is not.

In the author's summary of the evidence above, each layer of the stack runs into a scarce input that few suppliers control. Memory bandwidth limits how fast chips serve models, HBM and packaging capacity limit how many accelerators are made, and grid connections and turbines limit where they can run. Export controls are possible because the hardware chokepoints sit mostly in the United States and allied countries, and the rules have followed the bottleneck from arithmetic to memory. Efficiency gains, from FP8 training to cheaper queries, have so far been outrun by demand, so electricity use and capital spending keep rising. Open weights spread access to models far more widely than access to hardware, so the decisions of a few firms and governments over chips, power and capital still set the terms for everyone else.

## Further reading

- International Energy Agency (2026). *Key Questions on Energy and AI*. The most detailed public analysis of data-centre electricity, with transparent scenarios, data tables and a clear account of supply-chain bottlenecks. [@iea2026key]
- Shehabi, A., et al. (2024). *2024 United States Data Center Energy Usage Report*. A bottom-up estimate of US data-centre electricity and water use that shows how wide the uncertainty is and why. [@shehabi2024united]
- Gholami, A., et al. (2024). *AI and Memory Wall*. A short explanation of why memory bandwidth, not arithmetic, limits much of modern AI computing. [@gholami2024ai]
- Kapoor, S., et al. (2024). *Position: On the Societal Impact of Open Foundation Models*. The standard framework for weighing the benefits and marginal risks of open-weight models. [@kapoor2024position]
- Seger, E., et al. (2023). *Open-Sourcing Highly Capable Foundation Models*. A careful statement of the case for caution, best read alongside Kapoor et al. [@seger2023opensourcing]
- Sastry, G., et al. (2024). *Computing Power and the Governance of Artificial Intelligence*. Explains why hardware is a lever for governing AI, and what could go wrong. [@sastry2024computing]

# Chapter 8: Work, Productivity and the Economy

In the first half of 2025 the research organisation METR ran a randomised trial, reported in a preprint, with 16 experienced open-source software developers. Each of 246 real issues from their own projects was randomly assigned to be done with or without AI tools. Before starting, the developers expected AI to cut their time per issue by 24%, and economists and machine-learning experts surveyed by METR expected savings of 38–39%. When the developers' recorded times were compared, the issues on which AI was allowed had taken 19% *longer*. After the study the developers still believed that AI had made them about 20% faster [@becker2025measuring].

Two years earlier a widely cited experiment had found the opposite. College-educated professionals given ChatGPT for short writing tasks finished them 40% faster, and blind graders rated their work 18% better [@noy2023experimental]. Both studies were randomised and both timed work carefully. They studied different people, doing different tasks, with different generations of tools. The gap between their answers illustrates the central fact about the evidence on AI and work. Effects depend heavily on setting, and the settings that are easiest to study are not typical of the economy.

This chapter arranges the evidence, in the author's framework, along a chain that runs from technical potential to economic outcomes (Figure 8.1), building on the task-based view of work described in Section 8.1 [@acemoglu2019automation]. It runs from what AI could do (exposure) to whether it is used (adoption), what it does to tasks when used (experiments), how firms respond (jobs and wages) and what this adds up to (macroeconomics). Some effects lie outside the chain, among them the hidden labour behind AI [@gray2019ghost], the erosion or building of skills [@bainbridge1983ironies], and the distribution of gains and losses [@acemoglu2025simple].

![Figure 8.1: From exposure to economic outcomes. Exposure measures estimate what AI could do; adoption determines whether it is used; task-level productivity effects determine what happens when it is used; and firm decisions translate those effects into employment, wages and output. Data on firms and the economy are plentiful, but causal evidence linking them to AI becomes scarcer at each step. Schematic by the author, drawing on the task framework of @acemoglu2019automation, the exposure measures of @eloundou2023gpts and the productivity J-curve of @brynjolfsson2021productivity.](../figures/svg/fig-08-01.svg){#fig:08-01}

## 8.1 Tasks and exposure: how the measures are built

Economists who study technology and work treat a job as a bundle of **tasks**, the specific activities a worker performs, such as drafting a letter, checking an invoice or calming an angry customer. In the framework of @acemoglu2019automation, automation lets machines take over tasks that people used to do. This has a *displacement effect*, which lowers the demand for labour in those tasks. New technologies also create new tasks in which people have the advantage, a *reinstatement effect* that raises labour demand. Whether a technology helps or hurts workers overall depends on the balance between the two and on how fast new tasks appear.

Both effects are visible in the historical record. Using eight decades of US census data, @autor2024new find that the majority of current employment is in job specialties introduced since 1940. The same study finds that the demand-reducing effect of automation innovations has grown stronger since 1980, while the demand-raising effect of augmentation innovations has not. @acemoglu2022tasks estimate that between 50% and 70% of the change in the US wage structure between 1980 and 2016 is accounted for by relative wage declines of worker groups specialised in routine tasks in industries undergoing rapid automation. Their model also explains how large changes in inequality can coexist with modest productivity gains, a combination that recurs in the AI forecasts discussed in Section 8.5.

### Three ways to score an occupation

An **exposure measure** scores each occupation by how much of its work a technology could, in principle, perform or speed up. The two most widely used US measures start from O\*NET, the US Department of Labor's database that describes about a thousand occupations by their tasks, abilities and work activities [@felten2021occupational; @eloundou2023gpts]; the third described here starts from Poland's occupational classification [@gmyrek2025generative]. They differ in what they score and who does the scoring.

The *AI Occupational Exposure* (AIOE) index of @felten2021occupational was built before the current generation of large language models. It links ten AI applications tracked by the Electronic Frontier Foundation, such as image recognition, language modelling and translation, to the 52 human abilities that O\*NET uses to describe more than 800 occupations. A crowd-sourced survey rated how related each application is to each ability. An occupation's score is an average of the abilities' AI relatedness, each ability weighted by its prevalence and importance in that occupation. In a 2023 preprint the authors set the weight of every application except language modelling to zero; the re-weighted scores correlate at 0.979 with the original index. Telemarketers come top, and post-secondary teachers of English, foreign languages and history rank near the top [@felten2023language]. The method measures *relatedness* of abilities, not whether a task can actually be done.

@eloundou2023gpts scored tasks directly, labelling each of the roughly 19,000 task statements in O\*NET with a rubric. A task counts as *directly exposed* (E1) if access to a large language model (LLM) through an interface such as ChatGPT could cut the time needed by at least half at equivalent quality. Equivalent quality means that "a third party, typically the recipient of the output, would not notice or care about LLM assistance". It counts as *exposed with complementary software* (E2) if the 50% saving would require additional tools built on the model, including image generation. Otherwise it is *not exposed* (E0). Human annotators and an early version of GPT-4 both applied the rubric, and their labels agreed about four times in five. The labels are summarised in three measures. *α* counts only E1; *β* adds half of E2, to reflect that software takes time to build; *ζ* counts all of E2.

The preprint's headline numbers use the middle measure, *β*. About 80% of US workers are in occupations with at least 10% of their tasks exposed, and about 19% in occupations where more than half are exposed. The choice of measure moves the results far more than the choice of labeller. Counting the software that could be built on the model raises the share of tasks exposed from about 15% to around half (Table 8.1) [@eloundou2023gpts]. Unlike earlier measures of exposure to machine learning, exposure on this rubric rises with wages, and occupations that depend heavily on science and critical-thinking skills are less exposed. A shorter version appeared in *Science* in 2024 [@eloundou2024gpts].

| Measure | Tasks counted as exposed | Share of tasks exposed, human labels | Share of tasks exposed, GPT-4 labels | Share of workers with more than half their tasks exposed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| *α* | E1 only (LLM alone) | 15% | 14% | 3% (human labels) |
| *β* | E1 plus half of E2 | 31% | 35% | about 19% |
| *ζ* | E1 plus all of E2 | 47% | 56% | up to 49% (human labels) |

: Table 8.1: Exposure of US work to large language models on the three measures of Eloundou et al. E1 tasks could be done at least 50% faster at equal quality with an LLM alone; E2 tasks would need additional software built on the model. Task shares are means over all O\*NET task statements, core tasks weighted double; worker shares are as reported in the preprint's text, which does not give every combination. Source: @eloundou2023gpts; @eloundou2024gpts.

The third approach is the refined index from the International Labour Organization (ILO) and Poland's NASK research institute, published in May 2025 [@gmyrek2025generative]. Its authors first asked three LLMs to score every task in Poland's occupational classification from 0 (cannot be automated) to 1 (could be done without a human operator). They then checked the scores against ratings from workers surveyed in Poland and from experts, and trained a model on the human scores to re-score the tasks of the international classification. Occupations are placed in four exposure "gradients" using both the average score of their tasks and its spread; the highest gradient is reserved for occupations in which almost every task is highly exposed. The design matters because an occupation with a moderate average but a few highly exposed tasks is more likely to be reshaped than replaced.

The refinement lowered some earlier scores. Average occupational scores fell slightly from 0.30 in the 2023 index to 0.29. Clerical work, though still the most exposed group, lost ground because tasks such as taking meeting notes or scheduling, once scored as high as 0.9, were judged after two years of practical use to need substantial human effort [@gmyrek2025generative]. On the new index, one in four workers worldwide is in an occupation with some exposure. Only 3.3% of global employment falls in Gradient 4. Overall exposure is 34% of employment in high-income countries and 11% in low-income ones [@gmyrek2025generative]. Announcing the index, the ILO concluded that "transformation, not replacement, is the most likely outcome" [@ilo2025one].

An International Monetary Fund staff note from January 2024 reached higher numbers, with almost 40% of global employment exposed, about 60% in advanced economies, 40% in emerging markets and 26% in low-income countries. In advanced economies it judged that about half of exposed jobs might benefit from AI and half might be negatively affected [@cazzaniga2024genai]. The IMF figure rests on the ability-based AIOE index of Felten and colleagues and counts an occupation as highly exposed whenever its score lies above the median. The note itself calls this cut-off relative, so the share depends on where the line is drawn. The ILO counts an occupation as exposed only if a substantial part of its tasks scores high on an absolute 0–1 scale of automation potential, which places fewer workers above the line [@gmyrek2025generative].

::: {.box .concept}
**Concept: Exposure**

An occupation's exposure to AI is an estimate of the share of its work that AI could technically perform or speed up. It is not a forecast. It contains no information about cost, timing, regulation or whether firms will adopt the technology, and a high score is compatible with a job that disappears, shrinks, grows or simply changes. The three families of measures embed different assumptions. The AIOE scores abilities rather than tasks. The Eloundou rubric sets a threshold (a 50% time saving at unchanged quality) and lets the model judge its own usefulness. The ILO–NASK index asks workers and experts and then generalises their judgements with a model [@felten2021occupational; @eloundou2023gpts; @gmyrek2025generative].
:::

### What exposure cannot tell

Every exposure measure relies on judgements about what AI can do, by people or by models, and those judgements date quickly, as the ILO's downward revision of clerical tasks shows. The measures treat tasks as independent, whereas a job whose tasks are 60% exposed may still need a person for the remaining 40%. And none of them can tell whether AI will substitute for a worker or complement one. A tool that drafts legal documents might reduce demand for junior lawyers, or make legal services cheap enough that demand for them grows. Official statistics have now adopted the measures. In August 2026 the US Bureau of Labor Statistics began publishing exposure categories for 831 occupations, combining three theoretical indices, among them the AIOE and the Eloundou rubric, with usage data from Anthropic and Microsoft. It warns that "exposure does not imply job loss" and that the categories do not distinguish automation from augmentation [@bls2026artificial]. Exposure thus sits at the start of the chain in Figure 8.1, the easiest step to estimate for every occupation and the furthest from outcomes.

## 8.2 Adoption: who uses AI, and for what

A tool affects productivity only if people use it. Adoption is surprisingly hard to measure, because the answer depends on whether workers or firms are asked, on how the question is worded, and on whether occasional or intensive use counts [@bick2025state; @garcialuna2026ai]. Table 8.2 sets out the main measures.

### Worker surveys

The best US survey shows a sharp contrast between how many people use generative AI and how much of their work it touches. @bick2026rapid run a nationally representative survey of US adults aged 18 to 64, and find that workplace adoption has been faster than that of the personal computer. By May 2026, 62% of adults used generative AI, according to the authors' update on a Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis blog [@bick2026what]. Yet on their quarterly tracker it was used in only about 6% of all work hours in the second quarter of 2026, and workers reported time savings of about 2% of all work hours, counting non-users [@stlouisfed2026does]. Table 8.2 gives the series.

The measurement is fragile. After a test of question order showed that earlier rounds had underestimated use, the authors reweighted all of them [@bick2025state]. They infer that generative AI "may have increased labor productivity by up to 1.3%" since ChatGPT's release, with the caveat that saved time may go to less productive activities [@bick2025state].

In Denmark, Humlum and Vestergaard ran large surveys with Statistics Denmark in late 2023 and 2024. They covered 11 occupations thought to be highly exposed to AI chatbots, among them accountants, journalists, software developers and teachers. The latest round covered about 25,000 workers at 7,000 workplaces and was linked to official employment records. The revised version of their working paper (March 2026) shows how much employers matter. In workplaces that neither encouraged use nor provided tools or training, about 40% of workers had used chatbots at work and about 7% used them daily. In workplaces that encouraged use, supplied enterprise chatbots and trained staff, 93% had used them, 28% used them daily and 19% reported saving more than an hour a day. About 8% of users without employer initiatives, and about 17% with them, had taken on entirely new tasks created by chatbots, such as reviewing AI output or writing usage policies [@humlum2025still].

### Firm surveys

The US Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey (BTOS) asks firms whether they use AI. Until November 2025 the question asked about AI used in *producing goods or services*; by late 2025 about 10% of firms said yes, double the rate of mid-2024. From 17 November 2025 the question covered AI in *any business function*. Between about 18% and 22% of firms reported use in the first half of 2026, and 24.6% in the two weeks to 4 October 2026 [@census2026business]. (Since a September 2026 executive order the survey's wording calls the technology "Super Intelligence", a change that could itself affect how firms answer [@trump2026inaugurating].) Use was highest in information and professional services, at nearly four in ten firms; in agriculture, transport and construction it was below 10% [@garcialuna2026ai].

A Census Bureau working paper on a special AI supplement to the BTOS, covering November 2025 to January 2026, shows how large firms drive the totals and how shallow most use is [@bonney2026microstructure]. In that period 18% of firms used AI in a business function, or 32% when firms are weighted by employment, and among very large firms in information, professional services and finance the rate reached 50–60%. Of the adopters, 57% used AI in three or fewer functions, most often sales and marketing (52%). Two-thirds used AI only to augment tasks, and just 2% reported that AI had reduced their employment.

### Usage data from AI companies

AI providers can observe use directly. Anthropic, the developer of the Claude models, publishes an "Economic Index" based on privacy-preserving analysis of conversations. Its first report, a preprint by company researchers analysing more than four million conversations, found that software development and writing together accounted for nearly half of usage, and that slightly more usage suggested augmentation (57%) than automation (43%) [@handa2025which]. The company's January 2026 report drew on one million consumer conversations and one million business transcripts from November 2025. Consumer conversations were split between augmentation (52%) and automation (45%), whereas about three-quarters of business interactions through the programming interface, in which firms connect the model to their own software, were automation [@anthropic2026economic].

These data cover real use at scale, for one company's products and customers only. The "automation" and "augmentation" labels are assigned by a language model from conversation patterns, not measured from effects on jobs [@handa2025which]. The two words mean different things in different sources. Anthropic's labels describe conversation style, the Census Bureau's come from firms' own answers, the ADP study in Section 8.4 borrows Anthropic's shares, and the Bureau of Labor Statistics says its exposure categories cannot separate the two [@bls2026artificial]. Claims that effects are "concentrated where AI automates" inherit these differences. A June 2026 report linked usage to a survey of about 9,700 users, but computer and mathematical occupations made up about 30% of respondents against 4% of US employment [@massenkoff2026anthropic].

| Source (data period) | Population | Measure | Reported value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bick, Blandin, Deming & Schumacher (May 2026) | US adults aged 18–64 | Use generative AI | 62% |
| Bick, Blandin & Deming tracker (Q2 2026) | US employed adults | Used it for work in previous week | 39.2% |
| Bick, Blandin & Deming tracker (Q2 2026) | US employed adults | Share of all work hours using it / time saved | 6.3% / 2.2% |
| Census BTOS (late 2025) | US firms | Use AI to produce goods or services | about 10% |
| Census BTOS (21 Sep–4 Oct 2026) | US firms | Use AI in any business function | 24.6% |
| Census BTOS AI supplement (Nov 2025–Jan 2026) | US firms | Use AI in a business function | 18% (32% weighted) |
| Humlum & Vestergaard (late 2023 and 2024) | Danish chatbot users in 11 exposed occupations | Average time saved | about 3% of work hours |
| Anthropic Economic Index (Nov 2025) | Claude.ai conversations | Classified as augmentation / automation | 52% / 45% |

## 8.3 What experiments show about task productivity

The strongest evidence about cause and effect comes from **randomised controlled trials (RCTs)**, in which chance decides which people or tasks get access to AI, so that the groups differ on average only in that access. Many other studies are **observational**. They compare people or firms who chose to adopt with those who did not, so differences may reflect who chose rather than what they chose. Some observational studies are **quasi-experiments**, exploiting a natural source of variation, such as a staggered roll-out, to approximate a trial. Even an RCT measures the effect only for its sample, task and tool [@angrist2009mostly, ch. 2]. Table 8.3 compares the main studies, and Figure 8.2 plots their estimates.

| Study (status) | Design | Sample and setting | Tool and period | Main estimate | Main caveat |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Noy & Zhang (2023, *Science*) | Preregistered online RCT | 453 college-educated professionals; 20–30-minute writing tasks | ChatGPT | Time −40%; graded quality +18% | Short, self-contained tasks |
| Peng et al. (2023, preprint) | RCT | 95 freelance programmers recruited on Upwork (45 treated) | GitHub Copilot, 2022 | Time −55.8% (95% CI −89% to −21%) | One standardised task; only completers timed |
| Brynjolfsson, Li & Raymond (2025, *QJE*) | Staggered roll-out, difference-in-differences | 5,172 customer-support agents at one firm; 89% outside the US | GPT-3-based assistant, 2020–21 | Issues resolved per hour +15%; lowest-skill fifth +36% | Not randomised; one firm |
| Dell'Acqua et al. (2026, *Organization Science*) | Preregistered RCT, three arms | 758 consultants at Boston Consulting Group | GPT-4, 2023 | Inside frontier: +12.2% tasks, 25.1% faster; outside: 19% less likely to be correct | Tasks designed for the study |
| Cui et al. (2026, *Management Science*) | Three field RCTs, pooled | 4,867 developers at Microsoft, Accenture and a Fortune 100 firm | GitHub Copilot, 2–8 months | Completed tasks +26.08% (SE 10.3%) | Each experiment noisy; uneven take-up |
| Becker et al. (2025, preprint) | RCT at issue level | 16 experienced open-source developers, 246 issues | Cursor with Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet, Feb–June 2025 | Time +19% (95% CI +2% to +39%) | Small sample; mature projects |
| METR follow-up (2026, report) | RCT at task level | 57 developers, 800+ tasks | Tools of late 2025 | Time −18% (returning, n = 10); −4% (new, n = 47); neither significant | Developers withheld tasks |

CI = confidence interval; SE = standard error. Estimates use different outcomes, samples and tools and are not directly comparable. Source: @noy2023experimental; @peng2023impact; @brynjolfsson2025generative; @dellacqua2026navigating; @cui2026effects; @becker2025measuring; @metr2026changing; @otis2026uneven; @shen2026how.

### Writing and consulting

@noy2023experimental recruited marketers, grant writers, consultants, data analysts, HR professionals and managers. Each wrote two occupation-specific pieces, such as a press release or a delicate email, with large bonuses for quality. Between the tasks, a random half were walked through ChatGPT and allowed to use it. Experienced professionals in the same occupations graded the work blind. Time fell by 40% and quality rose by 18%. The gains were largest for participants who had done worst on the first task, so inequality between workers narrowed. Two weeks later, treated participants were twice as likely as controls to be using ChatGPT in their real jobs.

@dellacqua2026navigating ran a preregistered experiment with 758 consultants at Boston Consulting Group, first circulated as a working paper in 2023. After a baseline task, participants were randomly assigned to work without AI, with GPT-4, or with GPT-4 plus a short overview of prompting. On 18 realistic consulting tasks chosen to lie within the model's capabilities, those with AI completed 12.2% more tasks, worked 25.1% faster and produced work of significantly higher quality. On a complex managerial task selected to lie outside those capabilities, consultants using AI were 19% less likely than the control group to reach the correct answer. The authors call this pattern the **jagged technological frontier**. AI's competence does not decline smoothly as tasks become harder for humans, and a worker who cannot see where the frontier runs may rely on the tool exactly where it is weakest.

### Customer support

The most detailed field study looked at a real workplace over many months. @brynjolfsson2025generative studied an AI assistant introduced at a Fortune 500 firm selling business software, whose agents answered technical questions by online chat. Access was rolled out to different agents at different times, mainly between late 2020 and early 2021. The authors used **difference-in-differences** [@angrist2009mostly, ch. 5], comparing the change in performance of agents who gained access with the change, over the same period, among agents who had not yet gained it. The design rests on the assumption that the timing of access was unrelated to other changes in performance, which the authors probe with several alternative estimators.

::: {.box .case}
**Case study: An AI assistant in a customer-support centre**

The firm's agents, 89% of them outside the United States and mainly in the Philippines, served small and medium-sized US businesses. The assistant, built on GPT-3 and fine-tuned by a third-party company, suggested replies and links to documentation in real time; agents could ignore the suggestions [@brynjolfsson2025generative]. Across 5,172 agents, access raised issues resolved per hour by 15% on average. The least skilled fifth of agents gained about 36%. For the most experienced and highest-skilled agents, gains in speed were small and the quality of their conversations declined slightly. Agents with two months' tenure who had the assistant performed about as well as agents with more than six months' tenure who did not.

Gains were largest for moderately rare problems, where agents had little experience but the system had enough training data. English fluency improved, particularly among international agents, and customers were more polite and less likely to ask for a manager [@brynjolfsson2025generative].
:::

### Software development

Software is the most-studied occupation, because output can be logged automatically. In an early experiment reported in a preprint, @peng2023impact recruited 95 freelance programmers through Upwork in 2022 and randomly gave 45 of them GitHub Copilot, a code-completion tool. The task was to write a simple web server in JavaScript. Among those who finished, the treated group was 55.8% faster, with a **confidence interval** (the range of effects consistent with the data at the stated level of confidence) from 21% to 89% [@peng2023impact].

@cui2026effects analysed three field experiments in which Microsoft, Accenture and an anonymous Fortune 100 electronics manufacturer gave a random subset of developers access to Copilot as part of normal business. After two to eight months, everyone got access. Take-up was far from complete; at Microsoft fewer than half of the treated group had signed up even after two reminder emails. The authors therefore use random assignment as an *instrument* for actual use, which estimates the effect on those who adopted [@angrist2009mostly, ch. 4]. Pooling 4,867 developers, they estimate that using the tool raised completed tasks (pull requests, the unit in which code changes are submitted for review) by 26.08%, with a standard error of 10.3%. At Microsoft, recent hires and junior staff gained significantly, while longer-tenured and senior developers did not.

The METR trial described at the start of the chapter is the main counterweight [@becker2025measuring]. Its 16 developers typically had more than a decade of experience and had worked on their repositories, which averaged more than 1.1 million lines of code, for five years on average. Of 20 possible explanations for the slowdown, the authors judged five likely contributors, namely over-optimism about AI, high familiarity with the code, large and complex repositories, low reliability of the AI, and tacit context that the tools could not use. Developers accepted fewer than 44% of the AI's generations and spent about 9% of their time reviewing and cleaning its output. The authors stress that the result does not show that AI slows down most developers, or that it would do so with later tools.

METR's follow-up, beginning in August 2025, enrolled 57 developers and more than 800 tasks. For the ten developers returning from the first study the estimated effect was an 18% speed-up; for the 47 new recruits it was 4%. Neither estimate was statistically distinguishable from zero. Between 30% and 50% of developers said they had not submitted some tasks because they did not want to do them without AI, and some developers declined to take part at all for the same reason. Once a tool becomes indispensable to some workers, randomising it away becomes hard. METR concluded that developers were probably sped up more in early 2026 than in early 2025 but that its data were "only very weak evidence" of how much [@metr2026changing].

### When AI widens gaps

Most studies find gains concentrated among weaker or less experienced workers. A field experiment with small-business owners in Kenya found the reverse [@otis2026uneven]. Entrepreneurs were randomly given access to a GPT-4-based business assistant. There was no statistically significant average effect on revenues or profits, but the effect for those who had been performing poorly at baseline was more than 0.2 standard deviations lower than for high performers. In subsample analyses, high performers may have gained more than 15% while low performers did nearly 10% worse. The questions asked and the advice received were similar across the two groups; the difference lay in which advice entrepreneurs chose to act on. Unlike a support agent choosing among suggested replies to a familiar query, an entrepreneur has to judge open-ended advice without quick feedback.

### Reading the evidence together

The estimates in Table 8.3 range from a 56% reduction in task time to a 19% increase [@peng2023impact; @becker2025measuring]. Gains are largest on short, well-defined tasks with clear success criteria, and smallest, or negative, for experts on complex work in contexts they know well. Within a task they usually shrink inequality, possibly because AI passes on the practices of strong performers to weak ones, a mechanism for which only the customer-support study offers direct evidence [@noy2023experimental; @brynjolfsson2025generative]; the exception is work in which users must judge the quality of advice themselves [@otis2026uneven]. And the tools change faster than studies are published. Copilot in 2022, GPT-4 in 2023 and the coding agents of 2026 (Chapter 5) are different technologies, and, in the author's reading of the literature, few published trials yet test agents that carry out multi-step work on their own.

The evidence base also carries a warning about its own reliability. In May 2025 MIT announced that it had "no confidence in the provenance, reliability or validity of the data" in a November 2024 preprint by a former doctoral student on AI, scientific discovery and product innovation. It asked arXiv to mark the paper as withdrawn [@mit2025assuring].
