## 8.4 Jobs and wages: the evidence so far

A productivity gain in a task leaves firms several options. They can employ fewer people, keep the same staff and produce more, or move workers into new tasks. Public forecasts have often assumed the first. In May 2025 Dario Amodei, chief executive of Anthropic, which sells AI tools to businesses, told the news site Axios that AI could eliminate half of entry-level white-collar jobs and raise US unemployment to 10–20% within one to five years [@vandehei2025behind]. Nearly four years after the launch of ChatGPT, the evidence on which option firms are choosing is partial and in places conflicting, and it does not yet show change on that scale.

### Little sign of economy-wide disruption

The Danish study provides the most precise test. Linking survey answers to administrative records of monthly earnings, hours and occupations up to December 2024, Humlum and Vestergaard compare adopters and non-adopters before and after chatbots became available. The revised paper (March 2026) finds null effects. The pooled estimates rule out effects on earnings or recorded hours larger than 2% two years after ChatGPT's launch; no occupation shows a significant effect, and the nulls hold even among daily users who report substantial productivity gains [@humlum2025still]. What does move is the structure of work. Adopters were more likely to have switched occupations, especially into IT-support and clerical roles, and switchers' earnings grew 12 percentage points faster than those of other employed workers, though they were too few to move the average.

In the United States, the Yale Budget Lab measured how fast the mix of occupations changed in the 33 months after ChatGPT's release and compared it with the spread of computers and the internet [@gimbel2025evaluating]. The mix was changing somewhat faster than in earlier periods, but the difference was small and had begun before generative AI. Measures of exposure, automation and augmentation showed "no sign of being related to changes in employment or unemployment". Its tracker, updated in October 2026, still finds no clear AI footprint, and a May 2026 comparison of exposed occupations with a weighted set of unexposed ones found no significant effects so far [@budgetlab2026tracking; @gimbel2026what]. The Economic Innovation Group, a Washington think tank, reached a similar conclusion with Current Population Survey data and five exposure measures [@eckhardt2025ai]. Between 2022 and early 2025, unemployment in the most exposed fifth of workers rose by 0.30 percentage points, against 0.94 points for the least exposed fifth. Unemployment was rising for young workers and recent graduates in both exposed and less exposed occupations. Presenting the OECD's *Employment Outlook 2026*, its secretary-general likewise said, according to the French business site Journal du Net, there was no sign that firms' use of AI was causing a general fall in the demand for labour across member countries, and the OECD noted that young people's difficulty entering work predates generative AI [@barhiye2026ocde].

Employers' own statements point the other way. In announcements tracked by the outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas, AI was the most-cited reason for planned US job cuts in the first nine months of 2026. It was named for about 120,000 cuts, some 21% of the total, while announced cuts overall were 39% lower than a year earlier, or 15% lower excluding government, whose cuts in 2025 had been exceptional [@challenger2026september]. In the Federal Reserve's October 2026 Beige Book, five of the twelve districts reported firms that had cut staff through attrition, delayed hiring or expected less job creation after raising productivity with AI [@federalreserve2026beige]. Both record what firms say, not measured effects, and announcements are not net of hiring.

### Where substitution shows up

Clearer effects appear in online freelancing, where tasks are bought one at a time and buyers can switch to AI at once. Studying a large platform, @hui2024short find that after the release of ChatGPT and of image generators, freelancers in the most affected occupations saw falls in both employment and earnings, and that past performance did not protect them. Suggestive evidence indicates that top freelancers were hit harder. On another leading platform, @demirci2025who estimate a 21% fall in job posts for automation-prone writing and coding work relative to manual-intensive work within eight months of ChatGPT's release, and a 17% fall in posts for image creation after image generators appeared. Freelance markets are small and unusually exposed, so these results show what substitution looks like where it is easy, not how fast it will happen in employment relationships. Wage evidence in employment is thinner still. The Danish records show no effect on earnings, and the payroll data below show adjustment in employment rather than in base pay; only freelancers show clear losses of income.

### Early-career workers

Payroll data point to a group that may be affected first. In a working paper using monthly records from ADP, a payroll processor serving firms with more than 26 million US workers, @brynjolfsson2026canaries document "six facts" from a balanced panel of firms employing 3.5 to 5 million people a month. The August 2026 version has data to June 2026. By then employment of 22- to 25-year-olds in the two most AI-exposed fifths of occupations had fallen about 11% since November 2022, while young workers in the three least exposed fifths grew about 10%. Their employment stood 19% below where it would have been had it kept pace with less-exposed peers, a gap that has widened since the authors first reported it in 2025. Experienced workers showed no comparable gap. The adjustment came through reduced hiring rather than layoffs, appeared in employment rather than base pay, and was concentrated in occupations where AI is mostly used to automate; where it mostly complements workers, employment was flat or rising.

A separate working paper using résumé data on 65 million workers at more than 280,000 US firms found a related pattern [@hosseinimaasoum2025generative]. After firms posted job advertisements for staff to integrate generative AI, a signal of active adoption, junior employment at those firms fell sharply relative to non-adopting firms, while senior employment changed little, again mainly through slower hiring. Job advertisements suggest that entry-level roles are also being redesigned. PwC's 2026 *Global AI Jobs Barometer* analysed more than one billion advertisements. In the United States, entry-level roles most exposed to AI were seven times more likely than others to require skills traditionally expected of senior staff, such as leadership or face-to-face interaction [@pwc2026global]. These are correlations, and the consultancy's analysis does not identify their cause.

::: {.box .debate}
**Debate: Is AI already reducing entry-level hiring?**

*The case that it is.* The ADP working paper shows a 19% employment gap for 22- to 25-year-olds in highly exposed occupations by June 2026, widening steadily since the authors first documented it in August 2025 and concentrated where, by Anthropic's classification, AI substitutes for tasks. It persists when technology firms and computer occupations are excluded and when the authors control for exposure to interest-rate rises and for remote work [@brynjolfsson2026canaries]. Firm-level résumé data show junior employment falling specifically at firms that adopt generative AI [@hosseinimaasoum2025generative], and freelance platforms show direct substitution in writing and coding [@demirci2025who].

*The case that it is not yet shown.* The ADP authors present their findings as "early, descriptive indicators" rather than causal estimates. The gap shrinks when education is controlled for, some divergence predates generative AI, and it is larger in the ADP sample than in national surveys [@brynjolfsson2026canaries]. In Denmark, Humlum and Vestergaard replicate the decline in early-career employment in exposed occupations but find that it is *not* driven by firms that adopted chatbots. Workplaces that encourage chatbot use show no differential change in employment, job creation or destruction, or the composition of hires and separations, including among early-career workers [@humlum2025still]. National US data show unemployment rising for young workers in exposed and unexposed occupations alike [@eckhardt2025ai]. In an NBER working paper using Current Population Survey data for summer 2026, recent college graduates' unemployment showed no statistically significant rise relative to older graduates or to young workers without degrees [@fairlie2026early]. Even analyses that link AI to young people's unemployment may be measuring changing skill requirements rather than automation. A St. Louis Fed blog post attributes about a third of the rise in 18- to 24-year-olds' unemployment from April 2023 to December 2025 to growing demand for AI skills in job postings, but its authors note that the measure captures how job content is changing, "not whether firms are using AI to automate jobs or to screen applicants" [@rodgers2026how].

The firm-level studies point in opposite directions. The US résumé data find junior employment falling at adopting firms, while the Danish administrative records find no such effect [@hosseinimaasoum2025generative; @humlum2025still]. The two may describe different settings or stages; the Danish records end in December 2024. In the author's view, settling the question needs administrative-quality US data that link each firm's adoption to its hiring, observed after 2024, when the tools became more capable.
:::

## 8.5 The macroeconomic picture: why forecasts differ

If AI raises productivity in many tasks, the economy as a whole should grow faster. Published estimates of how much faster differ by more than an order of magnitude, and the reason can be traced to a handful of assumptions [@acemoglu2024simple; @aghion2024ai; @goldmansachs2023generative].

### Hulten's theorem and the task-based sum

@acemoglu2025simple anchors his estimate in a result from growth accounting, **Hulten's theorem** [@hulten1978growth]. In a competitive economy, the first-order effect of a small improvement in the technology for a particular task on aggregate productivity equals the task's share of GDP multiplied by the percentage cost saving in that task. (Strictly, the weight is the task's sales relative to GDP, a "Domar weight"; because sales include inputs bought from other producers, such weights can sum to more than one.) Reallocations of labour and capital across tasks, and knock-on changes in prices, matter only at the second order. Summing over tasks, the gain in total factor productivity (TFP), the part of output growth not explained by more capital or labour, is approximately

*TFP gain ≈ (GDP share of tasks affected) × (average cost saving in those tasks)* [@acemoglu2025simple].

The cost saving in a task is the saving in labour cost multiplied by labour's share of that task's costs, because AI saves labour time but not the machines, materials or premises the task also uses [@acemoglu2024simple].

::: {.box .deeper}
**Going deeper: Acemoglu's arithmetic**

The published version in *Economic Policy* puts the ten-year TFP gain at no more than 0.66%, and below 0.53% once hard tasks are allowed for [@acemoglu2025simple]. The April 2024 working paper, whose results are slightly higher, shows the arithmetic term by term [@acemoglu2024simple]. Weighting the tasks that @eloundou2023gpts classify as exposed by their occupations' share of the US wage bill gives 19.9% of tasks exposed. He then takes an estimate by Svanberg and colleagues, from an unrefereed working paper, that 23% of tasks exposed to computer vision could be automated profitably within ten years [@svanberg2024beyond]. Applying the same share to all AI, 0.199 × 0.23 ≈ 4.6% of tasks are affected. For the labour-cost saving he averages the 40% time saving in @noy2023experimental and the 14% in @brynjolfsson2025generative (as measured in that study's 2023 version), giving 27%; he leaves out the 55.8% in @peng2023impact as too narrow a task. With an AI-exposure-adjusted labour share of 0.57, the average total cost saving is 0.27 × 0.57 ≈ 15.4%. The TFP gain over ten years is then 0.046 × 0.154 ≈ 0.71%, or about 0.07 percentage points a year.

He then argues that early evidence comes from *easy* tasks with clear success criteria, and assumes a labour-cost saving of only 7% for *hard* tasks, half the customer-support figure. That lowers the ten-year gain to about 0.55%. Allowing for the extra investment AI would induce, GDP rises by 0.9–1.1% over ten years, or 1.6–1.8% if there is an investment boom like those of earlier automation technologies [@acemoglu2024simple].

The formula has known limits. It is a first-order approximation for small changes; it counts no new products or new tasks, which could make the true effect larger; and it ignores adjustment costs, which could make it smaller [@acemoglu2024simple; @hulten1978growth].
:::

### Same formula, different numbers

Philippe Aghion and Simon Bunel applied the same formula in an unrefereed note of June 2024, but with their own reading of the evidence [@aghion2024ai]. They take the share of exposed tasks from an IMF working-paper estimate for the United States and assume half of these become profitable to automate because computing costs fall by 22% a year. For the labour-cost saving they average three early studies, taking the customer-support gain at its later, higher level of about 25% rather than the 14% Acemoglu used, which gives 40% (Table 8.4). One of the three, the customer-support study, is quasi-experimental rather than randomised. Their baseline is 0.68 percentage points of additional TFP growth *a year*, ten times Acemoglu's figure, and the range across plausible inputs runs from 0.07 to 1.24 points. A second method, which assumes that AI will follow the path of electricity or of earlier digital technologies, gives 0.8 to 1.3 points a year. Both of their estimates, like Acemoglu's, leave out the possibility that AI automates the production of ideas as well as of goods and services, as their abstract notes. That possibility, AI speeding up research itself, drives the most dramatic scenarios discussed in Section 14.4.

| Input | Acemoglu (2024 working paper) | Aghion & Bunel (2024 baseline) |
|---|---|---|
| Share of tasks exposed to AI | 19.9% | 60% |
| Share of exposed tasks profitable to automate within ten years | 23% | 50% |
| Labour-cost saving in affected tasks | 27% | 40% |
| Labour share of costs in affected tasks | 0.57 | 0.57 |
| Implied TFP gain over ten years | ≈0.71% | ≈6.8% |
| Implied addition to annual TFP growth | ≈0.07 percentage points | ≈0.68 percentage points |

: Table 8.4: Two applications of the same task-based formula (TFP gain ≈ exposed share × profitable share × labour-cost saving × labour share) to the next ten years. Every input differs except the labour share, and the product of the differences is a tenfold gap. Acemoglu's figures and Aghion and Bunel's annual figure are as reported; their ten-year figure is the product of their inputs. Acemoglu's published version gives a slightly lower 0.66%. Source: @acemoglu2024simple; @aghion2024ai.

The Penn Wharton Budget Model at the University of Pennsylvania uses the same framework with an explicit diffusion path [@arnon2025projected]. It treats 40% of current US labour income as potentially exposed and assumes 23% of exposed tasks are automated. Labour-cost savings rise from about 25% to 40% as tools improve and spread at the pace of earlier technologies such as PCs and the internet. Its September 2025 projection has productivity and GDP 1.5% higher by 2035 and 3.7% higher by 2075 than without AI, with the largest contribution to TFP growth, about 0.2 percentage points, in 2032.

Estimates from financial firms and AI companies sit at the upper end. In research published by the investment bank Goldman Sachs in April 2023, its economists estimated that generative AI could raise global GDP by 7% and lift productivity growth by 1.5 percentage points over a ten-year period [@goldmansachs2023generative]. Anthropic's January 2026 report, using the company's own usage data, estimated that AI could add about 1.8 percentage points to annual US labour-productivity growth over the next decade, or about 1.0 to 1.2 points once task success rates are allowed for [@anthropic2026economic]. Both are estimates of labour productivity, which also rises when firms invest in more capital, and neither has been peer-reviewed.

### Why productivity statistics may lag

Even large eventual gains may not appear in official statistics for some time, and so far US data show no break in trend. Nonfarm business labour productivity grew 2.2% in the year to the second quarter of 2026. Since the end of 2019 it has grown at an annual rate of 2.1%, faster than the 1.5% of the 2007–2019 business cycle but equal to the average since 1947 [@bls2026productivity]. These aggregates cover every source of growth and cannot isolate AI's contribution. @brynjolfsson2021productivity describe a **productivity J-curve**. Firms adopting a general-purpose technology must make large complementary investments, in reorganising work, training staff and building data systems. These intangible investments are poorly measured, so measured productivity growth is at first *understated* and later, when the benefits are harvested, *overstated*. For computer hardware and software, they estimate that US TFP was 15.9% higher by the end of 2017 than official measures suggested. Humlum and Vestergaard read their Danish evidence, in which employers absorb chatbots by reorganising tasks and most users move saved time to other work, as consistent with the early, investment-heavy phase of such a curve [@humlum2025still]. A different gap needs no J-curve to explain it. Surveys find time savings of about 2% of all work hours, whereas experiments find gains of 15% or more within the tasks they study. The difference mostly reflects how few hours AI yet touches, since the survey figure averages over non-users and over tasks AI does not reach [@stlouisfed2026does].

## 8.6 Hidden labour and collective bargaining

### The work behind the machine

The figures so far count the people who use AI; they leave out those whose work builds it. AI systems depend on workers whom users rarely see. Models are trained and evaluated on data that people label, and the feedback training described in Chapter 3 relies on raters who compare and score model outputs. Mary Gray and Siddharth Suri call such task-by-task, platform-mediated labour **ghost work**. Their five-year study of on-demand workers in the United States and India found that many apparently automated services rely on people who are hired, managed and paid through software, often with few of the protections of standard employment [@gray2019ghost].

The best-documented case involves ChatGPT itself. In January 2023 an investigation by *TIME* reported that OpenAI had contracted Sama, an outsourcing firm, to have workers in Nairobi label text describing violence, hate speech and sexual abuse [@perrigo2023exclusive]. The labels trained a detector for such content that was later built into ChatGPT. According to *TIME*, the roughly three dozen workers took home between about $1.32 and $2 an hour, while OpenAI's contracts paid Sama $12.50 an hour, a rate Sama said covered all its costs. All four workers interviewed said the work had left them mentally scarred and described counselling as rare and unhelpful, which Sama partly disputed. Sama ended the work in February 2022, eight months early.

Systematic evidence points the same way. The Fairwork project at the Oxford Internet Institute scores online labour platforms out of ten against five principles: fair pay, conditions, contracts, management and representation. Its 2023 ratings covered 15 platforms. No platform scored above 5, and four scored zero. Microwork platforms supplying data annotation and model evaluation to AI companies "were among the lowest scores" [@fairwork2023work, p. 2]. Most demand for such work comes from clients in the Global North and most of the workforce is in the Global South. None of this labour appears in exposure indices or productivity experiments, which count the people who use AI, not those whose work goes into building it.

### Offshore work and who gains

The customer-support study of Section 8.3 is itself a study of offshore labour, since most of its agents worked in the Philippines [@brynjolfsson2025generative]. Its finding that new agents with the assistant matched experienced agents without it has two readings. For individual agents it means faster learning. For an outsourcing industry that competes partly on the experience of its workforce, it may mean that this advantage counts for less. Whether AI will reduce demand for the outsourced service work on which economies such as the Philippines and India depend has not yet been measured in the studies reviewed here, and whether gains reach agents as higher pay depends on wage-setting, which the study was not designed to measure.

### Collective bargaining

The clearest union response came from Hollywood. In 2023 the Writers Guild of America (WGA) struck for 148 days [@wga2023what]. The resulting agreement with the studios, covering 25 September 2023 to 1 May 2026, set rules for AI [@wga2023summary]. AI cannot write or rewrite literary material, and AI-generated material does not count as source material, so it cannot be used to undermine a writer's credit or to pay a lower rewrite fee [@wgaw2026artificial]. A writer may use AI with the company's consent, but the company cannot require it, and companies must disclose when material handed to a writer was generated by AI. The Guild reserved the right to argue that training AI on writers' work is prohibited.

The successor agreement, covering 2 May 2026 to 1 May 2030, "preserves all of the protections negotiated in 2023" and adds a duty to give the Guild written notice when companies license writers' work to train a commercial generative AI system. The Guild may then seek talks, including on pay [@wga2026summary]. Training data, left open in 2023, has thus become a subject of bargaining. The actors' union SAG-AFTRA ratified a four-year contract in June 2026 with more than 90% of votes, according to the Associated Press [@ap2026actors]. According to the union's board announcement, as reported by the trade publication SHOOT, it strengthens consent and compensation rules for AI and states that producers do not intend to use an AI-generated "synthetic" performer in a human role unless it adds "significant additional value" [@shoot2026sagaftra]. The contracts leave the technology in use but allocate control over it.

Other collective responses are smaller or less tested. In May 2023 more than 150 content moderators and data workers met in Nairobi and voted to form a union [@perrigo2023african]. In December 2023 the union federation AFL-CIO and Microsoft announced a partnership that, according to Microsoft, includes worker feedback to AI developers and a neutrality framework for future union organising [@microsoft2023aflcio].

## 8.7 Deskilling and the skills pipeline

A separate concern is that relying on AI may erode the skills of the people who use it. In a classic paper on industrial automation, @bainbridge1983ironies set out the **ironies of automation**. Automation leaves human operators the tasks designers could not automate, including monitoring and taking over when the system fails. Yet "physical skills deteriorate when they are not used" [@bainbridge1983ironies, sec. 1.1.1], so an experienced operator who has spent years watching an automated process may have become an inexperienced one by the time intervention is needed.

Evidence from medicine suggests a similar risk with AI. @budzyn2025endoscopist studied colonoscopies at four endoscopy centres in Poland that had introduced an AI system to help detect precancerous growths (adenomas). In a retrospective, observational analysis of 1,443 colonoscopies performed *without* AI assistance between September 2021 and March 2022, the adenoma detection rate fell from 28.4% in the months before AI was introduced to 22.4% afterwards. The authors concluded that continuous exposure to AI "might" reduce performance in unassisted procedures. The before-and-after design cannot exclude other changes over the same period. A later prospective trial with 13 endoscopists, using a related measure, found no deskilling in colonoscopies done after AI use ended [@pedersen2026learning].

For knowledge work, the cleanest test so far is a small randomised experiment reported in a preprint by Anthropic researchers [@shen2026how]. Fifty-two programmers with at least a year of Python experience learned an asynchronous programming library they had not used before, half with an AI assistant. The AI group was not significantly faster, and on a quiz afterwards, taken without AI, it scored 17% lower, about two grade points, with weaker conceptual understanding, code reading and debugging. Participants who delegated the coding entirely gained some speed at the cost of learning the library; three of the six patterns of use the authors identified, all involving active engagement such as asking conceptual questions, preserved learning. Chapter 10 discusses comparable findings on learning in education.

Deskilling matters for the economy as well as for safety, because expertise is built by doing routine work. The payroll evidence in Section 8.4 suggests that fewer junior workers are being hired into exposed occupations. If they no longer perform the tasks through which they once learned, the supply of future experts able to supervise AI may narrow. The evidence on learning is mixed. In customer support, the authors find evidence that AI assistance "facilitates worker learning" [@brynjolfsson2025generative]; in a small coding experiment, help from AI reduced what programmers learned about a new library [@shen2026how]; and the endoscopy trial found neither deskilling nor upskilling [@pedersen2026learning]. Neither the payroll data nor the PwC advertisement analysis can show that this pipeline is being damaged [@pwc2026global]; they show only that the conditions for it exist.

## 8.8 Inequality, distribution and policy

### Who gains?

Within tasks, AI usually narrows gaps, as in customer support, professional writing and software development (Section 8.3); the Kenyan experiment, where users had to judge open-ended advice, is the exception [@otis2026uneven]. Compression within a task does not imply compression across the economy, because the value of the task itself may fall. @acemoglu2025simple shows that AI can increase inequality even when it raises the productivity of low-skill workers in some tasks. Empirically he finds AI's exposure more evenly spread across demographic groups than earlier automation, so it is unlikely to raise inequality as much, but no evidence that it will reduce labour-income inequality. He predicts a widening gap between income from capital and from labour. The IMF note similarly warns that higher returns to capital could increase wealth inequality [@cazzaniga2024genai]. David Autor has argued the opposite possibility. Because AI can support expert judgement, it could let more workers take on higher-stakes decisions now reserved for elite experts in medicine, law or software and, "if used well", help restore middle-skill work [@autor2024applying].

Exposure is unevenly distributed across groups and countries. In high-income countries, according to the ILO–NASK index, jobs in the highest exposure gradient account for 9.6% of female employment but only 3.5% of male employment [@ilo2025one; @gmyrek2025generative]. The IMF finds that women and college-educated workers are more exposed but also better placed to benefit, and that older workers may find it harder to adapt. Advanced economies are more exposed but also better prepared, which could widen income gaps between countries [@cazzaniga2024genai].

Workers themselves are uneasy. In a Pew Research Center survey of US workers in October 2024, 52% said they were worried about the future impact of AI use in the workplace and 36% that they were hopeful [@lin2025us].

### The policy response

Governments have responded mainly through existing institutions, with a few targeted rules. The most concrete is the European Union's AI Act, whose wider structure Chapter 13 describes. It classifies as "high-risk" AI systems used to recruit or select workers, to make decisions on promotion or termination, to allocate tasks on the basis of individual behaviour or traits, and to monitor and evaluate workers' performance, uses often grouped under the name **algorithmic management** [@europeanparliament2024regulation, Annex III, point 4]. Employers deploying such systems must inform workers' representatives and the affected workers before using them [@europeanparliament2024regulation, art. 26(7)]. The Digital Omnibus on AI, the EU's 2026 amending regulation to the AI Act (Section 13.2), deferred the application of these high-risk obligations from 2 August 2026 to 2 December 2027 [@europeanparliament2026regulation].

Beyond specific rules, the main policy positions are best told apart by the question each one asks. One asks *which technologies are built*. In a 2023 policy memo, Acemoglu, Autor and Johnson argue that the private sector is pursuing a path that emphasises automation and workplace surveillance. They propose equalising tax rates on employing workers and on owning equipment and algorithms, limiting workplace surveillance, and funding research on technologies that complement workers [@acemoglu2023can]. Others put more weight on measuring effects before acting; the Yale Budget Lab, for example, stresses that "better data is needed" [@gimbel2025evaluating].

The US government's AI Action Plan of July 2025 is concerned instead with *how fast AI spreads*, and commits to removing "red tape and onerous regulation" [@whitehouse2025winning]. Its labour response is a "worker-first" agenda built on existing institutions: AI skills in training and apprenticeship programmes, retraining for displaced workers, and an AI Workforce Research Hub in the Department of Labor. On this view the state's task is to help workers move, not to shape the technology.

Collective bargaining addresses *who controls AI's use at work*. Agreements by sector, like the writers' contracts of 2023 and 2026, can fit rules to particular tasks [@wgaw2026artificial; @wga2026summary], and the AI Act's duty to inform workers' representatives gives it a legal foothold in the EU [@europeanparliament2024regulation, art. 26(7)]. It reaches only organised workers, which excludes most of the platform workers described in Section 8.6 [@fairwork2023work].

Proposals for redistribution start from *who bears the losses*. @korinek2019artificial show in simple economic models that, under plausible conditions, governments can tax the gains from AI without distorting incentives and use the revenue to compensate those who would otherwise lose. In a 2021 essay, Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, proposed an "American Equity Fund" paying out to every adult citizen, financed by an annual tax of 2.5% on the value of large companies and of land [@altman2021moores]. The most direct evidence on unconditional payments comes from a trial not designed with AI in mind. In a large US experiment, 1,000 low-income people received $1,000 a month for three years and 2,000 received $50 a month [@vivalt2026employment]. The larger payments reduced labour-market participation by 4.2 percentage points and working hours by one to two hours a week. Leisure rose most, and the quality of employment did not improve.

In the author's summary of this chapter's evidence, the best evidence sits early in the chain of Figure 8.1. Exposure can be scored for every occupation, and task-level gains have been measured in trials. The later links, from use to firms' choices to aggregate output, are still thinly observed. Measured use takes only a small share of work hours, the large gains of the experiments shrink or reverse for experts on complex work they know well and for users who must judge open-ended advice, and US productivity has yet to depart from its long-run trend. Where change is visible it lies in the content of jobs and possibly in the hiring of young workers into exposed occupations, while in the Danish records average earnings and hours have so far held steady. Whether that reorganisation ends in faster growth, a narrower path into expert work or both will depend on how tools are designed, how their use is bargained over and how gains are shared. Those are the questions on which the policy positions above divide.

## Further reading

- Acemoglu, D. & Restrepo, P. (2019). *Automation and New Tasks: How Technology Displaces and Reinstates Labor*. A clear, non-technical statement of the task-based framework on which exposure measures and macro forecasts are built. [@acemoglu2019automation]
- Brynjolfsson, E., Li, D. & Raymond, L. (2025). *Generative AI at Work*. The most detailed field study of AI in a real workplace, with a careful account of how a quasi-experimental design is tested. [@brynjolfsson2025generative]
- Becker, J. et al. (2025). *Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity*. A randomised trial whose result shows why expectations are a poor guide to effects; read it with METR's 2026 follow-up note on selection. [@becker2025measuring]
- Humlum, A. & Vestergaard, E. (2026). *Still Waters, Rapid Currents: Early Labor Market Transformation under Generative AI*. Links surveys to administrative records to show work being reorganised while earnings and hours stay flat. [@humlum2025still]
- Acemoglu, D. (2025). *The Simple Macroeconomics of AI*. A transparent macroeconomic estimate whose assumptions can be inspected and changed one by one. [@acemoglu2025simple]
- Gray, M. L. & Suri, S. (2019). *Ghost Work: How to Stop Silicon Valley from Building a New Global Underclass*. An ethnographic and survey study of the hidden on-demand workers behind apparently automated services. [@gray2019ghost]


# Chapter 9: Information, Media and Democracy

On 21 January 2024, two days before the New Hampshire presidential primary in the United States, an estimated tens of thousands of Democratic voters received a telephone call in a voice that sounded like President Joe Biden [@barrington2025people]. The voice had been cloned with generative AI, and the message urged recipients to "save your vote for the November election" instead of voting in the primary. The US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) traced the calls to a political consultant, Steve Kramer, and proposed a $6 million fine against him for unlawfully spoofing caller identification [@fcc2024proposes]. It confirmed the fine in a forfeiture order adopted on 26 September 2024 [@fcc2024issues]. In a separate state criminal trial, according to the Associated Press, a New Hampshire jury acquitted him in June 2025 of all voter-suppression and candidate-impersonation charges [@associatedpress2025new].

The episode compresses the main questions about AI and the information ecosystem into one case. The fake was cheap. According to a 2025 study, the audio was made with ElevenLabs, a commercial service offering "instant voice cloning for as little as $5 a month" [@barrington2025people]. In listening experiments, people cannot reliably tell such clones from real voices (Section 9.2) [@barrington2025people]. Its effect on turnout is, in the author's view, unknowable, because nobody can count the people who stayed at home. And the first federal response came from a telecoms regulator using existing law. In February 2024, citing the New Hampshire calls, the FCC declared that AI-generated voices count as "artificial" voices under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act, so that such calls need the prior consent of the person called [@fcc2024implications]. The fine itself was for spoofing caller identification [@fcc2024issues].

## 9.1 How synthetic media is made, and what cheapness changes

**Synthetic media** is any image, audio, video or text generated or substantially altered by AI. A **deepfake** is synthetic media that realistically depicts a real person, place or event in a way that could be mistaken for authentic [@chesney2019deep]. The EU's AI Act defines a deep fake as AI-generated or manipulated image, audio or video content that resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events and "would falsely appear to a person to be authentic or truthful" [@europeanparliament2024regulation, Article 3(60)]. A **cheap fake** is a misleading edit that relies on cheap, accessible software or none at all, such as slowing down a video or presenting real footage out of context [@paris2019deepfakes]. Researchers also distinguish **misinformation** (false information shared without intent to harm) from **disinformation** (false information knowingly created or shared to cause harm) [@wardle2017information], and both from **influence operations**, "covert or deceptive efforts to influence the opinions of a target audience", run by governments and other actors, often through inauthentic accounts [@goldstein2023generative].

### Images and video: diffusion models

Many image generators are **diffusion models**. The method, set out by Ho, Jain and Abbeel in 2020, has two halves [@ho2020denoising]. In training, a real image is gradually destroyed by adding small amounts of random (Gaussian) noise over many steps (1,000 in their model). After the last step less than 1% of the original image's signal remains, and the result is practically indistinguishable from pure noise. A neural network is trained on large numbers of such corrupted images to solve one narrow task: given a noisy image and the step number, predict the noise that was added. Generation runs the process backwards. The model starts from pure noise and, step by step, removes part of its own estimate of the noise, until an image emerges that looks as if it came from the training distribution.

Rombach and colleagues made text-to-image generation practical by running the process on a compressed "latent" representation of the image instead of its pixels, which cut computing costs substantially, and by letting a text prompt steer each denoising step through cross-attention, a variant of the attention mechanism described in Chapter 3 [@rombach2022high]. This **latent diffusion** design made high-resolution text-to-image generation affordable outside the largest laboratories. Later systems changed the recipe. Stable Diffusion 3 replaced the curved path from noise to image with a straight-line "rectified flow" and used a transformer as the network [@esser2024scaling], and OpenAI describes the image generator it built into GPT-4o in 2025 as autoregressive, producing an image piece by piece much as a language model writes text [@openai2025addendum].

### Voices: speech as a language-modelling problem

Voice cloning followed a parallel path. Microsoft's VALL-E, described in 2023 and published in a journal in 2025, converts speech into sequences of discrete codes using a neural audio codec, then trains a language model to predict those codes much as a text model predicts words. It could imitate an unseen speaker from "only a 3-second enrolled recording" used as a prompt, preserving the speaker's emotional tone and acoustic surroundings [@chen2025neural]. By 2024 such methods were consumer products. In one study, Barrington, Cooper and Farid built clones of more than 200 speakers with the ElevenLabs "Instant Voice Cloning" service [@barrington2025people].

### What cheapness changes, and what it does not

The common thread is cost. Generative AI mainly changes one part of the information system, the cost of producing plausible content. In a 2023 preprint, Goldstein and colleagues argued that language models could make influence operations cheaper, larger and harder to attribute. They located four points where intervention is possible: how models are built, who can access them, how content is disseminated and how audiences form beliefs [@goldstein2023generative]. The question is whether cheaper production translates into more influence. The companies' own reports show adoption rising steeply. In December 2024 Meta reported that the covert influence networks it had taken down made "only incremental productivity and content-generation gains" from generative AI [@clegg2024what]. Its August 2026 threat report said that AI-generated content had moved "from an occasional tactic" to "a near-standard component of influence operation tradecraft". Every network in that report used generative AI in some form, from profile photos to automated video production, yet the company reported that "behavioral detection approaches remain effective" against them [@meta2026adversarial]. OpenAI said in October 2026 that two operations it had banned, from Russia and Iran, had used its models to make routine work easier, and that planting stories in established media outlets appeared to reach more people than fake social media accounts [@openai2026disrupting; @huo2026openai]. These are accounts by the platforms of misuse of their own products. Evidence of effects on audiences is thinner. The 2026 International AI Safety Report, written by more than 100 independent experts chaired by Yoshua Bengio, found that in experiments AI systems are often at least as effective as non-expert humans at changing people's views, but that real-world use of AI to influence people "is documented but not yet widespread" [@bengio2026international, sec. 2.1.2]. So far, adoption has become near universal among the operations that platforms catch, while evidence that it has bought them more influence is scarce.

The reason, according to a strand of research on misinformation, is that production was never the binding constraint. In an essay for the Knight First Amendment Institute, Kapoor and Narayanan (2024) argue that AI lowers the cost of creating false content but not the cost of distributing it. Misinformation, they argue, spreads mainly because of demand, as people seek out claims that fit what they already believe [@kapoor2024looked]. Altay, Berriche and Acerbi (2023) reach a similar conclusion from the research literature. People do not believe everything they see online, and misinformation largely "preaches to the choir", reaching those who already agree [@altay2023misinformation]. The picture is complicated by AI that can hold a conversation, adapting to each person's objections as static content cannot (Section 9.5), and by generative models that have become distribution channels themselves, from search summaries to chatbots that answer questions about the news (Section 9.7).

## 9.2 Detection: why people and machines struggle

### Human judgement

In laboratory tests, people are poor judges of synthetic media. In a pre-registered experiment with 210 participants, Köbis, Doležalová and Soraperra (2021) found that people could not reliably tell deepfake videos from real ones; neither raising awareness nor paying for correct answers improved accuracy, and participants overestimated their own ability [@kobis2021fooled]. Nightingale and Farid (2022) showed participants a mix of real photographs of faces and faces generated by StyleGAN2. Accuracy was 48.2%, no better than a coin toss, and training with feedback raised it only to 59.0%. Synthetic faces were even rated more trustworthy than real ones [@nightingale2022ai].

Voices are no easier. Barrington and colleagues ran perceptual studies with 604 listeners. Participants judged a cloned voice to belong to the same person as the real recording "approximately 80% of the time", and correctly identified a voice as AI-generated "only about 60% of the time" [@barrington2025people]. For video, Groh and colleagues (2022) found in online studies with 15,016 participants that ordinary viewers were about as accurate as the leading computer-vision detector. Showing them the model's prediction improved average accuracy, but when the model was wrong it often led people astray [@groh2022deepfake].

### Automated detectors

Automated detectors are classifiers trained on examples of real and generated media to pick up statistical traces that generators leave behind. On academic benchmarks they often score well. Performance is usually reported as the AUC, the ranking score defined in Section 2.8: here, the probability that the detector gives a randomly chosen fake a higher "fake" score than a randomly chosen genuine item, so that 1.0 is perfect and 0.5 is guessing [@hanley1982meaning; @chandra2025deepfake].

The problem is **distribution shift**: a detector learns the fingerprints of the generators in its training data, and new generators leave different ones. A 2025 preprint by Chandra and colleagues at the non-profit TrueMedia.org tested this directly. They assembled Deepfake-Eval-2024, a set of video, audio and images circulating on social media in 2024, from 88 websites in 52 languages. Compared with their scores on older academic benchmarks, the AUC of open-source detectors fell by roughly half in every medium. The best open-source model in any modality reached an AUC of 0.58, and many were close to 0.5. Commercial detectors from seven vendors did better, but none reached 90% accuracy, which the authors treat as a lower bound for what trained human forensic analysts achieve on the same material [@chandra2025deepfake].

Better engineering will not remove the next obstacles, because they are structural. Detection is an adversarial game. Saberi and colleagues proved, for classifier-based detectors of AI-generated images, a trade-off between robustness (resisting small perturbations) and reliability (catching fakes with few false alarms) that sharpens as real and fake images become more alike [@saberi2024robustness]. A generator's developer, or anyone with access to a detector, can test outputs against it and adjust them until they pass. Base rates compound the problem. Consider an illustrative detector, the author's example, that flags 99% of fakes and wrongly flags only 1% of genuine items. Applied to a platform's stream of one million genuine videos and one thousand fakes, it would catch 990 fakes but also flag 10,000 genuine videos, so that more than nine in ten alarms would be false. Detection of AI-written *text* faces the same problems in sharper form. A test of 14 tools found them "neither accurate nor reliable" [@weberwulff2023testing], and Chapter 10 discusses evidence on their bias against non-native English writers.

## 9.3 Watermarks and provenance: labelling at the source

If synthetic content cannot reliably be recognised after the fact, an alternative is to mark it when it is made. **Watermarking** hides a signal in AI-generated content at the moment of creation, so that software holding the right key can later recognise it [@kirchenbauer2023watermark]. **Content provenance** attaches a cryptographically signed record of where content came from and how it was edited [@c2pa2025c2pa]. The two answer different questions, and they fail in different ways (Table 9.1).

### Text watermarks: the green-list scheme and SynthID

The best-studied text watermark was proposed by Kirchenbauer and colleagues in 2023 [@kirchenbauer2023watermark]. Its logic is statistical, and the Deeper box below works through it with the paper's own numbers.

::: {.box .deeper}
**Going deeper: How a text watermark is embedded and detected**

A language model writes by repeatedly choosing the next token (a word or word fragment). In the scheme of Kirchenbauer and colleagues, a secret key and the preceding token are fed into a hash function before each choice. The function splits the vocabulary pseudo-randomly into a "green list" containing a fraction γ (gamma) of all tokens and a "red list" containing the rest. The model then adds a bonus δ (delta) to the scores of green tokens before sampling. Where many words would fit, this tilts the choice towards green ones; where one word is almost certain, such as the second half of a name, the bonus barely matters and quality is preserved [@kirchenbauer2023watermark].

A detector that knows the key recomputes the green list at every position and counts green tokens. Unwatermarked text should contain about γ*T* green tokens in a passage of *T* tokens, with a standard deviation of √(*T*γ(1 − γ)). The test statistic *z* is the excess count divided by that standard deviation. With γ = 0.5 and *T* = 200, chance predicts 100 green tokens with a standard deviation of about 7.1. The authors flag text as watermarked when *z* exceeds 4, which happens at about 128 green tokens and corresponds to a false-positive probability of 3 in 100,000. In their tests with δ = 2, watermarked 200-token passages contained 159.5 green tokens on average, far above the threshold, and 98.4% of them were detected [@kirchenbauer2023watermark]. The failures were mostly low-entropy passages, such as memorised text, where the model had little freedom to choose green words.
:::

Google DeepMind's SynthID-Text, published in *Nature* in 2024, uses a different embedding method called tournament sampling. The model proposes many candidate tokens, which compete in a knockout tournament. In each round a pseudo-random function keyed to the four preceding tokens scores the candidates, and the final winner is emitted. Detection again needs the key but not the model [@dathathri2024scalable]. In a live experiment on nearly 20 million Gemini chatbot responses, users rated watermarked and unwatermarked answers equally well. The authors released the code openly and listed the limits themselves: watermarks are weakened by paraphrasing, they work less well in low-entropy text, and they require "coordination between actors running the LLM text generation services" [@dathathri2024scalable]. Google also applies SynthID to images and video, a scheme described in a 2025 preprint by its researchers [@gowal2025synthidimage]. In October 2026 it opened a public SynthID Detector for images, video and audio from Google and partners including OpenAI and Nvidia, with Apple to follow, and said it had watermarked more than 180 billion images and videos [@kohli2026were].

### How robust are watermarks?

Robustness is the central technical weakness. Kirchenbauer and colleagues themselves tested an attack in which a second, smaller language model (T5-Large) replaced randomly chosen words in watermarked 200-token passages. Measured by the AUC, replacing 10% of tokens barely mattered and replacing 30% only modestly (Figure 9.1). At the fixed threshold a deployed detector would use (*z* = 4), the damage was larger. Only about a third of passages with 30% of their tokens replaced were still flagged, but the text had become markedly less fluent [@kirchenbauer2023watermark]. Crude word replacement thus removes the watermark only by damaging the text. Fluent paraphrasing is a stronger attack, as the next paragraph shows. The authors' own follow-up found, however, that watermarks often survive paraphrasing by people or machines once enough text is available, because paraphrases leak fragments of the original. After strong human paraphrasing, about 800 tokens were needed on average for a confident detection [@kirchenbauer2024reliability]. Watermarks are therefore most useful for long texts and least useful for short ones, such as a social media post.

![Figure 9.1: Trade-off between removing a text watermark and preserving text quality. A smaller model (T5-Large) replaced words in 500 watermarked passages of about 200 tokens, up to a growing share of the tokens. Detection quality (AUC, left axis; 0.5 = chance) falls as more words are replaced, while perplexity (right axis; higher = less fluent text) rises from 6.3 to 33.9. At the paper's detection threshold (*z* = 4), the share of watermarked passages still flagged falls faster than the AUC suggests: from 98.4% unattacked to 82% at a 10% replacement rate and 35% at 30%. Watermark settings γ = 0.5, δ = 2.0, multinomial sampling. Source: @kirchenbauer2023watermark.](../figures/svg/fig-09-01.svg){#fig:09-01}

Later work found more economical attacks. Zhang and colleagues proved that, under natural assumptions, no watermark can be "strong", meaning impossible to remove without degrading quality. An attacker with a way to judge quality and a way to make small random changes can always walk the text away from the watermark while keeping it good. The authors argue that both can be supplied by a model weaker than the watermarked one, because judging and lightly rewriting text is easier than writing it, so a small model can launder a frontier model's output [@zhang2024watermarks]. Jovanović, Staab and Vechev showed that an attacker can partly reverse-engineer a green-list-style watermark by querying the model's public interface and studying its outputs. With that knowledge the attacker can both strip the watermark from text ("scrubbing") and make text of the attacker's choosing appear watermarked ("spoofing"). For "under $50", they reached average success rates above 80% against schemes previously considered safe [@jovanovic2024watermark]. Image watermarks face analogous limits. Saberi and colleagues showed that "diffusion purification", adding noise to a watermarked image and letting a diffusion model clean it up, removes watermarks that make only subtle changes to an image, while stronger watermarks can be defeated by an attack on a substitute model. Spoofing works here too. A watermarked noise pattern can be added to real photographs so that they are wrongly flagged as AI-generated [@saberi2024robustness].

Watermarks also depend on who controls them. A watermark exists only if the generator adds it, and open-weight models (Chapter 7) can be run without one. And the detector key is a security asset. If it is widely shared, attackers can test their evasion against it; if it is held tightly, as with SynthID, whose checks run through Google's own tools, outside verification depends on the company. According to The Next Web, OpenAI began adding SynthID to images from ChatGPT and its API in May 2026, alongside Content Credentials, and previewed a public checker for its own images [@constantin2026openai]. This is the kind of cross-company coordination the SynthID authors said watermarks need.

### Content Credentials: how C2PA provenance works

Provenance starts from the opposite assumption. Instead of trying to prove that content is fake, it lets honest sources prove where their content came from. The main standard is maintained by the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA), founded in February 2021 by Adobe, Arm, the BBC, Intel, Microsoft and Truepic [@microsoft2021technology]. Its signed provenance records are called "Content Credentials" [@c2pa2025c2pa].

Specification version 2.2 (May 2025) sets out how it works [@c2pa2025content]. When a camera or AI tool creates a file, it attaches a signed record of who made it and how; for AI output, the record states that the content was generated by a trained algorithm. Each later edit adds a new signed record that keeps the earlier ones, so the file carries its own history. Any change made outside this chain, even to a single pixel, breaks the seal, and validation fails. The record is easily stripped, for instance when a platform re-encodes an upload, so the standard also lets a watermark or fingerprint point to a copy kept online. Signers are identified by certificates that the coalition's default trust list expects to be issued to hardware or software, not to a person. Version 2.0 (January 2024) removed identified humans from the metadata, a choice relevant to photographers and witnesses whose safety depends on anonymity [@c2pa2025content]. And the coalition states plainly that provenance "cannot tell you whether the digital content is true, accurate or factual" [@c2pa2025c2pa]. Figure 9.2 shows the pipeline.

::: {.box .deeper}
**Going deeper: Inside a C2PA manifest**

Each signed record is a **manifest**. It contains **assertions**, labelled statements about the content. One records what was done to the file, starting with a "created" action (or "opened", when an existing file is edited), and for AI output gives the source type `trainedAlgorithmicMedia`. Others list the earlier files from which this one was composed, with their own manifests copied in. A **claim** lists every assertion by its cryptographic hash and is signed with a certificate, the public-key technology that secures web browsing. A trusted time-stamp lets the signature be checked after the certificate expires. A **hard binding**, a hash of the file's bytes, ties the manifest to the content, which is why changing a single pixel breaks the match. A **soft binding**, a watermark or perceptual fingerprint, survives re-encoding and can be used to find a stored copy of the manifest. The specification insists that soft bindings "shall not be used as a hard binding" [@c2pa2025content].
:::

![Figure 9.2: A simplified content provenance pipeline (C2PA Content Credentials). A camera or AI tool creates content and signs a manifest whose actions begin with “created”; an editing step adds a new signed manifest (“opened”) that keeps the earlier file and its manifest as an ingredient; a validator checks the signatures, certificates and hashes, including whether the hard binding still matches the file. Inside each manifest, a claim lists every assertion by its hash and is digitally signed and time-stamped. If the manifest is stripped, a soft binding (watermark or fingerprint) can be used to find a copy in a cloud repository. Provenance shows where content came from, not whether it is true. Schematic by the author, based on @c2pa2025content and @c2pa2025c2pa.](../figures/svg/fig-09-02.svg){#fig:09-02}

Adoption has moved from software to hardware. In September 2025 Google announced that the Pixel 10 phones attach Content Credentials to every JPEG photograph taken with the built-in camera app, not only to AI-edited images. It said the app had the highest security rating then defined by the C2PA, using keys protected by the phone's security chip. The company gave an explicit reason for signing everything. If only synthetic content is labelled, users come to believe that unlabelled content is authentic, which Google described, citing research, as "the implied truth effect" [@lynch2025how]. That effect is well documented for fact-check labels. In an experiment with 5,271 participants, Pennycook and colleagues found that attaching warnings to some false headlines made untagged false headlines seem more accurate. Marking some true headlines as verified removed the effect [@pennycook2020implied]. Apple took a different route. On its iPhone 18 Pro, announced in September 2026, an opt-in mode signs the camera's sensor data and keeps an unalterable "reference image" to compare with edited versions. The announcement did not mention C2PA, but said Apple would add support for Google's SynthID watermark in a later software update [@apple2026apple].

Provenance has its own limits. It works only where cameras, editing tools, platforms and browsers read and display the credentials, and a signed record that a photograph came from a particular phone does not show that the scene was not staged. Attaching credentials is optional, and the coalition does not intend content without them to be treated as less trustworthy [@c2pa2025c2pa], so their absence proves nothing. The seal is also only as good as its implementation. A 2026 security analysis, a preprint, found that the specification's "exclusion range", which lets parts of a file be left out of the hash, allows alterations that validators do not detect, and that validators disagreed on time-stamps and could accept compromised certificates [@golaszewski2026verifying]. Provenance is therefore strongest for sources that choose to sign, such as news agencies and official bodies, and weakest at exposing fakes from those that do not.

| | Post-hoc detection | Watermarking | Provenance (C2PA) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Question answered | Does this look AI-made? | Did a participating generator make this? | Who signed this, and what was done to it? |
| Needs cooperation of | Nobody | The generator's developer | Creators, tools and platforms |
| Typical failure | New generators (distribution shift); base-rate false alarms | Paraphrase or regeneration; open models without marks; spoofing | Metadata stripped; low adoption; staged content signed honestly |
| Evidence | Best open-source AUC 0.58 on 2024 in-the-wild content | Removable or forgeable for under $50 in some schemes; quality cost for crude attacks | Hash binding breaks on any change; soft binding needed to survive re-encoding |

: Table 9.1: Three technical approaches to identifying synthetic or authentic content. Source: [@chandra2025deepfake; @jovanovic2024watermark; @kirchenbauer2023watermark; @c2pa2025content].

## 9.4 Deepfakes and the 2024 election year

### What monitoring found

In 2024 voters went to the polls in the United States, India, Indonesia, Mexico, the United Kingdom, the European Union and many other places [@clegg2024what]. Many commentators predicted that generative AI would flood these campaigns with deceptive content [@kapoor2024looked]. The evidence gathered since points towards a limited measurable impact on results, with important caveats about what can be measured [@stockwell2024threat; @stockwell2024ai].

The most systematic monitoring came from the Alan Turing Institute's Centre for Emerging Technology and Security (CETaS). Its September 2024 briefing paper on the UK general election, the French legislative elections and the European Parliament elections identified "just 16 confirmed viral cases" of AI-enabled disinformation or deepfakes during the UK election and "only 11" across the EU and French elections combined. It found "no evidence" that they "meaningfully impacted" any result [@stockwell2024threat]. The institute's November 2024 report on the US election likewise reported a "lack of evidence" of a measurable impact on the result. It attributed this "primarily" to "insufficient data" on real-world voter behaviour. It recorded "far higher – albeit still relatively moderate – volumes" of viral AI-enabled disinformation in the US campaign than in the earlier elections. It also warned that users' uncertainty about what was authentic had "damaged trust in the integrity of online sources" [@stockwell2024ai].

Platform data point the same way. Meta reported that ratings of AI content about elections, politics and social topics made up "less than 1%" of all misinformation fact-checked by its partners during the major elections of 2024 [@clegg2024what]. That figure covers only content that fact-checkers chose to examine.

### Cheap fakes outnumbered deepfakes

Kapoor and Narayanan (2024) analysed 78 election-related uses of AI collected by WIRED's AI Elections Project. Half of them (39) showed no deceptive intent. They included parody and satire, and campaigns using AI openly, for example to translate a speech. For each of the 39 deceptive cases, the authors estimated that similar content could have been produced without AI for no more than a few hundred dollars. They also cited a count by the News Literacy Project in which cheap fakes were used about seven times as often as AI-generated content in the US election [@kapoor2024looked]. The bottleneck for a would-be deceiver in 2024 was reach and credibility, not the technical ability to fabricate.

### The liar's dividend

A subtler effect works through authentic content. When the public knows that convincing fakes exist, a person caught on a genuine recording can claim that it was faked. Chesney and Citron (2019) called this the **liar's dividend** and noted, perversely, that it grows as public education about deepfakes succeeds, because a sceptical public is more willing to doubt real evidence [@chesney2019deep].

Schiff, Schiff and Bueno (2025) tested the idea in five survey experiments with more than 15,000 American adults. Participants read about real scandals involving politicians, followed by a hypothetical response in which the politician claimed the story was fake. Both strategies tested, sowing uncertainty and rallying supporters against the accusers, raised support for the politician across partisan groups, and both worked better than staying silent or apologising. The claims were effective against text-based reports but "largely ineffective against video evidence", and they did not reduce general trust in the media [@schiff2025liars]. The dividend exists, then, but video still carried more evidential weight than text when the experiments were run. In the author's view, that is the margin most likely to erode as video generation improves.

::: {.box .debate}
**Debate: Were fears about AI and the 2024 elections overblown?**

*Largely, yes.* Simon, Altay and Mercier (2023) argued before the election year that supply of false content was never the main constraint on misinformation; attention and belief are [@simon2023misinformation]. Reviews of the misinformation literature find that false content mostly "preaches to the choir", reaching people who already agree with it [@altay2023misinformation]. The 2024 record set out above fits their view, with a few dozen viral AI cases, no measurable effect on any result, and cheap fakes that far outnumbered AI content [@stockwell2024threat; @stockwell2024ai; @kapoor2024looked].

*Not proven.* Every one of these sources measures visible content, not effects on behaviour. The WIRED database that Kapoor and Narayanan analysed contains only uses that someone detected and reported, so undetected deepfakes are excluded by construction, and a cost estimate for one item says little about campaigns of thousands of personalised items, the scale that worried Goldstein and colleagues. CETaS itself said the US finding reflected "insufficient data", and monitoring covered mainly the UK, France, the EU and the US. The cheapest harm, eroding confidence that any evidence is real, is the hardest to count, yet it is the one that survey experiments on the liar's dividend show can benefit politicians [@schiff2025liars]. Private conversations with chatbots, which experiments show can shift attitudes (Section 9.5), are invisible to monitoring of public posts [@kapoor2024looked; @goldstein2023generative; @stockwell2024ai; @hackenburg2025levers]. In the author's view, settling the question would take panel data, across several elections, linking individuals' exposure to AI-generated content to later changes in their knowledge, trust and turnout.
:::

Later elections showed more AI use but no clearer evidence of effects. Hungary showed that heavy use does not guarantee success. According to analysts at the Political Capital Institute, a Budapest think tank, no EU campaign had yet used AI as heavily as the governing Fidesz party did before Hungary's parliamentary election in April 2026. It circulated AI-generated videos and images, for example showing the opposition leader Péter Magyar as a puppet of Ukraine's president, and lost. In the institute's March survey of 1,000 adults, 52% of those who had seen deepfake videos were unsure whether a video was authentic. The authors credit the result mainly to a credible challenger and voter fatigue with government messaging [@kreko2026hungarys]. Colombia showed AI becoming ordinary campaign material. The EU election observation mission's final report described "frequent disinformation and an unprecedented use of AI and deepfakes" in the June 2026 presidential run-off, but found that AI's "most notable use was as a campaign tool", producing campaign advertising at a speed and cost unfeasible shortly before. Much of this content was not deceptive, and the mission found major regulatory and oversight gaps [@euelectionobservationmission2026final].

The United States and Brazil showed the regulatory gap and one attempt to close it. In the 2026 US midterms, according to Reuters, deepfakes became an open campaign tool. National Republican committees ran ads, labelled in small print, in which AI versions of Democratic candidates spoke; no federal rule applied, and 28 states had laws on AI in political ads, mostly requiring disclosure [@ax2026ai]. Brazil, whose presidential run-off falls on 25 October 2026, went furthest. According to CNN Brasil, its electoral court requires prominent labels on AI campaign material, bans new synthetic content from 72 hours before a vote and forbids AI systems to recommend candidates [@cnnbrasil2026tse]. The most consequential interference of the period, however, did not depend mainly on generative AI. The annulment of Romania's 2024 presidential election, discussed in Section 9.8, turned on the alleged coordinated amplification of content by platform accounts and undisclosed paid promotion [@solea2024romanias].

## 9.5 AI as a persuader

### The baseline: persuasion is hard

Political scientists have long found that changing voters' minds during a general election is difficult. Kalla and Broockman (2018) combined a meta-analysis of 40 field experiments with nine new experiments of their own and concluded that the best estimate of the effect of campaign contact and advertising on Americans' candidate choices in general elections is zero. In primaries and ballot-measure campaigns, where party labels give voters no cue, the field experiments they reviewed did find persuasive effects [@kalla2018minimal]. Any claim that AI is unusually persuasive has to be read against that baseline, with one caution. Kalla and Broockman measured vote choice after real campaign contact, while the AI studies below are survey experiments that measure attitudes on 0–100 scales, so the baseline sets expectations rather than a common yardstick. In this section "points" are points on such scales, not percentage points, unless stated otherwise.

### Static messages: as good as humans, little more

The first generation of studies examined static messages: a fixed text that every participant reads. Goldstein and colleagues (2024) gave 8,221 US respondents either nothing, a real article from a foreign covert propaganda campaign, or an article on the same thesis written by GPT-3. Among respondents who read no article, 24.4% agreed with the propaganda thesis. Reading the original propaganda raised agreement to 47.4%, and reading the GPT-3 version raised it to 43.5%. With an English speaker editing the prompts or selecting the outputs, GPT-3 articles were under some conditions as persuasive as the originals [@goldstein2024persuasive].

Later studies found that neither tailoring nor model scale adds much to a static message. Hackenburg and Margetts (2024) had GPT-4 tailor messages on four political issues to each participant's self-reported demographic and political data in real time. In a pre-registered experiment with 8,587 participants, these **microtargeted** messages moved opinion by 4.83 percentage points against 6.20 points for generic GPT-4 messages, a difference that was not statistically significant (*P* = 0.226) [@hackenburg2024evaluating]. Hackenburg and colleagues (2025) then generated 720 messages on ten US policy issues with 24 language models of very different sizes and tested them on 25,982 participants. Persuasiveness showed "sharply diminishing returns" to model size. Once the authors adjusted for basic task completion (staying coherent and on topic), the association between size and persuasiveness was no longer statistically significant [@hackenburg2025scaling]. For static text, frontier models appeared to be close to a ceiling.

### Conversation is different

The picture changed when AI was allowed to talk back. Costello, Pennycook and Rand (2024) asked people who believed a conspiracy theory to describe it in their own words, together with the evidence they found convincing. Participants then had three rounds of conversation with GPT-4 Turbo, which was instructed to reduce their belief using evidence tailored to their stated reasons. Belief in the chosen conspiracy fell by about 20% on average, and the effect persisted undiminished for at least two months. A professional fact-checker rated 99.2% of a sample of the AI's claims as true. Where the chosen conspiracy was in fact true, the AI did not reduce belief. The effect also spilled over to reduce belief in unrelated conspiracy theories, and it "occurred even among participants with deeply entrenched beliefs" [@costello2024durably]. In 2026 *Science* issued an expression of concern, since rescinded, and then a correction, after the authors found that screening criteria had been applied inconsistently and that the public dataset contained erroneous rows. The corrected primary analyses include 2,044 believers and keep the main results, a reduction of about 20% lasting two months [@thorp2026editorial; @science2026erratum; @costello2026data].

The largest study to date found that the most persuasive set-ups were also the least accurate. Hackenburg and colleagues (2025) tested many language models on hundreds of political issues with 76,977 UK adults, and fact-checked the claims the models made [@hackenburg2025levers]. Conversation was markedly more persuasive than a static message from the same model, and post-training a model for persuasion or changing how it was prompted raised its effect further, while personalisation added almost nothing. The dominant mechanism was information density. The more fact-checkable claims a model packed into a conversation, the more it persuaded. In an estimated "maximal persuasion" condition combining the most effective levers, 30.0% of fact-checkable claims were rated inaccurate, against 16.0% on average. Table 9.2 gives the effect sizes and their durability.

Lin and colleagues (2025) moved from policy issues to real elections, and showed that the same capacity can be pointed in either political direction. In pre-registered experiments before the 2024 US presidential election, the 2025 Canadian federal election and the 2025 Polish presidential election, participants were randomly assigned to converse with an AI that advocated for one of the two leading candidates. In the US the gap in candidate preference between the pro-Harris and pro-Trump conditions was 2.88 points on a 0–100 scale. In Canada and Poland it was about 10 points, effects the authors note are larger than those typically found for video advertisements. For a Massachusetts ballot measure on psychedelics, the gap among the 193 participants without extreme prior views was 22.73 points. Slightly more than a third of the US effect persisted after more than a month. In Canada and Poland, instructing the AI not to use facts and evidence cut its effect by more than half. Models advocating for right-leaning candidates made more inaccurate claims in all three countries, as rated by a validated AI fact-checking system. Unlike Hackenburg and colleagues, however, the authors found no association between accuracy and persuasiveness [@lin2025persuading].

Salvi and colleagues (2025) compared AI directly with people. In short multi-round debates with 900 participants, GPT-4 given basic demographic information about its opponent was more persuasive than a human opponent in 64.4% of the pairs where the two differed. That corresponds to an 81.2% increase in the odds of higher post-debate agreement (95% CI 26.0% to 160.7%) [@salvi2025conversational]. This seems to contradict the two larger studies, in which personalisation added almost nothing, less than one point in Hackenburg's and no significant difference between a personalising and a non-personalising AI in Lin's Polish experiment [@hackenburg2025levers; @lin2025persuading]. The designs answer different questions. Salvi's headline result compares personalised GPT-4 with human debaters in short debates, so it shows that an AI with personal data can out-argue people. The larger studies varied personalisation directly within AI conversations, with thousands of participants, and found that it is not what makes AI conversations persuasive. Table 9.2 and Figure 9.3 summarise these studies.

| Study | Participants | Design | Main estimate | Durability |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Goldstein et al. 2024 | 8,221 (US) | GPT-3 article vs real propaganda | Agreement 24.4% (none) → 47.4% (real) and 43.5% (GPT-3) | Not measured |
| Hackenburg & Margetts 2024 | 8,587 | GPT-4 messages, tailored vs generic | 4.83 vs 6.20 points; difference not significant | Not measured |
| Hackenburg et al. 2025 (PNAS) | 25,982 | 720 messages from 24 models | Sharply diminishing returns to model size | Not measured |
| Costello et al. 2024 | 2,044 (corrected) | Three-round dialogue against a conspiracy belief | Belief down about 20% | Undiminished at 2 months |
| Salvi et al. 2025 | 900 | Debates, GPT-4 vs human | GPT-4 with personal data more persuasive in 64.4% of non-tied pairs | Not measured |
| Hackenburg et al. 2025 (Science) | 76,977 (UK) | 19 models, 707 issues, conversation vs static | Conversation 41–52% more persuasive than a static message (static effect 6.1–6.9 points) | 36–42% at 1 month |
| Hackenburg et al. 2025 (Science), levers | Same; 466,769 claims fact-checked | Persuasion post-training, prompting, personalisation | Post-training up to +51%; personalisation under 1 point; maximal persuasion 15.9 points, with 30.0% of claims inaccurate (16.0% on average) | See row above |

### External validity

The experiments were artificial in ways that matter for real elections. Participants were recruited online, paid, told they were talking to an AI and assigned to converse with it. In the experiments of Hackenburg and colleagues, conversations lasted nine minutes on average [@hackenburg2025levers]. Outside experiments people choose whether to discuss politics with a chatbot, and in the author's view those who do are probably the politically engaged, whose views are hardest to move. Such use is still a minority habit. In the Reuters Institute's 2026 survey, 10% of respondents used AI chatbots for news each week [@egan2026digital]. Effects decayed, with roughly a third to two-fifths remaining after a month in the two largest studies, and an election campaign exposes voters to many competing messages. One feature of the design points the other way. Lin and colleagues debriefed participants at the end of each experiment, telling them that the AI had been instructed to persuade them, and randomised the direction of persuasion so that any lasting effects would cancel out across the electorate. Their persistence estimates were therefore measured after a debriefing and are probably a lower bound. The authors suggest that AI dialogue may matter more in state and local contests, where voters have weaker prior views, than in national ones [@lin2025persuading].

Other features of the results make them more concerning. The effects came mainly from presenting information, not from psychological tricks or personal data, so they do not depend on any capability that providers could easily withhold.
