In the Hackenburg study the most persuasive configurations were the least accurate, so a campaign optimising for votes would be pushed towards less accurate set-ups unless model developers or regulators constrain it. In Lin's study persuasion ran on facts and was not linked to accuracy, but the facts offered for right-leaning candidates were less accurate [@hackenburg2025levers; @lin2025persuading].

## 9.6 Synthetic respondents: AI as a stand-in for the public

A different use of language models is to replace survey respondents. Argyle and colleagues (2023) conditioned GPT-3 on thousands of first-person "backstories" built from the demographic and political characteristics of real participants in the American National Election Studies (ANES) of 2012, 2016 and 2020 [@argyle2023out]. In the preprint version of the study [@argyle2022out], the model's predicted Republican vote share came within six percentage points of the ANES figure in each year (0.391 against 0.404 in 2012, for example). The correlation between individual simulated and reported votes was 0.90 to 0.94. The authors called this property **algorithmic fidelity**: with the right conditioning, a model reproduces the response patterns of many subgroups. They named the resulting synthetic respondents **silicon samples**; using them in place of human respondents has come to be called **silicon sampling**. The authors proposed such samples as a new tool for social-science research.

The later evidence found the limits. Bisbee and colleagues (2024) asked ChatGPT, adopting different personas, to rate 11 social and political groups. Average scores closely matched the ANES, but the synthetic answers varied far less than real ones, and the statistical relationships between variables often differed from those in the human data. Results changed with small changes to prompt wording, and the same prompt gave significantly different results over three months, a serious problem for reproducibility [@bisbee2024synthetic].

The most demanding test so far came from the Pew Research Center in September 2026 [@pew2026well]. Pew built a "digital twin" for each member of its American Trends Panel who had completed both its 2025 political typology survey and the 2026 survey being replicated, giving the model the person's demographics and earlier answers. It then had the twins answer three 2026 survey waves under the same instructions as the human panellists. The best-performing model, Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.6, missed the human results by 12.4 percentage points on average across the three waves. The deeper problem was homogeneity. The synthetic respondents were "far less politically diverse" than the population and turned majority views within a party into near-unanimity. Among synthetic Democrats and Democratic leaners, 86% said that having people with fortunes of a billion dollars or more is a bad thing for the country, against 45% of real ones [@pew2026well]. The twins also missed on topical questions: 46% of them approved of President Trump's handling of his job, against 34% of the real panellists [@pew2026can]. Pew stated that it has no current or future plans to use AI models to generate survey results [@pew2026well].

In the author's reading of these three studies, models capture the average direction of opinion in large, well-studied groups [@argyle2023out; @bisbee2024synthetic; @pew2026well]. They miss the variance within groups and the views of people whose opinions cut across party lines, and their answers shift with prompt wording and model version. Variance, cross-cutting views and change over time are exactly what surveys exist to measure. Silicon samples can still help design questionnaires or explore hypotheses before fieldwork, but the evidence does not support using them in place of asking people.

## 9.7 Recommender systems, AI search and journalism

### Recommender systems and polarisation

A **recommender system** is an automated system that suggests or prioritises information for each user, for example by determining the order of posts in a social media feed [@europeanparliament2022regulation, Article 3(s)]. A common fear is that such systems create "echo chambers" and increase **polarisation**, the growing distance or hostility between political groups [@nyhan2023like].

Some of the strongest evidence comes from a collaboration between Meta and independent academics during the 2020 US election. Guess and colleagues (2023) switched a sample of consenting Facebook and Instagram users from the algorithmic feed to a reverse-chronological one. Time on the platforms fell substantially, and users saw more political and more untrustworthy content; over three months, there was no significant change in polarisation, political knowledge or other key attitudes [@guess2023social]. Nyhan and colleagues (2023) reduced exposure to content from like-minded sources by about a third for 23,377 users and found no measurable effect on eight pre-registered attitude measures, including polarisation and belief in false claims [@nyhan2023like]. González-Bailón and colleagues (2023) used aggregated data on 208 million US Facebook users. Ideological segregation in political news was high and increased at each stage, from what users could have seen, to what the feed showed them, to what they engaged with. It was also asymmetric. A substantial corner of the news ecosystem was consumed exclusively by conservatives, and most content rated false by Meta's fact-checkers sat in that corner, with no equivalent on the liberal side [@gonzalezbailon2023asymmetric].

Other studies found effects from more targeted changes. A long-running randomised experiment on Twitter compared users of the algorithmic feed with a control group of nearly 2 million daily active accounts on a chronological feed. The mainstream political right enjoyed higher algorithmic amplification than the mainstream left in six of seven countries studied, with no evidence that far-left or far-right groups were amplified more than moderate ones [@huszar2022algorithmic]. Piccardi and colleagues (2025) used a language model to rerank, in real time, the X feeds of 1,256 participants during the 2024 US campaign, demoting or promoting posts expressing antidemocratic attitudes and partisan animosity. Over ten days, this shifted feelings towards the opposing party by more than 2 points on a 100-point "feeling thermometer", in both directions and with no detectable difference between Democrats and Republicans [@piccardi2025reranking]. The findings differ in what was changed and what was measured. Reducing exposure to like-minded sources did not move attitudes over three months, while changing exposure to hostile, antidemocratic content moved feelings towards the other party, at least over ten days. The Piccardi study also shows that independent researchers can now test ranking interventions without a platform's cooperation.

### AI search and the click

Search engines now often place an AI-written summary above the list of links. Pew Research Center tracked the browsing of 900 US adults in March 2025. When an AI summary appeared, users clicked a traditional result link about half as often as when none did, rarely clicked the links inside the summary, and more often ended their browsing session on the results page (Figure 9.4) [@chapekis2025google]. News sites accounted for 5% of the sources the summaries cited, the same share as in ordinary results [@chapekis2025google]. A randomised field experiment supports a causal reading of this one-month, one-country observation. In a working paper, Agarwal and Sen (2026) used a browser extension to hide AI summaries at random for 1,065 US desktop users; a summary cut clicks on ordinary results by 39.8%, with no measurable change in users' satisfaction [@agarwal2026impact].

![Figure 9.4: Share of Google search visits in which users clicked a link, with and without an AI-generated summary on the page, and share of visits that ended the browsing session. Based on the browsing data of 900 US adults, March 2025. Source: @chapekis2025google.](../figures/svg/fig-09-04.svg){#fig:09-04}

For publishers, fewer clicks mean less advertising and subscription revenue. The Reuters Institute's *Digital News Report 2026* cites data from the analytics company Chartbeat on more than 2,500 news sites, compiled for the institute's separate annual trends report. Google search traffic to them fell by a third (33%) globally between November 2024 and November 2025, and by 38% in the United States. Publishers expect a further fall of 43% over three years. The report notes that the role of AI summaries in this decline is widely assumed rather than proven, and that hard-news queries are mostly excluded from them [@egan2026digital]. Regulators have begun to act. In June 2026 the UK's Competition and Markets Authority required Google to let publishers keep their content out of its AI search features and to credit it with clear links [@cma2026cma]. Since December 2025 the European Commission has been investigating, under EU competition law, whether Google uses publishers' content for AI Overviews and AI Mode without appropriate compensation or a way to refuse [@europeancommission2025opens]. American antitrust law has so far not helped. According to TheWrap, on 30 September 2026 a federal judge dismissed Penske Media's suit over AI Overviews, holding that publishers' expectation of search traffic "is not an agreement" [@bryant2026penske].

The same report tracks how audiences use AI for news. Weekly use of AI chatbots for news rose from 7% of respondents in 2025 to 10% in 2026, though use did not grow in the United States, the United Kingdom, France or Germany. Only 20% of respondents said they trusted news answers from chatbots, against 37% for news in general; in the UK the figure was 6%. Among chatbot news users, 42% said they always or often clicked through to the original sources, against 44% of search users, although the report warns that the two figures come from quite different user bases and should be compared with caution [@egan2026digital]. Whether AI answers attribute and link to journalism, and whether they reproduce it accurately, thus matters for both the business and the public value of news.

Accuracy remains a problem. In a study coordinated by the European Broadcasting Union (EBU) and led by the BBC, journalists from 22 public service media organisations in 18 countries and 14 languages rated 2,709 answers to a common set of news questions from the free versions of ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini and Perplexity, generated in May and June 2025. Of these, 45% had at least one significant issue; 31% had significant sourcing problems and 20% significant accuracy problems, such as fabricated quotations or outdated information [@ebu2025news]. These figures describe one set of products in 2025 and may change quickly. Whether news content may lawfully be used to train AI systems belongs to the wider copyright disputes covered in Section 13.6.

### Chatbots and content farms as channels

The argument that production was never the binding constraint (Section 9.1) assumes that distribution stays with platforms and audiences. Chatbots weaken that assumption, because they are themselves a channel that selects and restates information, and two kinds of failure have been documented. The first is plain error. In January 2024, election officials and other experts convened by the newsroom Proof News and the AI Democracy Projects rated about half of the answers that five leading models gave to questions about US voting as inaccurate, including invented rules on where and how to vote; the test used the models' programming interfaces rather than consumer apps [@angwin2024seeking]. The second is deliberate manipulation of the material that models learn from or retrieve, sometimes called "LLM grooming". NewsGuard, a company that rates the reliability of news sites, reported in March 2025 that ten leading chatbots repeated false claims laundered through the pro-Kremlin "Pravda" network of websites 33% of the time in its tests [@sadeghi2025wellfunded]. Both are audits with limited sets of prompts, and neither measures how many real users received such answers.

Generative AI also fills the web that such systems read. By October 2026 NewsGuard counted 3,749 "AI content farms" in 16 languages. These are news-like sites whose content is substantially produced by AI and published without significant human oversight, often funded by programmatic advertising [@newsguard2026tracking]. In the author's view, their significance lies less in virality than in volume, and in the possibility that search engines and chatbots treat them as sources.

## 9.8 Regulating platforms and synthetic content

The rules on what platforms must do about harmful information differ sharply between jurisdictions. In the United States, Section 230 of the Communications Act provides that no online service shall be treated as the publisher of information provided by its users [@uscongress1996protection], and new federal rules have targeted specific harms. The European Union regulates broadly, through the Digital Services Act for platforms and the AI Act for the makers and users of generative AI. Table 9.3 compares the main instruments.

### The Digital Services Act

The **Digital Services Act (DSA)** has applied in full since 17 February 2024 [@europeanparliament2022regulation, Article 93] and scales duties to platform size. Its strictest rules apply to "very large online platforms" and search engines, those with at least 45 million average monthly active users in the EU [@europeanparliament2022regulation, Article 33(1)]. Each year these must assess "systemic risks" arising from their design and use, including how their recommender systems contribute. The listed risks explicitly include "any actual or foreseeable negative effects on civic discourse and electoral processes" [@europeanparliament2022regulation, Article 34]. Platforms must then take reasonable mitigation measures. These may include testing and adapting recommender systems, and ensuring that generated or manipulated images, audio or video that falsely appear authentic are distinguishable "through prominent markings" [@europeanparliament2022regulation, Article 35(1)(d) and (k)]. They must offer at least one recommender option not based on profiling the user [@europeanparliament2022regulation, Article 38] and give vetted researchers access to data. The European Commission can fine them up to 6% of worldwide annual turnover [@europeanparliament2022regulation, Article 74]. AI services are now among them. On 31 August 2026 the Commission designated ChatGPT a very large online search engine, because it searches the web for users, giving OpenAI until January 2027 to assess and mitigate systemic risks, including to electoral processes [@europeancommission2026designates].

::: {.box .case}
**Case study: Romania's annulled election and the DSA**

On 6 December 2024, Romania's Constitutional Court annulled the presidential election after its first round, two days before a scheduled run-off involving the first-round leader, Călin Georgescu. The decision followed the declassification of intelligence documents describing a campaign on TikTok coordinated through Telegram, together with alleged undeclared campaign financing. Georgescu called the decision a coup, and the interior ministry's attribution to Russia rested on similarities with earlier Russian operations in Ukraine and Moldova [@solea2024romanias]. On 17 December 2024 the European Commission opened formal DSA proceedings against TikTok, focused on the management of election risks linked to its recommender systems and on its rules for political advertising; opening proceedings does not prejudge the outcome [@europeancommission2024commission]. The case shows that the most consequential threats to an election may come from coordinated amplification and undisclosed paid promotion, with or without generative AI, and that annulling an election is itself contested.
:::

The DSA's first non-compliance decision came on 5 December 2025, when the Commission fined X €120 million. It found that X's paid "blue checkmark" was deceptive design, that its advertising repository lacked required information, and that its terms prevented researchers from accessing public data [@europeancommission2025commission]. The research-access finding matters for the evidence base itself, because much of what is known about recommender systems comes from studies that depended on a platform's voluntary cooperation [@guess2023social], and the DSA attempts to make such access a legal right.

The DSA is contested, and the two sides rely on different kinds of evidence. Critics argue that duties framed around "systemic risks" push platforms to remove lawful speech to avoid large fines. In July 2025 the Republican majority on the US House Judiciary Committee published an interim staff report arguing that the DSA "compels global censorship", because platforms apply one set of terms worldwide and, according to subpoenaed documents, Commission officials expected them to change those terms [@housejudiciary2025foreign]. The report is a partisan document resting on the committee's own selection of material. Criticism also comes from digital-rights groups. In August 2024 Access Now, ARTICLE 19 and the Electronic Frontier Foundation warned the Commission against politicised enforcement, argued that spreading information that is "highly newsworthy, timely, and relevant to public discourse is not, in itself, a systemic risk", and asked it to define the evidence a systemic-risk assessment requires [@accessnow2024civil]. The regulation's defenders point to its text, which requires platforms to weigh negative effects on fundamental rights, including freedom of expression, alongside risks to civic discourse [@europeanparliament2022regulation, Article 34(1)(b)]. Independent work on the DSA's transparency tools is mixed. Analysing a sample of the 131 million "statements of reasons" for moderation decisions filed in the DSA Transparency Database in November 2023, Kaushal and colleagues (2024) concluded that compliance "remains problematic" because platforms have "a lot of discretion" in what they report [@kaushal2024automated].

### The AI Act's transparency duties

Article 50 of the AI Act divides the labelling task between two groups. **Providers** of AI systems that generate synthetic audio, images, video or text must ensure that outputs "are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated". Their technical solutions must be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable "as far as this is technically feasible". The duty does not apply to tools that only assist with standard editing or do not substantially alter the input [@europeanparliament2024regulation, Article 50(2)]. **Deployers**, those who use such systems, must disclose that deepfake image, audio or video content is artificial, in a lighter form for evidently artistic, satirical or fictional works. Deployers who publish AI-generated text to inform the public on matters of public interest must also disclose it, unless a human has reviewed it and someone holds editorial responsibility [@europeanparliament2024regulation, Article 50(4)]. Breaches can be fined up to €15 million or 3% of worldwide turnover [@europeanparliament2024regulation, Article 99(4)].

These duties began to apply on 2 August 2026 [@europeanparliament2024regulation, Article 113]. The Digital Omnibus on AI, in force since 27 July 2026, gave generative systems already on the market before that date until 2 December 2026 to add machine-readable marking. It also added two prohibitions from the same date, on AI systems that generate non-consensual intimate images of identifiable people and on those that generate child sexual abuse material [@europeanparliament2026regulation]. To make Article 50 workable, the Commission published a voluntary Code of Practice on marking and labelling AI-generated content on 10 June 2026 [@europeancommission2026publishes]. As long as no single technique is robust enough on its own, providers that sign it commit to "at least two layers of machine-readable marking", digitally signed metadata and an imperceptible watermark. They must also make a free detection tool available to deployers, users, researchers and authorities, and deployers who sign commit to label deepfakes with a common EU icon or an equivalent label [@europeancommission2026code]. By October 2026 the Commission's list counted 95 signatories to the providers' section and 192 to the deployers', among them Anthropic, Google, Meta, Microsoft and OpenAI [@europeancommission2026strong]. In the author's view, the layered approach reflects the evidence in Section 9.3: no single marking technique is robust on its own. Chapter 13 sets out the AI Act's overall timetable.

### Non-consensual intimate imagery

The harm from deepfakes that is best documented, and most clearly growing, is not political but sexual. Chesney and Citron (2019) predicted that the technology would be used for non-consensual intimate imagery (NCII), fraud and harassment as well as political deception [@chesney2019deep]. Fraud is the other well-documented harm. The 2026 International AI Safety Report notes that scammers use voice clones and deepfakes to trick victims into transferring money [@bengio2026international, sec. 2.1.1]. Section 11.4 covers it; this section concentrates on NCII.

In the United States, the TAKE IT DOWN Act, signed on 19 May 2025, made it a federal crime knowingly to publish non-consensual intimate images of identifiable people, including AI-generated "digital forgeries". Covered platforms had one year to set up a notice-and-removal process. On receiving a valid request they must remove the image "as soon as possible, but not later than 48 hours", and make reasonable efforts to remove known identical copies. Failure to comply is treated as an unfair or deceptive practice enforceable by the Federal Trade Commission, and platforms are shielded from liability for good-faith removals [@uscongress2025tools]. The first conviction under the Act, of an Ohio man who had used AI to make such images, came in April 2026, and the FTC began enforcing the removal duty on 19 May 2026 [@senatecommerce2026cruz]. The Electronic Frontier Foundation, a digital-rights group, opposed the law. It argued that the takedown provision covers a broader category of content than the criminal offence and "lacks critical safeguards against frivolous or bad-faith takedown requests". In its view, the 48-hour deadline will push smaller services to remove lawful material rather than verify claims [@kelley2025congress].

The United Kingdom has gone further in one respect. Since 6 February 2026 it has been a criminal offence in England and Wales to create an intimate deepfake of an adult, such as a nude or sexual image, without consent, or to request that one be made, even if the image is never shared. These are summary offences, punishable by a fine or a short prison sentence [@ukparliament2025s138].

::: {.box .case}
**Case study: Grok and the "undressing" images of January 2026**

Around the turn of 2026, X rolled out an image-editing feature powered by its Grok chatbot that let users alter photographs of real people with simple text prompts, including requests to undress them. The Center for Countering Digital Hate, a campaigning non-profit, estimated that Grok generated about three million sexualised images over 11 days, including about 23,000 that appeared to depict children; the estimate did not establish how many were made without consent [@afp2026musks]. Regulators responded under platform law rather than AI law. According to The Register, on 12 January 2026 the UK regulator Ofcom opened an investigation under the Online Safety Act into whether X had assessed and mitigated the risk of illegal content; the Act allows fines of up to £18 million or 10% of qualifying worldwide revenue [@jones2026ofcom]. On 26 January the European Commission opened formal DSA proceedings into whether X had assessed and mitigated the risks of deploying Grok's functions, including "manipulated sexually explicit images", stating that "these risks seem to have materialised" [@europeancommission2026commission]. Neither inquiry had announced a finding by late October 2026. In October, according to Reuters, Ofcom said Grok's image tools now blocked pornographic content for UK users and that its investigation had moved on to X's handling of illegal content [@reuters2026concerns]. The UK's offence of creating such images came into force only in February 2026, after the episode. The case also shows which law binds whom. Platform rules bound X as a platform and applied after the images had spread. The AI Act's new prohibition of non-consensual intimate image generation, applicable from 2 December 2026, will also be enforced after the fact, but it binds the provider of the generating system itself, here xAI.
:::

| Instrument | Who is bound | Main duty relevant to synthetic media | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|---|
| EU Digital Services Act (2022/2065), in full since 17 Feb 2024 | Platforms; strictest duties for very large platforms and search engines | Assess and mitigate systemic risks, including to electoral processes; mark realistic manipulated media; researcher data access | Commission; fines up to 6% of worldwide turnover |
| EU AI Act Art. 50 (2024/1689), from 2 Aug 2026 (2 Dec 2026 for marking by systems already on the market) | Providers and deployers of generative AI | Machine-readable marking of outputs; disclosure of deepfakes and public-interest text | National authorities; fines up to €15m or 3% |
| EU AI Act Art. 5 as amended (2026/1744), from 2 Dec 2026 | Providers and deployers | Ban on AI generating non-consensual intimate images or child sexual abuse material | National authorities |
| US TAKE IT DOWN Act (Pub. L. 119-12), platform duties from 19 May 2026 | Individuals; covered platforms | Criminal offence of publishing NCII including digital forgeries; 48-hour removal | Federal prosecutors; FTC for platforms |
| UK Online Safety Act 2023 | Online services in scope, including social media | Assess and mitigate risk of illegal content, including NCII | Ofcom; fines up to £18m or 10% of revenue |
| UK Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, s. 138, from 6 Feb 2026 (England and Wales) | Individuals | Offences of creating, or requesting, an intimate deepfake of an adult without consent | Criminal courts; fine or short prison sentence |

: Table 9.3: Main legal instruments governing platforms and synthetic media, as of October 2026. Source: [@europeanparliament2022regulation; @europeanparliament2024regulation; @europeanparliament2026regulation; @uscongress2025tools; @jones2026ofcom; @ukparliament2025s138].

In the author's reading, each of these regimes addresses one link of the chain [@europeanparliament2022regulation; @europeanparliament2024regulation; @uscongress2025tools; @ukparliament2025s138]. The AI Act targets production, the DSA and the Online Safety Act target distribution, the TAKE IT DOWN Act targets individual publication and removal, and the UK's new offence targets individual creation. The division fits the evidence on synthetic media. Cheap production has so far mattered less than reach, detection after the fact is unreliable, and marking at the source works only where generators, tools and platforms cooperate. Chapter 13 compares these approaches with those of China, the United Kingdom and international bodies. None of the regimes yet answers the measurement problem on which much of the evidence on AI and elections founders. Visible fakes can be counted, but their effects cannot, until independent researchers get the data needed to trace exposure to synthetic content, including private chatbot conversations, and link it to what people believe and do.

## Further reading

- Chesney, B. and Citron, D. (2019). *Deep Fakes: A Looming Challenge for Privacy, Democracy, and National Security*. The legal analysis that introduced the "liar's dividend" and anticipated the intimate-image harms that legislators addressed six years later. [@chesney2019deep]
- Kirchenbauer, J. et al. (2023). *A Watermark for Large Language Models*. A clear, short account of how text watermarking works, including the authors' own catalogue of attacks against it. [@kirchenbauer2023watermark]
- Kapoor, S. and Narayanan, A. (2024). *We Looked at 78 Election Deepfakes. Political Misinformation Is Not an AI Problem*. A short, data-based argument for focusing on the demand for misinformation rather than its supply. [@kapoor2024looked]
- Hackenburg, K. et al. (2025). *The Levers of Political Persuasion with Conversational Artificial Intelligence*. The largest experiment on what makes AI persuasive, documenting the trade-off between persuasiveness and accuracy. [@hackenburg2025levers]
- Pew Research Center (2026). *How Well Synthetic Samples Replicate Public Opinion*. A careful, transparent test of AI "digital twins" against a real national panel, with group-by-group error rates. [@pew2026well]
- Access Now, ARTICLE 19 and Electronic Frontier Foundation (2024). *Civil Society Statement: Commissioner Breton Needs to Stop Politicising the Digital Services Act*. A two-page statement of the free-expression concerns about broad "systemic risk" enforcement, from rights groups rather than politicians. [@accessnow2024civil]
- Egan, J. et al. (2026). *Reuters Institute Digital News Report 2026*. The standard annual source on how people in 48 markets get news, including from AI chatbots and search summaries. [@egan2026digital]


# Chapter 10: Education, Health and Everyday Life

In June and July 2024, first-year senior secondary students from nine public schools in Benin City, Nigeria, took part in an after-school programme to practise English. They worked in pairs with Microsoft Copilot, a chatbot built on GPT-4. Teachers set the topic and the opening prompt. The students then questioned the chatbot freely for 90 minutes, up to twice a week, for six weeks. Places were allocated by lottery among the students who volunteered, which turned the programme into a randomised controlled trial. In a working paper, the World Bank team that evaluated it reported a gain of 0.31 standard deviations on an end-of-programme assessment, and 0.23 standard deviations on the English component alone [@desimone2025chalkboards].

A few months earlier, in autumn 2023, a field experiment in a large high school in Turkey gave nearly 1,000 mathematics students access to GPT-4 during practice sessions. Students with an unrestricted chatbot scored higher on practice problems, then scored 17% lower than students without access when they sat an exam on their own [@bastani2025generative]. The two studies used similar technology and point in different directions. The difference lies in how the tools were set up, what was measured and when, and the same questions decide how to read the evidence on AI in clinics and in private life. Effects on jobs and productivity are treated in Chapter 8, the general taxonomy of AI risks in Chapter 11, and the enforcement of data-protection law against AI developers in Chapter 13.

## 10.1 AI tutors: the benchmark and the trials

The hope behind AI tutoring has a long pedigree. In 1984 the educational psychologist Benjamin Bloom reported that students taught one-to-one by a tutor performed about two standard deviations better than students taught in a conventional class. He called the search for group methods that could match this the "2 sigma problem" [@bloom1984sigma]. Later research confirmed that tutoring works, but with much smaller effects. Kurt VanLehn's 2011 review of experiments comparing human tutoring, computer tutoring and no tutoring found an effect of 0.79 standard deviations for human tutors, far below Bloom's figure. Intelligent tutoring systems, the rule-based programs that give feedback on each step of a solution, reached 0.76, nearly as much [@vanlehn2011relative]. A meta-analysis of 50 controlled evaluations of such systems found a median effect of 0.66 standard deviations, but the effect depended heavily on whether learning was measured on tests developed locally for the evaluation or on standardised ones [@kulik2016effectiveness].

The best current estimate for human tutoring in schools comes from a 2024 meta-analysis of randomised field experiments from pre-kindergarten to the end of secondary school. It found a pooled effect of 0.288 standard deviations. Effects were largest for programmes that used teachers or paraprofessionals as tutors, took place in earlier grades, met at least three days a week and ran during the school day [@nickow2020impressive]. In the author's view, the gap between this figure and VanLehn's 0.79 probably reflects the kind of study more than the quality of tutors. The 2024 meta-analysis admitted only randomised field experiments with school pupils, and, as the box below shows, smaller studies and tests designed by the researchers produce larger effects than large field trials. The same contrast recurs in the AI tutoring trials below. The obstacle, in the author's assessment, is cost, because a trained tutor for every pupil several times a week is unaffordable for most school systems. Large language models (LLMs, the text-generating systems described in Chapter 3) revived the question of whether software could supply part of what a tutor provides at a fraction of the price.

::: {.box .deeper}
**Going deeper: How to read an effect size and an education trial**

Education studies report results in standard deviations (SD) of the test score so that different tests can be compared [@kraft2020interpreting]. If scores are roughly normally distributed, an effect of 0.3 SD moves the average treated student from the 50th to about the 62nd percentile of the comparison group, and 0.63 SD to about the 74th (the author's calculation from the normal distribution). The psychologist Jacob Cohen's conventions, which call 0.2 "small" and 0.8 "large" [@cohen1988statistical], come from laboratory psychology and, Kraft argues, mislead in schools [@kraft2020interpreting].

In a 2019 working paper, later published in *Educational Researcher*, Matthew Kraft assembled effect sizes from 747 randomised trials of education interventions with standardised achievement outcomes. Their median was 0.10 SD, and he proposed treating less than 0.05 as small, 0.05 to just under 0.20 as medium and 0.20 or more as large [@kraft2019interpreting; published as @kraft2020interpreting]. By that yardstick, the positive AI tutoring results below are large, often implausibly so, and two of the trials found harm. Kraft's benchmarks come from standardised tests, while most of these trials used tests written for the study, which brings us to the reasons for suspicion.

Study design inflates effect sizes. In 645 studies drawn from 12 reviews, Cheung and Slavin found effects roughly twice as large in published articles as in unpublished reports, in small trials as in large ones, and on measures made by the experimenters as on independent tests. Quasi-experiments, which compare groups not formed by chance, produced larger effects than randomised experiments [@cheung2016how]. How much weight a trial deserves also depends on how it assigned participants, what it estimated and who dropped out. Assigning whole classes to arms, as in the Turkish trial, prevents students from sharing tools across arms; but students in the same class resemble one another, so the effective sample is smaller than the head count [@campbell2012consort]. The estimand is the precise description of the effect a study sets out to estimate [@ich2019e9r1]. An "intention-to-treat" estimate compares everyone offered a programme with everyone who was not, whether or not they attended. It answers the policy question "what happens if we offer this?", whereas the effect on those who actually took part is usually larger. Attrition matters because if weaker students in one arm skip the final test, the remaining groups are no longer comparable [@moher2010consort]. The Nigerian trial below illustrates both points.
:::

Table 10.1 summarises the main controlled studies of LLM-based tutoring published by October 2026. The Nigerian programme is one of the most discussed because it took place in a lower-income country. About half of the 1,328 volunteers were offered places; the rest formed a control group that continued normal lessons [@desimone2025chalkboards]. Effects were positive across the range of prior attainment but largest for girls and for students who were already doing well; the authors caution that the result for girls may partly reflect one girls-only school. Attendance averaged 72%, so effects for students who actually attended are larger than the intention-to-treat figures. Three features call for caution, and they should be read together. First, attrition was high and uneven. Half of the control group (334 of 671) missed the final test, against just over a third (235 of 657) of those offered places. The authors' corrections, bounds that trim the group with fewer drop-outs and reweighting by observed characteristics, leave the effect positive, but they rest on assumptions about who stayed away. Second, the claim that six weeks produced gains equivalent to 1.5 to 2 years of ordinary schooling is a conversion, not a measurement. It divides the effect by an assumed typical annual learning gain for Nigerian pupils (about 0.16 SD a year, by the author's calculation from the paper's figures), and the same conversion underlies the estimate that the programme, at about $48 per pupil ($9 at the margin), is among the more cost-effective education interventions in developing countries. Third, the paper is a working paper and has not been peer-reviewed [@desimone2025chalkboards].

| Study | Setting and sample | Design | AI set-up | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| De Simone et al. (working paper) | Nigeria, 9 public schools, 2024; 1,328 volunteers | Individual lottery; 6 weeks after school | Copilot (GPT-4), teacher-designed prompts, pairs | +0.31 SD overall, +0.23 SD English (intention-to-treat) |
| Kestin et al. | Harvard introductory physics, 2023; 194 students | Crossover: each student had both conditions | Tutor fed instructors' step-by-step solutions | +0.63 SD versus in-class active learning |
| Henkel et al. (preprint) | Ghana, 11 schools, grades 3–9; about 1,000 students | Schools randomly assigned (5 treatment, 6 control); 8 months, two 30-minute sessions a week | Rori: scripted maths micro-lessons on WhatsApp; language models interpret pupils' messages | +0.37 SD on maths growth scores |
| Wang et al. (preprint) | US online tutoring; 900 tutors, 1,800 students | Tutors randomised | AI suggests moves to human tutors | +4 percentage points topic mastery; +9 for lower-rated tutors |
| Bastani et al. | Turkey, one high school, 2023; nearly 1,000 students in about 50 classes | Classes assigned to three arms; students randomly assigned to classes | GPT-4 unrestricted vs hint-only tutor | Exam −17% (unrestricted); no significant change (hint-only) |
| Liu et al. (working paper) | US public university, autumn 2025; 2,379 undergraduates, 30 instructors | Instructors randomised within blocks of similar courses; one semester | GPT-4o tutor drawing on instructor-selected course materials | Final grades −0.37 SD within same-course blocks; not significant in full sample; about 15% of students offered the tutor used it |

: Table 10.1: Controlled studies of LLM-based tutoring with random or matched assignment (see the design column). Effect sizes are measured on different tests and are not directly comparable. Source: [@desimone2025chalkboards; @kestin2025ai; @henkel2024effective; @wang2024tutor; @bastani2025generative; @liu2026effects].

The Harvard trial tested a different question: could a carefully built AI tutor beat a good lesson, not merely no lesson? Kestin and colleagues compared an AI tutor, used at home, with an in-class "active learning" session in an introductory physics course for life-science students in autumn 2023 [@kestin2025ai]. In the crossover design, 194 students each took one lesson in each format, on two topics, so that every student served as their own comparison. A regression adjusting for prior knowledge gave an effect of 0.63 SD, which the authors consider an underestimate because many students reached the top of the scale. Students using the tutor spent a median of 49 minutes, against 60 minutes in class, and rated their engagement higher. The tutor was no general chatbot. It was given step-by-step solutions written by the instructors and a system prompt built on research about how students learn. The material was introductory and new to the students, and the lessons targeted understanding and application. Some of the authors developed the active-learning methods used as the comparison, which makes it a demanding benchmark but also gives the team a stake in both arms. Each format covered one lesson on one topic, and learning was measured by short tests written for the study by a team member not involved in the lessons, which did not count towards grades. Tests written for a study are the kind of measure that Cheung and Slavin found to inflate effects, so the largest positive result in Table 10.1 is also one to read with care [@cheung2016how].

In Ghana, Rori, a maths tutor that runs on WhatsApp on basic phones, was used by about 1,000 pupils in grades 3 to 9 for two 30-minute sessions a week over eight months. Rori takes pupils through a fixed curriculum of short lessons with hints and worked solutions, using language models mainly to interpret their free-text messages, so it is less of a chatbot than the other tutors in Table 10.1. The preprint reports an effect of 0.37 on maths growth scores [@henkel2024effective]. Because only 11 schools were randomly assigned, five to treatment and six to control, the uncertainty is larger than the pupil count suggests. Tutor CoPilot, evaluated in another preprint, took the opposite route and advised human tutors working online with pupils from under-served communities in the United States. Pupils whose tutors had access were 4 percentage points more likely to master topics, and pupils of lower-rated tutors gained 9 points. The system cost about $20 per tutor per year, and an analysis of the tutors' messages showed that those with access asked more guiding questions and gave away answers less often [@wang2024tutor].

Most of these trials were short, and most measured learning on tests close to what had just been taught, the conditions under which the meta-analyses above found the largest effects. None tells us what a full school year with an AI tutor would achieve on an independent examination. Outside trials, students already use general chatbots for learning on a large scale, without the scaffolding the trial tutors had. In a Pew Research Center survey of 1,458 US teenagers in autumn 2025, 54% said they had used chatbots for help with schoolwork and 10% did all or most of their schoolwork with them [@mcclain2026how]; a year earlier, 26% had used ChatGPT for schoolwork [@sidoti2025quarter]. A working paper by OpenAI researchers and academic economists, analysing ChatGPT consumer messages, estimated that about 10% of all messages in mid-2025 were requests for tutoring or teaching [@chatterji2025how].

Teachers are the other large group of users, and one randomised trial has measured what AI does to their workload. In England in 2024, 68 secondary schools were randomly assigned either to let their Year 7 and 8 science teachers use ChatGPT, with a guide, to prepare lessons, or to prepare without generative AI. Teachers with ChatGPT spent about 56 minutes a week on preparation against 82 minutes, a saving of 31%, and an expert panel that did not know which group had produced which materials found no difference in their quality [@roy2024chatgpt]. The trial measured teachers' time, recorded in their own diaries, not pupils' learning.

## 10.2 When help harms learning

The Turkish study is the clearest experimental evidence that an AI assistant can raise performance while lowering learning. Bastani and colleagues ran four 90-minute sessions in about fifty classes in grades 9 to 11, covering roughly 15% of the semester's mathematics curriculum [@bastani2025generative]. Each class was assigned to one of three arms in a way that balanced observable characteristics; because the school allocates students to classes at random, the assignment of students to arms was effectively random. "GPT Base" was a plain GPT-4 chat interface. "GPT Tutor" used the same model with a prompt that told it to give hints instead of answers. Two part-time mathematics teachers supplied, for every problem, one or more correct solutions, common student mistakes and guidance on feedback, which were placed in the prompt so that the model would not mislead students. The control arm used textbooks and notes only. Each session began with the teacher reviewing a topic, followed by assisted practice and then a closed-book, closed-laptop exam in which every problem matched a conceptually similar practice problem.

Figure 10.1 shows the results. During practice, measured as the share of points obtained, GPT Base raised scores by 48% relative to the control group and GPT Tutor by 127%. On the unassisted exam, GPT Base students scored 17% lower than the control group, a statistically significant loss that takes the average from about 32% of points to about 27%. GPT Tutor students were indistinguishable from the control group [@bastani2025generative]. The authors traced the loss to students using the chatbot as a "crutch". The most common message in the GPT Base arm was a request for the answer. The base model was also unreliable. Asked "What is the answer?" ten times for each of the 57 practice problems, it was correct 51% of the time, and most of its errors were logical rather than arithmetic.

![Figure 10.1: Two kinds of evidence on AI tutors. Panel A: in a randomised trial in a Turkish high school, students using an unrestricted GPT-4 interface ("GPT Base") or a hint-giving version ("GPT Tutor") scored far higher than a control group during practice, but in the later unassisted exam the GPT Base group scored 17% lower than the control group and the GPT Tutor group about the same. Panel B: estimated effects in two other tutoring trials (three estimates), in standard deviations. The same underlying technology can raise or lower measured learning depending on design and on what is measured. Source: @bastani2025generative; @desimone2025chalkboards; @kestin2025ai.](../figures/svg/fig-10-01.svg){#fig:10-01}

Students also misjudged their own learning. Those in the GPT Base arm did not perceive that they had performed worse or learned less, and those in the GPT Tutor arm believed they had done significantly better, although their exam scores matched the control group's. Preregistered tests for differences by ability, resources and effort found little heterogeneity, so the harm was not confined to weaker students. The guarded tutor removed the harm but produced no gain on the exam [@bastani2025generative]. In this trial, design prevented damage without adding learning. The study took place when chatbots were new to most students and covered one subject in one school.

A larger trial in a routine university setting found a negative effect, but it is much harder to interpret. At the University of Maryland in autumn 2025, 30 instructors teaching 2,379 undergraduates in many disciplines were randomly assigned, within groups of similar courses, to offer a course-integrated tutor built on GPT-4o and fed with materials the instructors chose. Comparing sections of the same course, the offer lowered final grades by 0.37 SD, with larger losses for first-generation students. In the full sample, which mixes different courses, the grade effect was not significant. Only about 15% of students offered the tutor used it even once. By the author's calculation, if the whole effect had run through those students, each would have lost about 2.5 SD, which is implausible, so the grade effect is probably not an effect of using the tutor; the authors suggest it may reflect how instructors' promotion of it changed students' other AI use. The paper is an unreviewed working paper [@liu2026effects], and its result deserves more caution than the Turkish trial's.

The mechanism has a name in cognitive psychology. Cognitive offloading is "the use of physical action to alter the information processing requirements of a task so as to reduce cognitive demand", such as writing a reminder instead of remembering [@risko2016cognitive]. Offloading is often sensible, but learning depends on some of the effort it removes. Psychologists call the useful kind of effort a "desirable difficulty" [@bjork1994memory], and the Nigerian programme deliberately built retrieval practice and other such difficulties into its prompts [@desimone2025chalkboards]. Several smaller experiments with university students point the same way. In a laboratory study of 117 students writing an essay with help from ChatGPT, a human expert, writing-analytics tools or nothing, the ChatGPT group improved its essays most but gained no more knowledge and transferred no more of it to new tasks. The authors warn of "metacognitive laziness", a dependence on the tool that weakens learners' regulation of their own learning [@fan2025beware]. In another experiment, 91 students researched a socio-scientific question with either ChatGPT or Google. Those using the chatbot reported lower cognitive load but produced lower-quality reasoning in their final recommendations [@stadler2024cognitive].

Evidence from outside controlled experiments is weaker. A preprint from the MIT Media Lab recorded brain activity with electroencephalography (EEG, sensors on the scalp) while 54 participants wrote essays with ChatGPT, with a search engine or unaided over several sessions [@kosmyna2025brain]. Chatbot users showed the weakest connectivity between brain regions, the least sense of ownership of their essays and difficulty quoting from them. Only 18 participants completed the final session, and EEG connectivity is an indirect proxy for learning. Surveys can show only associations. In surveys of knowledge workers and of the general public, greater confidence in or use of AI went with less critical thinking [@lee2025impact; @gerlich2025ai], but people who think less critically may simply rely more on AI, so such correlations cannot show which way the influence runs. Chapter 8 discusses the parallel, contested evidence from medicine, where an observational study found that endoscopists' unaided detection rates fell after AI support was introduced and a later small trial found no such effect.

Developers have responded with modes that imitate the GPT Tutor design. In July 2025 OpenAI launched a "study mode" for ChatGPT in which the system asks questions to check understanding and may withhold direct answers until the learner engages [@zeff2025openaia]. Such modes rely on instructions to the model and can be switched off by the student, which is the same freedom the GPT Base arm had. To the author's knowledge, whether optional guardrails change behaviour at scale has not been tested in a published randomised trial. Some school systems have chosen restriction instead. In September 2026 New York City, the largest US school district, announced a one-year moratorium on student-facing generative AI from pre-school to eighth grade, with supervised pilots in a limited number of high-school classes and companion chatbots banned in all grades [@nyc2026mayor].

## 10.3 Cheating, detection and assessment

Universities face the practical side of the same question: how to assess what a student knows when a capable writing assistant is always available. The Higher Education Policy Institute (HEPI) has surveyed full-time UK undergraduates each year since 2024. In its 2026 survey of 1,054 students, polled in December 2025, 94% said they used generative AI to help with assessed work, most often to have concepts explained or articles summarised [@stephenson2026student]. The share who said they had included AI-generated text directly in assessed work rose from 3% in 2024 to 12% in 2026. Teenagers draw distinctions of their own. In Pew's 2024 survey, 54% of US teens thought it acceptable to use ChatGPT to research new topics, but only 18% thought it acceptable for writing essays [@sidoti2025quarter].

One early response was to detect AI-written text automatically. Chapter 9 summarises independent tests of detection tools in general; in education, the decisive problem is whom the errors fall on. Many detectors rely partly on perplexity, a measure of how predictable a text is to a language model, because machine-generated text tends to be highly predictable. Liang and colleagues tested seven widely used detectors on 91 essays written by non-native English speakers for the TOEFL exam. The detectors wrongly labelled more than half of them as AI-generated, with an average false-positive rate of 61%, while classifying essays by US eighth-grade students accurately [@liang2023gpt]. A false positive here means a human-written essay flagged as machine-written. The authors attribute the bias to the more limited vocabulary and syntax typical of non-native writers, which lowers perplexity in the same way that model generation does. When the researchers asked ChatGPT to enrich the word choices in the TOEFL essays, the false-positive rate fell to 12%. The tools thus penalised honest non-native writers and could be evaded with the technology they were meant to detect. The evidence on bias is mixed, however. Researchers at ETS, which runs the GRE and TOEFL tests and has an interest in detection, built detectors for GRE essays and concluded that carefully developed detectors are not necessarily biased against non-native English speakers [@jiang2024detecting; @hao2026detecting]. A 2026 preprint found no systematic bias against non-native writers of Czech in three families of detectors [@alali2026different]. Purpose-built detectors may avoid the bias that general tools showed in 2023, but even an unbiased detector makes some false accusations, and a student cannot disprove a statistical score. OpenAI withdrew its own AI-text classifier in July 2023, citing its "low rate of accuracy" [@coldewey2023openai].

Institutions have therefore shifted attention from detection to the design of assessment. In HEPI's 2026 survey, 65% of students said that assessment at their institution had changed significantly in response to AI [@stephenson2026student]. The report's authors describe a move back towards traditional exam-style assessment, alongside assessments designed to exclude AI and others that include its use by design [@stephenson2026student]. In the author's view, each option has costs. Supervised exams test a narrower range of skills, and assessments that permit AI must judge how it was used. The author knows of no study that has shown which combination best protects the validity of degrees.

Monitoring students also raises questions of privacy and fairness, and the law has begun to respond. Since 2 February 2025, the EU AI Act has banned AI systems that infer the emotions of people in education institutions, except for medical or safety reasons [@europeanparliament2024regulation, Articles 5(1)(f) and 113]. It classes as "high-risk" the AI systems used to decide admission, evaluate learning outcomes, assign students to levels of education, or monitor and detect prohibited behaviour during tests [@europeanparliament2024regulation, Annex III(3)]. Automated marking and online proctoring therefore fall under the Act's strictest duties for permitted systems. After a 2026 amendment, these duties apply from 2 December 2027 [@europeanparliament2026regulation]; Chapter 13 describes what they require.

## 10.4 Medical AI: regulation and the evidence base

Medicine has a longer record of AI-based software than education, and a formal system for deciding which tools may be sold. In the United States, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) maintains a public list of AI-enabled medical devices authorised for marketing. As of the update published in September 2026, it contained 1,614 devices, the earliest from 1995 and the most recent decided in June 2026 [@fda2026artificial]. Radiology accounted for 1,230 of them, about 76%, followed at a distance by cardiovascular devices and neurology. Figure 10.2 shows how annual authorisations grew from 6 in 2015 to 335 in 2025.

![Figure 10.2: Number of AI-enabled medical devices authorised by the US FDA each year, 2015–2025, by date of final decision. Authorisations rose more than fiftyfold over the decade, and about three-quarters of all listed devices are in radiology. Nearly all were cleared through the 510(k) pathway, which requires equivalence to an existing device. Counts reflect the FDA list as updated in September 2026; the FDA adds devices whose summaries are published late, so recent years may be revised upwards. Source: @fda2026artificial.](../figures/svg/fig-10-02.svg){#fig:10-02}

The route by which these devices reached the market matters more than their number. Table 10.2 counts the list by submission type. Almost all were cleared through the 510(k) pathway, in which a manufacturer shows that its device is "as safe and effective, that is, substantially equivalent" to a legally marketed device, known as the predicate [@fda2024premarket]. The FDA's review compares technological characteristics and performance data, which "can include clinical data" but can also consist of bench testing and software validation. A novel low-to-moderate-risk device can use the De Novo route, and once classified it can serve as a predicate for later 510(k) submissions, so each new kind of device can open a path for its successors [@fda2025novo]. Premarket approval, the most demanding route, is reserved for class III devices, those that support or sustain life or present a potential unreasonable risk [@fda2019premarket], and accounts for barely 1% of the list.

| Pathway | What the manufacturer must show | AI-enabled devices | Share |
|---|---|---|---|
| 510(k) clearance | Substantial equivalence to a legally marketed predicate device | 1,553 | 96.2% |
| De Novo classification | Reasonable assurance of safety and effectiveness for a novel low-to-moderate-risk device without a predicate | 40 | 2.5% |
| Premarket approval (PMA) | Safety and effectiveness of a class III (highest-risk) device | 21 | 1.3% |
| Total | | 1,614 | 100% |

: Table 10.2: AI-enabled medical devices on the FDA list (1995 to June 2026) by marketing pathway, counted from submission numbers (K = 510(k), DEN = De Novo, P = PMA). Source: [@fda2026artificial; @fda2024premarket; @fda2025novo; @fda2019premarket].

The count is easy to over-read in other ways too. The FDA describes its list as not comprehensive, because it identifies devices mainly by searching their public summaries for AI-related terms. Authorisation is a judgement about safety and effectiveness for a stated intended use; it is not proof that the device improves patient outcomes. The list does not yet show which devices, if any, use generative AI. The FDA has said it will explore ways to tag devices that incorporate LLMs and other foundation models [@fda2026artificial]. The author's search of the September 2026 list found no ambient documentation tools of the kind discussed in Section 10.5. That absence reflects a regulatory boundary as much as an evidence gap. Since the 21st Century Cures Act of 2016, US law has excluded from the definition of a medical device software intended for administrative support of a health-care facility, and software that keeps electronic patient records without interpreting them [@uscode21360jo]. Tools that only draft notes for a clinician to check can fall on the non-device side of that line, so the FDA list is not where evidence on them will appear. According to a client alert from the law firm Covington, in August 2026 the agency published a discussion paper on how generative-AI devices might be assessed by risk, tested before marketing and monitored afterwards, stressing that the paper is not guidance [@covington2026fda].

Machine-learning models also raise a problem the device system was not built for, because they can be retrained. The FDA, Health Canada and the UK's Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency have set out principles for "predetermined change control plans", in which a manufacturer specifies in advance the planned modifications, the protocol for implementing and controlling them, and how their impact will be assessed. Updates within such a plan need no new submission [@fda2025predetermined]. In December 2024 the FDA issued final guidance on what such a plan for AI-enabled device software must contain [@fda2024marketing]. In the EU, AI in a medical device is high-risk under the AI Act when the device must undergo a third-party conformity assessment under EU medical-device law [@europeanparliament2024regulation, Article 6(1)], which excludes most devices in the lowest risk class. The obligations were deferred by the 2026 amendment to 2 August 2028 [@europeanparliament2026regulation]; Table 13.1 gives the dates.

Most published evidence on medical AI comes from diagnostic accuracy studies, which compare a system's outputs with a reference standard on a set of stored cases and report them mainly as sensitivity and specificity, two measures that are easy to confuse [@bossuyt2015stard; @liu2019comparison].

::: {.box .concept}
**Concept: Sensitivity, specificity and external validation**

Sensitivity is the share of people who have a condition whom a test correctly flags; specificity is the share of people without the condition whom it correctly clears [@altman1994diagnostic]. A smoke alarm that goes off at every slice of burnt toast has high sensitivity and low specificity. In a screening population where few people are ill, even high specificity produces many false alarms. In the author's illustration, a test with 98.5% specificity used on 10,000 healthy people flags 150 of them. Studies often summarise performance across all possible alarm thresholds with the AUC, the ranking score defined in Section 2.8 (0.5 is chance, 1.0 perfect) [@hanley1982meaning]. External validation means testing a model on data from a different hospital, population or time period from the data it was built on. It matters because a model can perform well where it was developed and poorly elsewhere, when patients, settings and measurement practices differ [@altman2000what].
:::

A 2019 systematic review in *The Lancet Digital Health* examined studies from 2012 to 2019 that compared deep learning models with health-care professionals on medical images [@liu2019comparison]. In the 14 studies that tested both on the same external sample, pooled sensitivity was 87.0% for the models and 86.4% for clinicians, and pooled specificity was 92.5% and 90.5%. The authors' main conclusion concerned the evidence base. Of 82 included studies, only 25 performed any external validation, and poor reporting was widespread.

Generative models have since been pooled in the same way. A 2025 meta-analysis of 83 studies of generative AI models on diagnostic tasks found an overall accuracy of 52.1%. This was not significantly different from physicians overall or from non-specialist physicians, and significantly lower than specialists [@takita2025systematic]. Both reviews pool very different tasks and models, so their averages describe the literature more than any single product.

Accuracy on stored images is a step removed from what matters to patients, and randomised trials remain scarce. A systematic review found 41 randomised trials of machine-learning interventions published up to October 2021. They were mostly small (a median of 294 participants), half were conducted at a single site, and none adhered to all items of CONSORT-AI, the reporting guideline for trials of AI interventions [@plana2022randomized]. Published in 2020, CONSORT-AI added 14 items to the standard trial-reporting checklist, among them how the AI was integrated into the clinical setting, how inputs and outputs were handled, and an analysis of error cases [@liu2020reporting]. A later scoping review identified 86 randomised trials of AI in clinical practice published between 2018 and November 2023. Of these, 81% reported positive primary endpoints. Most, however, were single-centre, 43% were in gastroenterology, and more than half had a primary endpoint of diagnostic yield or performance rather than a patient outcome. The authors warn that publication bias probably inflates the share of positive results [@han2024randomised].

::: {.box .deeper}
**Going deeper: What makes medical AI evidence strong**

The reviews above suggest a hierarchy of questions. Does the model agree with a reference standard on stored cases (retrospective accuracy)? Does it do so on data from other hospitals, populations and periods (external validation)? Do clinicians reading cases with the model do better than without it (reader studies, such as the vignette trials in Section 10.5)? Does introducing it in real care, compared at random with care without it, change what happens to patients and staff (prospective trials such as MASAI)? And does the effect hold up after deployment, as patient mixes and recording practices drift (post-market monitoring)? Each rung costs more and answers a question closer to patient benefit. Strong evidence also has features that cut across the rungs: an outcome that matters to patients rather than a surrogate; a comparator that reflects current good practice; preregistration; independence from the vendor; multiple sites; reporting of subgroups and error cases; and enough follow-up to count what the tool misses. Most devices on the FDA list reached the market through claims of equivalence to earlier devices (Table 10.2), and the randomised trials cluster in a few specialties [@han2024randomised].
:::

## 10.5 Medical AI in practice: screening, prediction, conversation and paperwork

The most informative trial so far comes from breast screening. In the Swedish MASAI trial, women attending screening were randomly assigned either to standard double reading by two radiologists or to AI-supported reading. In the AI arm, a commercial system gave each examination a malignancy risk score from 1 to 10. Only the highest-scoring examinations went to two radiologists and the rest to one, and the AI's marks of suspicious areas were shown for the high-risk scores of 8 to 10 [@lang2023artificial]. A prespecified safety analysis of the first 80,033 women found detection rates of 6.1 cancers per 1,000 in the AI arm against 5.1 in the control arm, a difference with a p-value of 0.052. The false-positive rate was 1.5% in both arms, and radiologists' reading workload fell by 44.3%. Part of the extra detection was in situ cancer (60 against 38 cases), early lesions of which some would never have caused harm; this is why the trial's primary endpoint was interval cancers, those diagnosed between screening rounds.

The final results, covering 105,934 women followed for two years, were published in *The Lancet* in 2026. Interval cancers occurred at a rate of 1.55 per 1,000 in the AI arm against 1.76 in the control arm. The ratio of 0.88 had a 95% confidence interval of 0.65 to 1.18, which met the trial's non-inferiority criterion but does not show a significant reduction; fewer of the AI arm's interval cancers were invasive. Sensitivity was 80.5% against 73.8%, with identical specificity [@gommers2026interval; @lunduniversity2026ai]. The trial tested one product in one national programme, with radiologists who knew which arm they were reading. Because the comparator was double reading, the standard in the Swedish programme, the result does not transfer directly to health systems in which one radiologist reads each examination.

A German observational study of 463,094 women screened in 2021–2023, funded by Vara, the company whose AI system it evaluated, found higher detection without a higher recall rate when radiologists chose to use AI support [@eisemann2025nationwide]. Because radiologists chose when to use it, that study cannot rule out differences between the cases they selected.

::: {.box .case}
**Case study: The Epic Sepsis Model**

Sepsis is a life-threatening response to infection, and early recognition matters. Epic, a large US electronic health record vendor, offered hospitals a proprietary model that scored inpatients' risk of sepsis every 15 minutes, and it was implemented at hundreds of US hospitals although its performance had not been adequately evaluated. In 2021, researchers at Michigan Medicine reported an external validation covering 38,455 hospitalisations, of which 2,552 involved sepsis [@wong2021external]. The model's AUC was 0.63, against the 0.76 to 0.83 that Epic had reported in its internal documentation. At the alert threshold used, it missed two-thirds of the sepsis patients while generating alerts for 18% of all hospitalised patients, a heavy burden of alert fatigue. It identified only 183 sepsis patients (7%) whom clinicians had not already treated with timely antibiotics.

An updated version was validated prospectively at four large US health systems, covering 227,091 inpatient encounters between 2023 and 2025 [@wong2026multicenter]. Discrimination was better, with encounter-level AUC between 0.82 and 0.92, but performance varied between sites, and the positive predictive value was only 0.13 to 0.26, so most patients the model flagged did not meet sepsis criteria. The two evaluations are not like for like. The first was retrospective at one hospital, the second prospective at four health systems with a different version of the model. The lesson that holds across both is the gap between a vendor's claims and independent results. A model can pass external validation and still impose a high cost in staff attention; whether its alerts improve care is a further question that only an impact trial can answer.
:::

A natural assumption is that a clinician with an AI assistant will outperform either alone. Trials suggest this is not automatic. In a randomised trial in late 2023, 50 US physicians worked through clinical case vignettes with or without access to GPT-4 [@goh2024large]. The median diagnostic reasoning score was 76% with the chatbot and 74% without, a difference that was not statistically significant. In a secondary analysis, GPT-4 working alone scored a median of 92%. A follow-up trial with 92 physicians tested management reasoning, meaning decisions about further testing and the balance of risks. Those using GPT-4 scored 6.5 percentage points higher than those using conventional resources and took about two minutes longer per case; physicians with GPT-4 did no better than GPT-4 alone [@goh2025gpt].

The pattern extends beyond medicine. A 2024 meta-analysis of 106 experiments across many fields found that human–AI combinations performed on average worse than the better of the two working alone. The pooled effect was a Hedges' *g* of −0.23, where *g* is the difference between two group means divided by their pooled standard deviation, with a correction for small samples. Combinations lost value in decision tasks and when the AI was the stronger partner, and gained in content creation and when the human was stronger. Compared with the humans working alone, however, human–AI combinations did clearly better (*g* = 0.64). The loss is relative to the AI working alone, not to the human [@vaccaro2024combinations]. Chapter 11 discusses automation bias, the tendency to defer to automated suggestions even when they are wrong, which is one explanation.

Google's AMIE (Articulate Medical Intelligence Explorer) shows how a conversational system has been taken up the evidence ladder. In a randomised, double-blind crossover study by Google researchers, using text-based consultations with validated patient-actors across 159 case scenarios, specialists rated AMIE better than 20 primary-care physicians on 30 of 32 axes, including diagnostic accuracy, and patient-actors rated it better on 25 of 26. The authors note that clinicians were working in an unfamiliar text-chat format [@tu2025towards]. In a second Google study, 20 clinicians worked on 302 difficult published case reports. AMIE alone listed the correct diagnosis among its top ten in 59.1% of cases against 33.6% for unassisted clinicians. With AMIE's help, clinicians reached 51.7%, against 44.4% for those using search engines [@mcduff2025towards].

The first real-world step was a single-centre feasibility study in Boston, published in *The Lancet* in October 2026. There, 98 patients talked with AMIE before an urgent primary-care appointment while physicians supervised every conversation with authority to stop it [@brodeur2026conversational]. No conversation needed to be stopped under the predefined safety criteria; supervisors noted one hallucination and added clinical information in five conversations. Primary-care physicians returned surveys for only 60 of the 98 visits; in the 44 of these in which they had read AMIE's transcript beforehand, they found it helpful for visit preparation in 33. The study had no control group and was funded by Alphabet, Google's parent company. A randomised test in routine care came from Kenya. At 16 primary-care clinics run by Penda Health, 103 clinical officers were randomly assigned to work with or without a GPT-4o-based assistant that checked their electronic records in the background. Across 9,691 patients enrolled in 2025, treatment failure within 14 days, the primary outcome, occurred in 2.2% of patients with the assistant and 2.0% without. After adjustment for differences between the groups the odds ratio was 0.77 (95% CI 0.55 to 1.08), pointing the other way, and neither difference was significant. No safety signal emerged, and the authors conclude that any benefit is probably modest [@agweyu2026generative]. Figure 10.3 places these tools in the clinical workflow.

![Figure 10.3: Where AI sits in the clinical workflow. The patient journey runs from intake and history-taking through investigation, diagnosis and treatment decision to documentation and follow-up. Examples of AI tools are shown at each stage, together with the kind of evidence that would show they help. "Medical AI" is many different tools, each needing its own evaluation. Schematic by the author, based on the studies in Sections 10.4 and 10.5: @brodeur2026conversational; @lang2023artificial; @goh2024large; @wong2021external; @lukac2025ambient; @han2024randomised.](../figures/svg/fig-10-03.svg){#fig:10-03}

One fast-spreading clinical use of generative AI involves no diagnosis at all. "Ambient scribes" listen, with consent, to a consultation and draft a clinical note for the doctor to review. A randomised trial at UCLA Health assigned 238 outpatient physicians, across 14 specialties and about 72,000 encounters, to one of two commercial scribes or to usual practice for two months from late 2024 [@lukac2025ambient]. With one product (Nabla), average time spent writing each note fell from 4 minutes 30 seconds to 3 minutes 49 seconds, a reduction 9.5% larger than in the control group. With the other (Microsoft's DAX Copilot), the difference from the control group was not statistically significant. The scribes were used in only about a third of eligible visits (33.5% for DAX and 29.5% for Nabla), so the trial estimates the effect of offering a scribe, not of using one at every visit. Users of both products reported modest improvements on burnout and workload measures. Physicians reported that drafts occasionally contained clinically significant inaccuracies, and one mild adverse event occurred. A clinician who signs an AI-drafted note remains accountable for its content, so the value of the tool depends on whether checking is quicker and more reliable than writing.

## 10.6 Companions, loneliness and mental health

### The evidence on companions and well-being

Not all personal use of AI is practical. Some people use chatbots for conversation, emotional support or companionship, either through general assistants or through apps designed as "AI companions", such as Character.AI and Replika. How common this is depends on the population studied. In the analysis of ChatGPT consumer messages, only 1.9% concerned relationships and personal reflection, and fewer still games and role play [@chatterji2025how]. Among US teenagers the picture differs. NORC surveyed 1,060 teens aged 13 to 17 for the advocacy organisation Common Sense Media in April and May 2025. It found that 72% had used an AI companion at least once and 52% did so at least a few times a month [@robb2025talk]. A third of users said they had chosen to discuss something important with an AI instead of a person, yet 67% of all respondents found AI conversations less satisfying than those with friends. The survey's definition included general chatbots used as companions, and 341 of its respondents came from a non-probability panel, so the figures are indicative. A Pew survey in autumn 2025 found that 12% of teens had used chatbots for emotional support or advice and 16% for casual conversation [@mcclain2026how].

In the author's view, the studies below should be read with three problems in mind. Loneliness and dependence are measured by questionnaires, which shift with mood and expectation, and most studies last weeks, which is short for effects on relationships to appear. Above all, heavy users are not a random sample. Someone already isolated may both use a chatbot more and feel lonelier, so an association between use and loneliness does not show which causes which. Randomised trials can assign conditions, but not how much people choose to use a tool, which is the variable that seems to matter most [@fang2025ai; @phang2025investigating; @zhang2025rise].

The most detailed experimental evidence comes from two linked preprints by researchers at the MIT Media Lab and OpenAI. In the first, 981 participants used ChatGPT daily for four weeks under randomly assigned conditions that varied the chatbot's voice (text, a neutral voice or an engaging voice) and the type of conversation (open, personal or non-personal) [@fang2025ai]. The assigned conditions had no significant effect on loneliness, social contact with other people, emotional dependence on AI or problematic use. The strongest pattern was correlational. Participants who chose to use the chatbot more had worse outcomes on all four measures, whatever their condition. The second study combined this trial with an automated analysis of more than three million conversations and a survey of over 4,000 users; a small number of very heavy users accounted for a disproportionate share of emotionally laden conversations [@phang2025investigating]. A separate study, published in *Nature Human Behaviour* in 2026, surveyed 1,131 US adult users of Character.AI and analysed 4,664 chat sessions donated by 237 of them. People with smaller social networks were more likely to name companionship as their main use, and companionship use was associated with lower well-being, more strongly when interactions were intensive and highly self-disclosing [@zhang2025rise].
